light: Monstera deliciosa grows under the canopy in Central American rainforests, climbing tree trunks toward gaps in the leaves above. That habit explains what it wants indoors: bright, filtered light rather than bare sun. An east window, or a spot two to three feet back from a south or west window, is close to ideal.

Light is also what controls fenestration — the famous holes and splits. Juvenile leaves are solid hearts, and the plant only starts producing split leaves once it has enough light and maturity to support them. A Monstera in a dim corner will stay alive for years and never fenestrate. If yours is pushing out small, solid leaves, low light is the first thing to correct.
water: Water when the top two inches of mix have dried out. In a bright spot through spring and summer that usually lands somewhere around every seven to ten days, but treat that as a starting point rather than a schedule — pot size, mix and light all move the number. Water thoroughly until it runs from the drainage holes, then empty the saucer.

From late autumn through winter, growth slows and the mix stays wet far longer. Stretch the interval to every two or three weeks and check with a finger each time rather than watering on autopilot. More Monsteras are killed by winter watering habits carried over from summer than by any pest.

Monstera tolerates average household humidity, but it grows faster and produces better leaves above 60%. Grouping plants, a pebble tray or a humidifier all help. Misting looks appealing but raises humidity for only a few minutes.
soil: Use a chunky, fast-draining aroid mix rather than straight potting soil. A reliable blend is roughly one third quality potting mix, one third orchid bark and one third perlite, with a couple of handfuls of coco coir or worm castings for moisture retention and nutrition. The bark keeps air pockets around the roots, which is exactly what an epiphytic climber expects.

Whatever you mix, the pot must have drainage holes. Monstera roots rot quickly in a sealed cachepot that collects water at the bottom. Feed with a balanced liquid fertiliser at half strength every four weeks during spring and summer, and stop entirely over winter.

propagation: Monstera propagates readily from stem cuttings, and the single thing that determines success is whether your cutting includes a node. The node is the slightly raised band on the stem where a leaf meets it, often with a brown aerial root emerging. A leaf with no node will sit in water looking healthy for months and never root, because all the growth tissue is in the node.

Cut just below a node with clean shears, taking one or two leaves with it. Put the cutting in water, keeping the node submerged and the leaves out, in bright indirect light. Change the water weekly. Roots usually appear within two to four weeks; once several are two to three inches long, pot into your usual aroid mix and keep it slightly moister than normal for the first fortnight while the plant transitions from water roots to soil roots. You can also root cuttings directly in damp sphagnum moss, which skips that transition entirely and tends to produce sturdier plants.

problems.symptom: New leaves have no splits or holes
problems.cause: Not enough light, or a plant that is simply still young. Fenestration develops with maturity and adequate light, and it will not appear on a plant kept in a dim corner.
problems.fix: Move it closer to a bright window with filtered light and give it something to climb — a moss pole encourages the plant to produce larger, more mature leaves. Expect the change to show on new growth, not on existing leaves.

problems.symptom: Yellowing lower leaves
problems.cause: Most often overwatering, especially if several leaves yellow at once and the mix is still damp days after watering. A single old leaf yellowing near the base is just normal ageing.
problems.fix: Check the mix before every watering and let the top two inches dry out. If the soil smells sour or the roots are brown and soft, repot into fresh, chunky mix and trim the damaged roots.

problems.symptom: Brown, crispy leaf edges
problems.cause: Low humidity, underwatering, or salt buildup from fertiliser and hard tap water.
problems.fix: Raise humidity, water more consistently, and flush the pot thoroughly with plain water every few months to wash out accumulated salts.

problems.symptom: Dark brown patches with yellow halos
problems.cause: Bacterial or fungal leaf spot, usually following water sitting on the foliage in a cool, still room.
problems.fix: Remove affected leaves, improve air circulation, and water the soil rather than the leaves. Avoid misting until it clears.

problems.symptom: Fine webbing and stippled, dull leaves
problems.cause: Spider mites, which thrive in dry indoor air and are easy to miss until the webbing appears.
problems.fix: Rinse the plant in the shower, then treat every five to seven days with insecticidal soap or neem oil for at least three cycles to catch newly hatched mites. Raising humidity makes reinfestation less likely.

problems.symptom: White cottony clusters in leaf joints
problems.cause: Mealybugs, which shelter where the leaf stem meets the main stem and in the folds of new growth.
problems.fix: Dab each cluster with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol, then follow with insecticidal soap. Check weekly for a month — they hide well and one missed cluster restarts the infestation.

problems.symptom: Stems growing long and leggy with small leaves
problems.cause: Insufficient light, and often a lack of support. Monstera is a climber, and an unsupported plant sprawls rather than building size.
problems.fix: Increase light and add a moss pole or trellis, tying the stem in so aerial roots can grip. Prune leggy sections back to a node and propagate the cuttings.

repotting: Repot every two to three years, or when roots grow out of the drainage holes, water runs straight through without wetting the mix, or the plant dries out far faster than it used to. Spring and early summer are the best time, so the plant recovers during active growth.

Go up only one pot size — roughly two inches wider in diameter. An oversized pot holds more wet mix than the roots can use, which is a common route to root rot. Slide the plant out, loosen the outer roots, cut away anything brown and mushy, and settle it into fresh aroid mix at the same depth it was growing before.

This is also the natural moment to add or replace a moss pole, since you can position it against the stem while the root ball is out of the pot. Water thoroughly after repotting, then hold off on fertiliser for four to six weeks while the roots settle.
varieties: The plain species is the most common, but several forms are worth knowing. 'Thai Constellation' carries creamy, speckled variegation, is tissue-cultured, and is more stable and more widely available than it once was. The 'Albo Variegata' form produces dramatic blocks of pure white, propagates only by cutting, and is far more temperamental — a cutting with too much white lacks the chlorophyll to sustain itself.

Do not confuse Monstera deliciosa with Monstera adansonii, sold as the Swiss cheese vine, which has smaller leaves with enclosed holes rather than splits that reach the edge. Young deliciosa plants are also frequently mislabelled as split-leaf philodendron, a different genus entirely. 'Borsigiana' is a faster, more compact growth form of deliciosa rather than a separate species.

light: Snake plant has a reputation as a low-light plant, and it is genuinely one of the most shade-tolerant houseplants available — but tolerating and thriving are different things. In a dark corner it survives almost indefinitely while putting out very little new growth. In bright indirect light it grows noticeably faster and keeps its variegation sharp.

It also handles a few hours of direct sun better than most houseplants, provided the change is gradual. Moving one straight from a shaded corner to a sunny south window will bleach or scorch the leaves, so shift it in stages over two or three weeks.
water: This is a succulent, and it stores water in its leaves. Water deeply, then let the mix dry out completely before watering again. Through spring and summer that is typically every two to three weeks; check by pushing a finger a couple of inches into the mix rather than watering on a schedule.

In winter, growth effectively stops and the plant needs remarkably little — once every four to six weeks is often plenty, and in a cool room it can go longer. Overwatering in winter is by far the most common way snake plants are killed.
Always water into the mix rather than down into the central rosette, where trapped water causes the base of the leaves to rot. Humidity is irrelevant to this plant; average household air is fine.
soil: Use a free-draining cactus or succulent mix, or make your own with two parts potting mix to one part coarse sand or perlite. The aim is a medium that wets through and then dries quickly rather than staying damp.

Terracotta suits snake plants particularly well because the porous walls pull moisture out of the mix between waterings. Drainage holes are essential. Feed lightly — a balanced fertiliser at half strength two or three times across the whole growing season is ample, and none at all through winter.

propagation: Division is the fastest and most reliable method, and it is the only one that preserves variegation. Slide the plant out of its pot and look for natural clumps with their own roots and rhizome; separate them with a clean knife, leaving each division at least three leaves and a healthy piece of rhizome. Pot each into dry cactus mix and wait a week before the first watering so cut surfaces can callus.

Leaf cuttings also work, with one important caveat: cuttings taken from a variegated plant such as 'Laurentii' will root and grow, but they revert to plain green, because the yellow margin is not carried in the leaf tissue. Cut a healthy leaf into three-inch sections, keeping track of which end pointed down — a section planted upside down will never root. Let the pieces callus for a day or two, then stand them bottom-end down in barely moist mix. Roots take a month or more, and a new pup several months after that. Patience is the main requirement.

problems.symptom: Leaves soft and mushy at the base
problems.cause: Root or rhizome rot from overwatering, a mix that holds too much moisture, or water sitting in the central rosette.
problems.fix: Unpot immediately, cut away every soft root and rhizome section until only firm white tissue remains, let the cuts dry for a day, and repot into dry cactus mix. Wait a week before watering. If the rot has reached most of the rhizome, save healthy leaves as cuttings instead.

problems.symptom: Leaves wrinkled, curling inward or creased lengthwise
problems.cause: Underwatering. A snake plant draws down its own water reserves before showing any distress, so wrinkling means it has been dry for a while.
problems.fix: Water thoroughly until it drains, and check again in a week. The leaves plump back up over several days. If it has been bone dry for months, water twice a week apart rather than trying to correct it in one go.

problems.symptom: Yellowing along the leaf margins
problems.cause: Usually overwatering, occasionally a pot-bound plant that can no longer take up water evenly.
problems.fix: Let the mix dry out completely and extend the interval. If the roots have filled the pot and are circling tightly, repot in spring.

problems.symptom: Brown, dry leaf tips
problems.cause: Inconsistent watering — long droughts followed by a soaking — or fluoride and salts in tap water.
problems.fix: Water more evenly, and try filtered or rainwater if your supply is hard. Trim the brown tip at an angle with clean scissors; it will not turn green again but it will stop advancing.

problems.symptom: Leaves falling over away from the centre
problems.cause: Most often too little light, causing weak growth that cannot hold itself up. Overwatering and a pot too large for the root mass also cause it.
problems.fix: Move to brighter light and reduce watering. A pot that is snug rather than roomy helps keep tall leaves upright; snake plants genuinely prefer being a little pot-bound.

problems.symptom: Small brown bumps on leaves that scrape off
problems.cause: Scale insects, which attach themselves and feed under a hard protective shell.
problems.fix: Scrape them off with a fingernail or a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol, then treat with neem oil. Repeat every week for a month, since the mobile juveniles are almost invisible.

problems.symptom: Variegated leaves reverting to plain green
problems.cause: Insufficient light, or growth that originated from a leaf cutting rather than division.
problems.fix: Move to brighter indirect light. Remove fully green new shoots if you want to keep the variegated look, and propagate variegated plants by division rather than leaf cuttings.

repotting: Snake plants are happy tight in their pots and only need repotting every three to five years. The usual prompt is dramatic: the rhizomes are strong enough to crack a plastic pot or push the whole plant upward out of the soil.

Repot in spring into a container just one size larger. Choose something heavy and wide rather than tall — mature leaves are top-heavy, and a light plastic pot tips over. Terracotta is ideal for both weight and moisture control.
Use the opportunity to divide crowded clumps and inspect the rhizome for soft spots. Pot at the same depth, water lightly after a week, and skip fertiliser for a couple of months.
varieties: Sansevieria trifasciata 'Laurentii' is the classic, with bold yellow margins on dark green. 'Zeylanica' has wavy silver-green banding and no yellow edge. 'Moonshine' is a pale silvery-green throughout and needs decent light to hold that colour.

For smaller spaces, 'Hahnii' — the bird's nest snake plant — forms a squat rosette six to eight inches tall. At the other extreme, Sansevieria masoniana, the whale fin, produces a single enormous paddle-shaped leaf. Note that the genus was reclassified into Dracaena, so you may see these sold as Dracaena trifasciata; the care is identical whichever name is on the label.

light: Golden pothos is genuinely adaptable, which is why it turns up in offices and windowless bathrooms. It grows in anything from low light to bright indirect light. What changes with light levels is not survival but appearance: in bright indirect light the leaves are larger and the golden variegation is pronounced, while in low light new leaves come out smaller and mostly green.
Avoid direct midday sun, which scorches the foliage and bleaches the variegation to a washed-out cream. If your plant is losing its gold, move it brighter before assuming it is a watering problem.
water: Let the top one to two inches of mix dry before watering, then water thoroughly until it drains. In a moderately bright spot during spring and summer this tends to be every seven to ten days, less in lower light where the mix stays damp longer.
Reduce through autumn and winter, often to every two to three weeks. Pothos is forgiving of a missed watering and distinctly unforgiving of a permanently wet pot, so when in doubt, wait.

The plant gives clear signals: leaves go slightly limp and soft when thirsty and perk up within hours of watering. Use that as your guide rather than a fixed schedule, but do not let wilting become routine — repeated severe drought causes permanent leaf loss along the vine.
soil: An ordinary well-draining houseplant mix works. Adding a handful of perlite or orchid bark improves aeration and makes overwatering harder to achieve, which is worth doing if you tend to water generously.

Pothos also grows indefinitely in plain water, which is why cuttings in jars do so well. A plant grown permanently in water needs a weak dose of liquid fertiliser every month or so, since there are no nutrients in the water itself. In soil, feed monthly at half strength through spring and summer only.

propagation: Pothos is one of the easiest houseplants to propagate, and it is a good first attempt if you have never taken a cutting. Find a node — the small brown nub on the vine where a leaf stem joins, often with a stubby aerial root already showing — and cut half an inch below it. Each cutting needs at least one node and one leaf.

Stand the cuttings in a glass of water with the nodes submerged and the leaves above the surface, in bright indirect light. Change the water weekly to keep it oxygenated. Roots normally appear within one to two weeks, and once they reach two to three inches you can pot several cuttings together into one pot for a full-looking plant straight away. Keep newly potted cuttings a little moister than an established plant for the first couple of weeks. Cuttings can equally be pushed straight into damp soil, skipping water entirely; the rooting is slower to watch but the plant adapts faster.

problems.symptom: Yellow leaves, often several at once
problems.cause: Overwatering is the usual cause, particularly if the mix is still wet and the yellowing starts at the base of the plant.
problems.fix: Let the top inches dry properly before the next watering and empty any water standing in the cachepot. One yellow leaf occasionally is normal ageing and not a concern.

problems.symptom: Brown, crispy leaf tips and edges
problems.cause: Dry air, underwatering, or accumulated fertiliser salts and chlorine from tap water.
problems.fix: Water more consistently, flush the pot with plain water every few months, and consider filtered water if your tap water is heavily treated.

problems.symptom: Long bare vines with widely spaced leaves
problems.cause: Too little light. The plant stretches toward the nearest source, producing distance between leaves rather than new foliage.
problems.fix: Move it brighter and prune the bare vines back to within a few inches of the soil. Pothos branches readily from pruned nodes, and the cuttings you removed can be rooted and added back to the same pot.

problems.symptom: Variegation fading to plain green
problems.cause: Insufficient light. The gold-marked tissue contains less chlorophyll, so in dim conditions the plant favours green growth.
problems.fix: Increase light gradually. Cut back fully green vines to encourage variegated growth from lower nodes.

problems.symptom: Black or dark brown stem bases, plant collapsing
problems.cause: Root rot from prolonged wet soil, sometimes with a sour smell from the mix.
problems.fix: Take healthy cuttings from the upper vines immediately as insurance, then unpot, trim all soft black roots, and repot into fresh mix in a pot with drainage. Water sparingly until new growth appears.

problems.symptom: Small flies rising from the soil
problems.cause: Fungus gnats, which breed in permanently damp topsoil and are a symptom of watering too often.
problems.fix: Let the top layer dry fully between waterings, use yellow sticky traps for the adults, and water from below for a few weeks. The problem resolves once the surface stops staying wet.

problems.symptom: Leaves limp and drooping despite damp soil
problems.cause: Root rot rather than thirst. Damaged roots cannot take up water, so the plant wilts even in wet mix.
problems.fix: Check the roots. Healthy roots are firm and white; rotted ones are brown and fall apart. Trim, repot into fresh mix, and reduce watering frequency.

repotting: Pothos grows fast and generally needs a new pot every one to two years. Signs are roots emerging from the drainage holes, water running straight through, or growth slowing noticeably during the growing season.

Move up one size, about two inches wider. Spring is best but pothos is tolerant enough to repot at almost any time. Tease apart circling roots at the base of the root ball so they grow outward rather than continuing to spiral.

If the plant has gone bare and leggy at the top, repotting is a good moment to cut it back hard and replant rooted cuttings around the parent to thicken it up. Water well afterwards and wait a month before resuming fertiliser.
varieties: 'Golden' is the familiar green-and-yellow form. 'Marble Queen' is heavily streaked with white and grows more slowly, since it carries less chlorophyll. 'Neon' is a uniform chartreuse with no variegation at all and keeps its colour best in bright indirect light.

'N'Joy' and 'Pearls and Jade' are compact, with distinct white-bordered leaves. 'Satin pothos' is sold alongside these but is actually Scindapsus pictus, a different genus with velvety, silver-spotted leaves — care is very similar. Note that all pothos varieties are toxic to cats and dogs if chewed, so a hanging position is worth considering in a pet household.

light: Peace lily is one of the few genuinely flowering plants that tolerates low light, which is why it ends up in office lobbies. It survives in dim corners, but it will not bloom there. The white spathes need medium to bright indirect light to form, so if yours has produced only leaves for a year, light is almost certainly the reason.
Keep it out of direct sun, which scorches the thin leaves within days. A north or east window, or a few feet back from a brighter one, gives the balance of enough light to flower without burning.
water: Peace lily likes evenly moist soil and, unusually among houseplants, tells you clearly when it is thirsty: the whole plant droops dramatically, then recovers within hours of watering. Tempting as it is to use that as a schedule, repeated wilting stresses the plant and causes leaf-edge browning over time. Water when the top inch is dry rather than waiting for the collapse.
In spring and summer that is usually once a week; in winter, every ten to fourteen days. Water thoroughly until it drains and never leave the pot standing in a full saucer.

This is a plant that genuinely benefits from humidity. It comes from tropical forest floors and appreciates 50% or more — a pebble tray, a humidifier or a bathroom position all help. It is also sensitive to chlorine and fluoride, so if you see brown tips despite good watering, switch to filtered or rainwater.
soil: Use a standard peat-based potting mix with a handful of perlite for drainage. Peace lily wants a medium that holds moisture without becoming waterlogged, so avoid heavy garden soil and avoid pure bark mixes, which dry out far too fast for this species.

Feed every six to eight weeks during spring and summer with a balanced liquid fertiliser at half strength. Peace lilies are light feeders and over-fertilising is a common cause of brown leaf tips. Stop feeding completely in autumn and winter.

propagation: Peace lily is propagated by division, not by cuttings. A leaf or stem cutting will not root, because the plant grows as a clump of crowns rising from a shared root mass rather than from nodes along a stem.

The best time is spring, ideally while repotting. Slide the plant out and look at the base: you will see distinct crowns, each with its own leaves and roots. Work them apart with your fingers where you can, and use a clean knife where the root mass is too dense. Each division needs at least two or three leaves and a decent share of roots to establish. Pot each one into fresh mix in a pot only slightly larger than its roots, water well, and keep out of direct light for a few weeks while it settles. Expect a sulk — some drooping and perhaps a lost leaf — before new growth appears.

problems.symptom: Plant wilts dramatically, then recovers after watering
problems.cause: Underwatering. Peace lily collapses visibly when the mix dries out and bounces back quickly once watered.
problems.fix: Water more regularly, aiming to water when the top inch is dry rather than waiting for the wilt. Repeated wilting damages leaf tissue even though the plant recovers each time.

problems.symptom: Brown, crispy leaf tips
problems.cause: Chlorine or fluoride in tap water, over-fertilising, or dry air — often a combination.
problems.fix: Switch to filtered, distilled or rainwater, halve your fertiliser, flush the pot with plain water every few months, and raise humidity. Trim brown tips at an angle with clean scissors.

problems.symptom: No flowers for a year or more
problems.cause: Not enough light. Peace lily survives in low light but only blooms in medium to bright indirect light. A very young plant may also simply be too immature.
problems.fix: Move to a brighter spot out of direct sun and feed lightly through the growing season. Blooming usually follows within a few months.

problems.symptom: Flowers emerging green instead of white, or turning green as they age
problems.cause: Green-ageing is normal — spathes turn green then brown as they finish. Flowers that open green usually mean too much fertiliser or too much light.
problems.fix: Cut spent flower stalks to the base. If new blooms open green, reduce feeding and check the plant is not in harsh light.

problems.symptom: Yellowing leaves, especially lower ones
problems.cause: Overwatering if the mix stays wet, natural ageing if it is one or two older leaves at a time, or too much direct light if the yellowing is widespread and pale.
problems.fix: Check the soil first. If it is soggy, extend the watering interval and confirm the pot drains. Remove yellow leaves at the base.

problems.symptom: Black or dark brown leaf bases, mushy stems
problems.cause: Root rot from waterlogged soil or a pot left standing in water.
problems.fix: Unpot, cut away every soft brown root, and repot into fresh mix in a pot with working drainage. Water sparingly until new growth appears.

problems.symptom: Sticky residue on leaves and fine webbing
problems.cause: Spider mites or mealybugs, both encouraged by dry indoor air.
problems.fix: Wipe the leaves down, rinse the plant in the shower, and treat with insecticidal soap every five to seven days for three cycles. Raising humidity discourages spider mites specifically.

repotting: Repot every one to two years, in spring. Peace lily grows into its pot quickly and the signs are clear: roots circling the surface or emerging from drainage holes, water running straight through, and much faster wilting between waterings than before.

Go up only one pot size. Peace lily flowers more freely when slightly snug, and an oversized pot holds wet soil around the roots. Loosen the root ball, remove any dark soft roots, and set the plant at the same depth in fresh mix.
If the clump has become congested, repotting is the natural moment to divide it into two or three plants. Water thoroughly afterwards and hold off fertiliser for six weeks while the roots recover.
varieties: 'Mauna Loa' is the common large form, reaching around three feet with big spathes. 'Domino' carries irregular white variegation across the leaves and needs a little more light to keep the pattern. 'Sensation' is the giant of the group, capable of four to six feet with broad, deeply ribbed leaves — a genuine floor plant.

For smaller spaces, 'Petite' stays under a foot. Whichever you choose, all Spathiphyllum are toxic to cats and dogs: the calcium oxalate crystals cause mouth and throat irritation if chewed, so this is not a plant for a household with a nibbling pet.

light: ZZ plant tolerates lower light than almost anything else sold as a houseplant, including windowless offices lit only by fluorescent tubes. It genuinely survives there, thanks to the potato-like rhizomes under the soil that store water and energy.

That said, it grows faster and more upright in bright indirect light. In very low light expect perhaps one or two new stems a year, and those stems may lean toward the light source. Direct afternoon sun scorches the glossy leaflets, so filtered light is the target if you want actual growth rather than mere survival.
water: This is the most drought-tolerant common houseplant, and almost every ZZ that dies is drowned rather than starved. The rhizomes hold weeks of water in reserve. Let the mix dry out completely — all the way through, not just the top inch — before watering again.

In practice that means every two to three weeks in a bright spot during summer, and as little as once every four to six weeks in winter or in low light. Water thoroughly when you do, letting it run from the drainage holes, then leave it alone entirely.

If you are ever unsure, wait. A ZZ that has gone too long shows wrinkled stems and drooping leaflets and recovers completely from a good soak. A ZZ that has been kept wet develops rhizome rot, which is usually fatal by the time it shows above the soil. Humidity is irrelevant to this plant.
soil: Use a fast-draining mix — cactus and succulent compost, or ordinary potting mix cut with a third perlite or coarse sand. The rhizomes need air around them and rot in dense, water-retentive media.

Drainage holes are non-negotiable. Terracotta helps if you are a generous waterer. Feed very lightly: a balanced fertiliser at half strength two or three times across spring and summer is plenty, and none in winter. ZZ plants grow slowly and cannot use much.

propagation: ZZ plants propagate three ways, and all of them are slow. Division is the quickest: unpot a mature plant, separate the rhizome clusters by hand or with a clean knife making sure each piece has at least one stem and some roots, and pot each into dry cactus mix. Wait a week before the first watering so the cut surfaces callus.

Stem cuttings also work — take a whole stem at soil level, cut it into sections, and stand them in water or damp mix. Leaf cuttings are the slowest but most reproducible method: pull individual leaflets off with a small piece of the stem attached, lay them on barely moist mix, and wait. A pea-sized rhizome forms at the base after two to three months, and the first new shoot may take six months to a year. This is a propagation project for the patient; there is no way to speed it up, and warmth and bright indirect light are the only levers that help.

problems.symptom: Yellowing leaves and stems going soft at the base
problems.cause: Overwatering and rhizome rot. This is the classic ZZ failure and it is usually well advanced before anything shows above the soil.
problems.fix: Unpot immediately. Healthy rhizomes are firm and pale; rotted ones are brown, soft and smell sour. Cut away everything soft, let the remaining pieces dry for a day, and repot into dry cactus mix. Do not water for at least a week.

problems.symptom: Wrinkled stems, leaflets curling or drooping
problems.cause: Genuine underwatering — the plant has used up its stored reserves. This takes months to reach and is rare.
problems.fix: Water thoroughly until it drains, and repeat in a week. The stems plump back out over a couple of weeks. This is far easier to fix than the opposite problem.

problems.symptom: Stems flopping outward from the centre
problems.cause: Too little light causing weak, stretched growth, or a plant that has grown top-heavy and needs repotting.
problems.fix: Move to brighter indirect light. A snug, heavy pot helps keep tall stems upright. Stems that have flopped will not straighten, so prune them at soil level if they bother you.

problems.symptom: Brown tips on the leaflets
problems.cause: Fluoride and salts in tap water, over-fertilising, or occasionally very dry air combined with irregular watering.
problems.fix: Flush the pot thoroughly with plain water every few months, reduce fertiliser, and try filtered water if your supply is hard.

problems.symptom: Leaflets dropping from otherwise healthy stems
problems.cause: Sudden change in conditions — a move, a cold draught, or a dramatic shift in watering. ZZ plants shed leaflets as a stress response.
problems.fix: Settle it in one position, keep it away from doors and heating vents, and resume consistent care. New leaflets will not regrow on bare sections of stem, so prune those out once the plant has stabilised.

problems.symptom: Pale, washed-out or scorched patches on leaflets
problems.cause: Direct sun, particularly through an unshaded south or west window in summer.
problems.fix: Move it back from the glass or filter the light with a sheer curtain. Damaged leaflets will not recover; remove the worst and let new growth replace them.

problems.symptom: Small brown bumps along stems and leaflet undersides
problems.cause: Scale insects. The glossy foliage makes them relatively easy to spot once you look.
problems.fix: Scrape them off with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol and follow with neem oil, repeating weekly for a month to catch the crawlers.

repotting: ZZ plants are slow and happy being snug, so repotting every two to three years is plenty. The usual prompt is unmistakable: the rhizomes swell until they visibly distort or crack a plastic pot, or push the whole plant upward out of the soil.

Repot in spring into a pot one size larger, choosing something sturdy — a mature ZZ is heavy and top-heavy. Handle the rhizomes carefully; they bruise, and a damaged rhizome is an entry point for rot.

Use dry mix and wait a week before watering, which gives any roots damaged during the move a chance to seal. Skip fertiliser for a couple of months. Division into new pots is easiest at this point if the clump has become crowded.
varieties: The standard Zamioculcas zamiifolia has glossy mid-green leaflets. 'Raven' is the striking dark cultivar: new growth emerges bright lime green and matures to a near-black purple, and it needs decent indirect light to develop that colour fully.

'Zenzi' and 'Zamicro' are dwarf forms with shorter stems and tightly packed leaflets, useful for shelves and desks. A variegated form exists with cream and green marbling but is slow, expensive and more prone to scorching. All ZZ plants are toxic to cats and dogs, and the sap can irritate skin — worth wearing gloves when dividing rhizomes.

light: Spider plant does best in bright indirect light, which keeps the variegation crisp and encourages the arching flower stems that carry the plantlets. It tolerates medium light and even fairly dim corners, but growth slows and the white stripes fade toward green.

Keep it out of direct midday sun, which bleaches and scorches the narrow leaves. An east-facing window is close to perfect; a west or south window works if the plant sits back from the glass or behind a sheer curtain. If you want babies, err on the brighter side — plantlets are produced far more freely in good light.
water: Water when the top inch of mix has dried, keeping the soil lightly moist but never soggy. Through spring and summer that is typically once a week. Spider plants store water in thick, tuberous roots, so they cope with an occasional missed watering better than most.
Reduce to every ten to fourteen days in winter when growth slows. Water thoroughly until it drains and discard what collects in the saucer.

Spider plants are notoriously sensitive to fluoride and chlorine in tap water — this is the single most common cause of the brown tips they are famous for. If your water is heavily treated, use filtered, distilled or rainwater, or leave tap water standing uncovered overnight. Average household humidity is fine, though they appreciate a little extra.
soil: A standard well-draining potting mix with a handful of perlite suits them well. The thick storage roots want air as well as moisture, so avoid dense, compacted media.

Feed every four weeks through spring and summer with a balanced liquid fertiliser at half strength, and stop over winter. Go easy: over-fertilising is the second most common cause of brown leaf tips after tap water, because salts accumulate in the mix. Flushing the pot with plain water every few months clears them out.

propagation: Spider plants are the easiest houseplant of all to propagate, because they do most of the work themselves. A mature plant sends out long arching stems carrying plantlets — miniature spider plants, often with stubby roots already forming at the base.

You have three options. Leave the plantlet attached to the parent and pin it down into a small pot of moist mix beside it; once it has rooted in a few weeks, snip the connecting stem. Or cut the plantlet off and stand it in water until roots are an inch or two long, then pot it up. Or plant the cut plantlet straight into damp soil and keep it moist while it establishes. All three work reliably; the attached method is the most foolproof because the parent keeps feeding the baby while it roots. Mature clumps can also be divided at repotting, which is the quickest way to make two full-sized plants.

problems.symptom: Brown tips on the leaves
problems.cause: The signature spider plant complaint. Usually fluoride or chlorine in tap water, salt buildup from fertiliser, or dry air — often all three.
problems.fix: Switch to filtered, distilled or rainwater, flush the pot with plain water every few months, and cut back on feeding. Trim the brown tip at an angle following the leaf's natural point; it will not regrow green but it will stop spreading.

problems.symptom: No plantlets being produced
problems.cause: Insufficient light, a plant too young to flower, or too much root room. Spider plants tend to produce babies once they are comfortably pot-bound.
problems.fix: Move to brighter indirect light and resist repotting into a much larger container. A plant that is slightly snug flowers and produces plantlets far more readily.

problems.symptom: Pale, washed-out leaves losing their stripes
problems.cause: Either too little light, which fades variegation toward green, or too much direct sun, which bleaches the whole leaf.
problems.fix: Check the position. Faded-to-green usually means move brighter; bleached and papery means move back from the glass.

problems.symptom: Leaves yellowing and limp, mix constantly damp
problems.cause: Overwatering and the beginnings of root rot in the fleshy storage roots.
problems.fix: Let the top inch dry fully between waterings and confirm the pot drains freely. If the roots are brown and soft rather than firm and white, trim them and repot into fresh mix.

problems.symptom: Whole plant looks limp and the pot feels very light
problems.cause: Underwatering, or a root system so congested that there is barely any soil left to hold water.
problems.fix: Water thoroughly and check whether roots have filled the pot. A plant that dries out within two or three days of watering needs repotting regardless of the calendar.

problems.symptom: Fine webbing between leaves, stippled grey-green foliage
problems.cause: Spider mites, which favour the dry air around radiators.
problems.fix: Rinse the plant thoroughly in the shower, then treat with insecticidal soap every five to seven days for three cycles. Raising humidity makes recurrence much less likely.

problems.symptom: Brown mushy patches at the base of the leaf clump
problems.cause: Crown rot from water sitting in the centre of the rosette, or from soil kept saturated.
problems.fix: Water into the mix rather than over the crown, improve drainage, and remove affected leaves at the base. Divide out any healthy sections if the centre is badly affected.

repotting: Spider plants grow vigorously and typically need repotting every one to two years. The thick white storage roots fill a pot quickly and will eventually lift the whole plant above the rim or crack a plastic container outright.

Repot in spring, moving up one pot size. Do not be tempted by a much larger container — a slightly snug spider plant produces far more plantlets, and extra soil just stays wet. Loosen the dense root mass, trim any brown or mushy roots, and set the plant at its previous depth.
This is the natural moment to divide. A congested clump pulls apart into two or three plants, each with roots and a good fan of leaves. Water well afterwards and wait a month before feeding.
varieties: 'Vittatum' is the classic, with a broad white central stripe and green margins. 'Variegatum' reverses that, with green centres and white edges. Both are equally easy and equally prolific with plantlets.

'Bonnie' is the curly form, with leaves that spiral tightly — the same plant behaviourally, just more compact and better suited to a shelf. 'Hawaiian' has a pale champagne-coloured flush on new growth that fades to green as leaves mature. All spider plants are non-toxic to cats and dogs, which is why they are one of the most recommended plants for pet households — though cats are notoriously drawn to chewing the dangling leaves, so expect some nibbling.

light: Fiddle leaf fig needs more light than most people give it, and this is the root of its difficult reputation. It wants bright indirect light for most of the day — directly in front of an east window, or a few feet from a south or west window. In a dim corner it drops leaves steadily and never recovers properly.

A few hours of gentle direct morning sun is beneficial; harsh afternoon sun through unshaded glass will scorch the large leaves. Rotate the pot a quarter turn every week or two, because the plant leans hard toward its light source and develops a one-sided crown if left alone.
water: Water when the top two inches of mix are dry, then water thoroughly until it runs from the drainage holes. In a bright spot during spring and summer that is usually every seven to ten days. This plant hates both extremes — it will drop leaves from drought and rot from constant wet.
Cut back substantially in autumn and winter, often to every two to three weeks. The combination of low winter light and unchanged watering is what kills most fiddle leaf figs in their first year.

Consistency matters more than frequency here. Fiddle leaf figs respond badly to erratic care, so pick a checking routine and stick to it. They prefer humidity above 40% and dislike cold draughts intensely — keep them away from doors, single-glazed windows and air conditioning vents.
soil: Use a well-draining potting mix with plenty of structure: roughly two parts quality potting compost to one part perlite and one part orchid bark. Ficus lyrata roots need air, and a dense peat-heavy mix that stays soggy is a direct route to root rot.

The pot must drain freely. Feed every four weeks through spring and summer with a balanced liquid fertiliser at half strength, or use a fertiliser formulated for foliage plants with a higher nitrogen ratio. Stop feeding entirely from October to March.

propagation: Fiddle leaf figs propagate from stem cuttings taken in spring or early summer. Choose a section of stem six to twelve inches long with one or two healthy leaves, and cut just below a node with clean, sharp secateurs. The plant bleeds a milky white latex when cut — it irritates skin and is toxic if ingested, so wear gloves and rinse the cut end before proceeding.

Stand the cutting in water in a bright spot out of direct sun, changing the water weekly, or pot it straight into damp, free-draining mix. Rooting is slower than for most houseplants, typically four to eight weeks, and warmth makes a real difference. A clear bag loosely over a soil-potted cutting raises humidity and improves the odds. Once roots are two to three inches long, pot into your usual mix and keep it slightly moister than an established plant for the first few weeks. Air layering is the more reliable method for a tall, bare-stemmed plant, and has the advantage of producing a large plant immediately rather than a single-stem cutting.

problems.symptom: Brown spots in the middle of leaves with dark edges
problems.cause: Root rot from overwatering. On fiddle leaf figs the damage often shows in the leaf centre rather than the edges, and spreads outward.
problems.fix: Check the roots. Trim anything brown and soft, repot into fresh free-draining mix, and reduce watering. Affected leaves will not recover and can be removed.

problems.symptom: Brown, dry patches starting at the leaf edges
problems.cause: Underwatering or very low humidity, sometimes combined with a plant sitting near a radiator.
problems.fix: Water more consistently and move it away from heat sources. Raising humidity to 40-50% helps noticeably.

problems.symptom: Sudden leaf drop
problems.cause: Stress from change — a new position, a cold draught, a sharp temperature swing, or an abrupt shift in watering. Fiddle leaf figs are unusually sensitive to being moved.
problems.fix: Settle it in one spot with stable conditions and stop adjusting things. Some drop after a move home is normal; give it a month to acclimatise before intervening further.

problems.symptom: Leaves pale, small, and widely spaced up a leggy stem
problems.cause: Not enough light. The plant stretches toward the window and cannot support full-sized foliage.
problems.fix: Move it into genuinely bright indirect light. Prune the top back to encourage branching, and rotate the pot regularly so it grows evenly.

problems.symptom: Red or brown speckling on new leaves
problems.cause: Oedema — cells rupturing because the plant took up water faster than it could transpire it, usually after heavy watering in low light.
problems.fix: Water less and increase light. The spotting is cosmetic and does not spread; new leaves will come out clean once conditions are right.

problems.symptom: White fuzzy spots or fine webbing on leaf undersides
problems.cause: Mealybugs or spider mites, both of which shelter under the broad leaves where they go unnoticed.
problems.fix: Wipe every leaf on both sides with a damp cloth, then treat with insecticidal soap or neem oil weekly for three to four weeks. Inspect the undersides regularly — this is the spot people forget.

problems.symptom: Dusty leaves looking dull
problems.cause: Simple dust accumulation. The large flat leaves collect it quickly, and a heavy layer measurably reduces the light reaching the leaf.
problems.fix: Wipe both sides with a damp cloth every few weeks. This is genuine maintenance for this species rather than cosmetic.

repotting: Repot every one to two years while young, then every two to three years once mature. Signs are roots circling the surface or emerging from the drainage holes, water running straight through, and growth stalling during the growing season.

Spring is the right time. Move up one pot size only — typically two inches wider. Fiddle leaf figs are top-heavy, so choose a substantial pot that will not tip; a wide, heavy ceramic container is safer than a tall narrow one.

Handle the root ball gently and disturb it as little as possible, because this species resents root disturbance and often sulks for a few weeks afterwards. Water thoroughly, keep it out of direct sun for a fortnight, and do not fertilise for six weeks. For very large specimens that cannot practically be repotted, top-dress instead: scrape off the top two inches of mix and replace with fresh compost each spring.
varieties: 'Bambino' is the dwarf cultivar, reaching three to four feet with smaller, rounder leaves — a far more practical choice for an average room than the species, which can reach ten feet indoors. 'Compacta' is similar, with tightly spaced leaves on a bushier frame.

'Variegata' carries cream and green marbling, is considerably harder to keep and needs bright light to avoid the white sections browning. Whichever form you choose, Ficus lyrata is toxic to cats and dogs, and the milky sap irritates skin on contact — worth knowing before you prune.

light: Rubber plant is more forgiving than its relative the fiddle leaf fig, tolerating medium light while preferring bright indirect. In good light it produces large, glossy, well-spaced leaves; in dim conditions the stem stretches and the leaves come out smaller and further apart.

Variegated forms such as 'Tineke' and 'Ruby' need noticeably more light than the plain dark green species, because the cream and pink tissue contains little chlorophyll. If a variegated rubber plant is reverting to green, the light level is the reason. Avoid harsh direct sun, which scorches, though gentle morning sun is fine.
water: Let the top one to two inches dry out before watering, then water thoroughly until it drains. In spring and summer that usually works out at every seven to ten days. Rubber plants are moderately drought-tolerant thanks to their thick, waxy leaves and dislike sitting wet.
Cut back sharply in winter to every two to three weeks, or longer in a cool room. Overwatering in winter is the most common cause of the sudden lower-leaf drop that alarms new owners.

Wipe the leaves with a damp cloth every few weeks. The broad glossy surfaces collect dust quickly, and clean leaves photosynthesise better and look dramatically better. Average household humidity is adequate, though the plant appreciates a little extra.
soil: Use a well-draining potting mix with added perlite or bark — roughly three parts compost to one part perlite. The aim is a medium that holds some moisture but drains freely, since Ficus elastica roots rot in dense, waterlogged soil.

Feed monthly through spring and summer with a balanced liquid fertiliser at half strength. Rubber plants are moderately hungry and respond well to feeding during active growth, but stop completely in autumn and winter, when unused fertiliser salts accumulate and burn the roots.

propagation: Rubber plants root readily from stem cuttings taken in spring or early summer. Cut a six-inch section of stem with two or three leaves, just below a node. The cut bleeds copious milky latex, which irritates skin and stains — wear gloves and dab the wound with a damp cloth until it stops before potting.

Reduce water loss by rolling the remaining leaves into a loose cylinder and securing them with an elastic band. Pot the cutting into damp, free-draining mix, or stand it in water, and keep it warm in bright indirect light. A clear bag over a soil-potted cutting maintains humidity and improves success. Roots take four to six weeks. Air layering is the better technique for a tall, leggy plant: wound the stem, wrap it in damp sphagnum moss inside a plastic sleeve, and wait six to eight weeks for roots to form before cutting below them — you get a substantial new plant immediately and the parent branches from the cut.

problems.symptom: Lower leaves yellowing then dropping
problems.cause: Overwatering is the usual cause. Losing the occasional oldest leaf is normal, but several at once with damp soil is a warning.
problems.fix: Let the top two inches dry before watering and confirm the pot drains. In winter, extend the interval substantially.

problems.symptom: Sudden leaf drop after a move
problems.cause: Shock from a change in light, temperature or humidity. Rubber plants dislike cold draughts in particular.
problems.fix: Settle it in one position away from doors and vents, and maintain steady watering. It usually stabilises within a few weeks; avoid making further changes while it adjusts.

problems.symptom: Brown crispy leaf edges
problems.cause: Dry air, underwatering, or salt buildup from fertiliser and hard water.
problems.fix: Water more consistently, flush the pot with plain water every few months, and raise humidity slightly. Reduce feeding if you have been generous.

problems.symptom: Variegated leaves reverting to solid green
problems.cause: Insufficient light. The plant favours chlorophyll-rich green tissue when it is short of energy.
problems.fix: Move to brighter indirect light and prune out fully green shoots to redirect growth into variegated stems.

problems.symptom: Tall bare stem with leaves only at the top
problems.cause: Natural growth habit combined with low light and no pruning. Rubber plants grow as single stems unless encouraged to branch.
problems.fix: Cut the main stem back by a third in spring. The plant branches from below the cut, and the section you removed can be air-layered or rooted as a cutting.

problems.symptom: Black spots or soft dark patches on leaves
problems.cause: Fungal leaf spot or advanced root rot, typically following prolonged overwatering combined with poor air circulation.
problems.fix: Remove affected leaves, improve airflow, and inspect the roots. Trim soft brown roots and repot into fresh mix if rot is present.

problems.symptom: Sticky leaves and small brown bumps on stems
problems.cause: Scale insects excreting honeydew, which in turn attracts sooty mould.
problems.fix: Scrape the scale off with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol, wash the sticky residue off with soapy water, and treat with neem oil weekly for a month.

repotting: Repot every one to two years while the plant is young and growing quickly, then every two to three years. The signals are roots through the drainage holes, water running straight through, or a plant that has stopped growing in spring.

Repot in spring into a pot one size larger. Rubber plants grow tall and become top-heavy, so weight and width in the pot matter more than depth. Loosen circling roots and trim any that are dark and soft.

A mature rubber plant that has reached the ceiling can be kept at a manageable size by pruning the top and root-pruning at repotting: trim the outer inch of the root ball and return it to the same container with fresh mix. Water well and hold off fertiliser for six weeks.
varieties: The plain species has deep green leaves; 'Robusta' is the common commercial form with especially broad, thick foliage. 'Burgundy' and 'Abidjan' have near-black leaves with red midribs and hold that colour best in bright light.

'Tineke' carries cream and grey-green variegation, and 'Ruby' adds pink flushing to the margins — both need more light than the green forms to keep their colour. All Ficus elastica are toxic to cats and dogs, and the milky sap causes skin irritation and stains fabric, so gloves and a dust sheet are worth having when pruning.

light: Aloe vera is a true succulent from arid regions and wants as much light as you can give it indoors. A south or west-facing windowsill is ideal, with four to six hours of direct sun. In lower light the plant stretches, the leaves thin and flop outward, and the compact rosette shape is lost.

Introduce strong sun gradually. An aloe moved straight from a shop shelf to a blazing summer windowsill will develop brown or reddish scorch patches. Move it in stages over two or three weeks. A reddish-bronze tint on the leaves is normal sun stress and not harmful, but white or brown papery patches are burns.
water: Water deeply, then let the mix dry out completely before watering again. The thick leaves are water reserves, and this plant is built for drought rather than regular irrigation. In spring and summer that usually means every two to three weeks; in winter, every four to six weeks or even less in a cool room.
Water into the soil around the base, not into the rosette. Water trapped between the leaves at the centre causes crown rot, which is difficult to recover from.

The commonest mistake is watering a little and often. That keeps the surface damp without ever soaking the root zone, encouraging shallow roots and fungus gnats. Soak thoroughly, drain completely, then wait. Humidity is irrelevant; aloe is happiest in dry household air.
soil: Use a cactus or succulent compost, or make your own from two parts potting mix to one part coarse sand or perlite plus a handful of grit. The mix should feel gritty and drain within seconds when watered.

Terracotta is strongly preferable to plastic here, because the porous walls pull moisture out between waterings. Drainage holes are essential and a layer of grit on the surface helps keep the base of the leaves dry. Feed sparingly — a half-strength succulent fertiliser twice across the whole growing season is plenty, and none in winter.

propagation: Aloe vera propagates from offsets, commonly called pups — small plantlets that emerge from the base of a mature plant. This is the only reliable method; a detached aloe leaf will rot rather than root, unlike some other succulents.

Wait until a pup is at least a few inches tall and has developed its own roots. Slide the whole plant out of the pot, brush the soil away and locate where the pup joins the parent. Separate it with a clean knife, taking as many of its own roots as possible. Let the cut surfaces dry and callus for two to three days in a shaded spot — potting a fresh wound straight into damp soil invites rot. Then plant each pup in dry cactus mix and wait a week before the first light watering. Keep new divisions in bright indirect light rather than full sun until they are established, then move them into direct sun gradually.

problems.symptom: Leaves soft, mushy and translucent at the base
problems.cause: Root or crown rot from overwatering, a mix that holds too much moisture, or water sitting in the rosette.
problems.fix: Unpot immediately and inspect. Cut away every soft root and any mushy leaf bases until only firm tissue remains, let it dry for two days, and repot into dry gritty mix. Withhold water for a week. Severely rotted plants may only be salvageable as healthy pups.

problems.symptom: Leaves thin, curling inward and wrinkled
problems.cause: Underwatering. The plant is drawing on its internal reserves.
problems.fix: Water thoroughly until it drains and repeat in a week. Leaves plump up over several days. This is much easier to correct than overwatering.

problems.symptom: Leaves flat, splaying outward instead of upright
problems.cause: Too little light. The plant stretches sideways searching for it, and the rosette loses its structure.
problems.fix: Move to the brightest window available, increasing exposure gradually. Stretched growth will not re-tighten, but new growth from the centre will come in compact.

problems.symptom: Brown or white papery patches on leaves
problems.cause: Sunburn, usually after an abrupt move into direct sun.
problems.fix: Shade the plant temporarily and reintroduce sun over two to three weeks. Damaged tissue does not heal; remove badly scorched leaves at the base.

problems.symptom: Leaves turning reddish-brown or bronze all over
problems.cause: Usually sun stress, which is harmless, though it can also indicate underwatering or a pot-bound plant.
problems.fix: Check the soil and the roots first. If watering is adequate and roots have room, the colour is cosmetic and the plant is fine — move it slightly out of the strongest sun if you prefer green.

problems.symptom: Small flies around the pot
problems.cause: Fungus gnats breeding in soil that is being kept too damp — a symptom of watering too often rather than a pest problem in itself.
problems.fix: Let the mix dry out completely, add a gritty top dressing, and use sticky traps for the adults. The problem disappears once the watering routine changes.

problems.symptom: White cottony spots where leaves meet the stem
problems.cause: Mealybugs, which shelter deep in the tight leaf axils of the rosette.
problems.fix: Dab each one with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol. Check weekly for a month; the leaf axils hide them well and a single survivor restarts the colony.

repotting: Aloe vera is happy slightly pot-bound and only needs repotting every two to three years, or sooner if pups have filled the container. Other signs are roots through the drainage holes and a plant that has become top-heavy enough to tip.

Repot in spring into a pot just one size larger, and choose something wide and heavy rather than deep — aloe roots are shallow and spreading. Terracotta again helps with moisture control and stability.

Use completely dry mix and do not water for a week afterwards, giving any damaged roots time to seal. Remove pups at the same time if the pot has become crowded. Skip fertiliser for a couple of months after repotting.
varieties: Aloe barbadensis miller is the medicinal species and the one usually sold simply as aloe vera, with thick grey-green leaves and a gel used for minor burns. Aloe aristata, the lace aloe, is smaller and more ornamental with white tubercles along the leaves.

Aloe 'Christmas Carol' and Aloe 'Pink Blush' are compact hybrids grown for their red markings. Note the pet-safety point: despite its use on human skin, aloe vera is toxic to cats and dogs if eaten, causing vomiting and lethargy — the latex just under the leaf skin is the culprit. Keep it out of reach in a pet household.

light: Boston fern wants bright indirect light and no direct sun at all. In the wild it grows in humid forest shade, and the fine fronds scorch quickly on a sunny windowsill. A north-facing window is ideal; an east window works if the plant sits slightly back from the glass.

In too little light the fronds thin out, the plant looks sparse and it sheds heavily. In too much, the leaflets bleach to a pale yellow-green and then crisp. If you are hanging one, remember that light falls off sharply with distance from the window — a fern hung in the middle of a room is usually in lower light than it looks.
water: This is the demanding part. Boston fern wants consistently moist soil — not wet, not dry — and it punishes lapses in either direction. Check the top half-inch every couple of days and water as soon as it feels dry to the touch. In a warm room that can mean two or three times a week in summer.

Reduce slightly in winter, but never let the root ball dry out completely. A Boston fern that dries out fully will shed most of its fronds, and while the crown often survives to regrow, it is a setback of months.

Humidity matters more for this plant than for almost any other common houseplant. It genuinely needs 50% and preferably more. A bathroom or kitchen, a humidifier, or a pebble tray all help significantly. The dry air from central heating is the main reason Boston ferns fail indoors over winter.
soil: Use a peat-based or coir-based potting mix that holds moisture while still draining — add a handful of perlite to keep it open. The goal is a medium that stays evenly damp without becoming a bog.

Plastic pots suit Boston ferns better than terracotta, because they slow evaporation and help keep the root ball consistently moist. Feed monthly at half strength through spring and summer only. Ferns are sensitive to fertiliser salts, so flush the pot with plain water every couple of months to prevent buildup, which shows as browned frond tips.

propagation: Division is the practical method and the one to use. In spring, slide the plant out of its pot and look at the dense root mass. Mature Boston ferns naturally form multiple crowns, and these pull apart into separate plants. Use a clean serrated knife if the root ball is too dense to separate by hand.

Each division needs several fronds and a healthy share of roots. Pot each into fresh moisture-retentive mix at the same depth, water thoroughly and keep them somewhere humid and shaded for two to three weeks while they recover. Expect some frond loss after division; this is normal and new growth follows once the roots re-establish. Boston ferns also produce runners — thin, wiry stolons that creep over the soil surface. Pin one down into an adjacent pot of damp mix and it will root at the tip, after which you can sever the connection. Spore propagation is possible but slow and unreliable at home, and named cultivars do not come true from spores.

problems.symptom: Fronds dropping leaflets all over the floor
problems.cause: The signature Boston fern complaint. Almost always low humidity, sometimes combined with the soil drying out or a position near a radiator.
problems.fix: Raise humidity to 50% or more with a humidifier or pebble tray, move it away from heat sources and draughts, and keep the soil consistently damp. Some shedding of old fronds is normal; carpet-covering shedding is not.

problems.symptom: Brown, crispy frond tips
problems.cause: Dry air, underwatering, or fertiliser salt buildup in the mix.
problems.fix: Increase humidity, water more consistently, and flush the pot with plain water every couple of months. Trim damaged tips with scissors.

problems.symptom: Whole fronds yellowing and dying back
problems.cause: Overwatering and waterlogged roots if the mix is sodden, or severe drought if the root ball has shrunk away from the pot sides.
problems.fix: Feel the soil. If it is soggy, improve drainage and water less. If it is bone dry and water runs straight down the gap at the edge, submerge the whole pot in a basin for twenty minutes to rehydrate the root ball.

problems.symptom: Pale, washed-out fronds
problems.cause: Too much light, usually direct sun through a window.
problems.fix: Move to a shadier position with bright indirect light only. Bleached fronds will not recover, so trim them out as new growth comes through.

problems.symptom: Sparse, thin growth with long gaps between fronds
problems.cause: Too little light, or a plant that needs feeding and repotting after several seasons in the same tired mix.
problems.fix: Move somewhere brighter but still out of direct sun, refresh the potting mix in spring, and resume regular half-strength feeding through the growing season.

problems.symptom: Small brown bumps in rows under the fronds
problems.cause: Usually spores, which are entirely normal and a sign of a mature, healthy fern. Occasionally scale insects, which are irregularly placed rather than arranged in neat rows.
problems.fix: If the bumps are in tidy rows either side of the midrib, leave them alone. If scattered and they scrape off stickily, treat as scale with rubbing alcohol and neem oil.

problems.symptom: Fine webbing between fronds
problems.cause: Spider mites, which thrive in exactly the dry air that also causes shedding.
problems.fix: Rinse thoroughly in the shower, treat with insecticidal soap weekly for three weeks, and fix the humidity — otherwise they will return.

repotting: Boston ferns grow fast and generally need repotting every one to two years, in spring. Signs are roots filling the surface, water running straight through, or a plant that dries out within a day of watering.

Move up one pot size, choosing plastic rather than terracotta to conserve moisture, and make sure it drains. Boston ferns have shallow, fibrous root systems, so a wide pot suits them better than a deep one.

Loosen the root mass gently and trim any dead brown roots. This is the obvious moment to divide a crowded plant. Water well, keep humidity high for a few weeks while it settles, and do not feed for six weeks.
varieties: Nephrolepis exaltata 'Bostoniensis' is the classic with long arching fronds. 'Dallas' and 'Compacta' are smaller and noticeably more tolerant of average household humidity — a better choice if you cannot provide a humid spot.

'Fluffy Ruffles' and 'Rita's Gold' offer denser, frillier foliage, the latter with a chartreuse tint. Related lemon button fern is much smaller and considerably more forgiving about dry air. All Nephrolepis ferns are non-toxic to cats and dogs, which makes them a popular choice for pet households despite the humidity demands.

light: Heartleaf philodendron is one of the most adaptable trailing plants available, growing happily in anything from low light to bright indirect. Like pothos it survives in dim corners, but the difference shows in the foliage: good light produces larger, closer-spaced leaves and a fuller plant.

Keep it out of direct sun, which scorches and fades the deep green. An east window or a position a few feet back from a brighter one suits it well. If your plant has long bare stretches of vine with small leaves, low light is almost always the explanation.
water: Let the top inch of mix dry before watering, then water thoroughly until it drains. In spring and summer that usually means every seven to ten days; in lower light or in winter, every two weeks or more.

Heartleaf philodendron signals thirst clearly, with slightly limp leaves that recover within hours of watering. It is far more tolerant of occasional drought than of permanently wet soil, so when unsure, wait a few more days.

Average household humidity is adequate, though the plant grows faster above 50%. Brown crispy tips generally point to dry air or inconsistent watering rather than anything more serious. Empty the saucer after watering; standing water is the usual route to root rot.
soil: A standard well-draining houseplant mix with added perlite or orchid bark works well. As a climbing aroid it wants air around the roots, so anything dense and peat-heavy that stays soggy should be lightened.

Feed monthly at half strength during spring and summer and stop over winter. Heartleaf philodendron is a modest feeder, and over-fertilising shows up as brown leaf tips and a white crust on the soil surface. Flush the pot with plain water every few months if you feed regularly.

propagation: This is among the easiest of all houseplants to propagate, and a good candidate for a first attempt. The vines are covered in nodes — small bumps where each leaf stem meets the vine, often with a short aerial root already visible.

Cut a four to six inch section with two or three leaves, making the cut half an inch below a node. Remove the lowest leaf so that node sits bare. Stand the cutting in water with the node submerged and the leaves clear of the surface, in bright indirect light, changing the water weekly. Roots appear within one to two weeks. Once they are two inches long, pot three or four cuttings together into one small pot for an immediately full plant. Cuttings root just as readily pushed directly into damp soil, which avoids the brief adjustment period that water-rooted cuttings go through when transplanted.

problems.symptom: Long bare vines with small, widely spaced leaves
problems.cause: Too little light. The plant stretches toward the nearest source rather than producing full foliage.
problems.fix: Move to brighter indirect light and prune the bare vines back to a few inches from the soil. Philodendron branches readily from cut nodes, and the removed sections root easily to fill out the same pot.

problems.symptom: Yellow leaves, several at once
problems.cause: Overwatering, particularly if the mix is still damp and the yellowing starts low on the plant.
problems.fix: Let the top inch dry properly before watering and check the pot is not sitting in water. The occasional yellow leaf on an old vine is normal ageing.

problems.symptom: Brown crispy leaf tips and edges
problems.cause: Dry air, erratic watering, or salt buildup from fertiliser and hard tap water.
problems.fix: Water on a more consistent schedule, raise humidity a little, and flush the pot with plain water every few months.

problems.symptom: Leaves drooping despite damp soil
problems.cause: Root rot. Damaged roots cannot take up water, so the plant wilts even though the mix is wet.
problems.fix: Take healthy cuttings straight away as insurance, then unpot, trim every soft brown root, and repot into fresh airy mix. Water sparingly until new growth appears.

problems.symptom: Pale, washed-out or scorched leaves
problems.cause: Direct sun, typically through an unshaded south or west window.
problems.fix: Move it back from the glass or filter the light. Bleached leaves do not recover; trim them as new growth replaces them.

problems.symptom: Small flies hovering around the pot
problems.cause: Fungus gnats breeding in permanently damp topsoil, which indicates watering too frequently.
problems.fix: Let the surface dry fully between waterings, use yellow sticky traps for the adults, and water from below for a few weeks.

problems.symptom: White cottony clusters along the stems
problems.cause: Mealybugs, which tuck themselves into leaf joints and under the curl of new growth.
problems.fix: Dab with rubbing alcohol on a cotton bud, then treat with insecticidal soap. Inspect weekly for a month, since a single missed cluster restarts the infestation.

repotting: Repot every one to two years, in spring. Heartleaf philodendron grows quickly and the usual signs apply: roots emerging from the drainage holes, water running straight through, and slowing growth during the growing season.

Move up one pot size only. As a trailing plant it suits hanging pots and shelf positions, so weight and balance are worth considering — a pot that is too large holds excess wet soil and makes hanging awkward.

Tease apart circling roots so they grow outward. If the plant has gone bare at the crown, repotting is the moment to cut it back hard and plant rooted cuttings around the parent to thicken it. Water well and wait a month before feeding.
varieties: The plain Philodendron hederaceum has deep green heart-shaped leaves. 'Brasil' carries a bright chartreuse stripe down the centre of each leaf and is equally easy. 'Micans' has velvety bronze-green foliage with a faint iridescence and slightly prefers higher humidity.

'Lemon Lime' is a uniform chartreuse throughout. Heartleaf philodendron is frequently confused with pothos, but the differences are consistent: philodendron leaves are thinner, softer and more sharply heart-shaped with a distinct drip tip, and new leaves emerge from a papery sheath. All philodendrons are toxic to cats and dogs, so a hanging position is worth considering in a pet household.

light: Jade plant needs a lot of light — four or more hours of direct sun daily is ideal. A south or west-facing windowsill is the right home. This is the single biggest factor in whether a jade develops the thick, compact, tree-like form people want or a floppy, stretched one.

In insufficient light the stems elongate, the leaves space out and thin, and the plant eventually leans and topples under its own weight. Good light also brings out the red edging on the leaves, which is a healthy sun response rather than a warning. Introduce strong sun gradually to avoid scorching a plant that has been in dimmer conditions.
water: Treat jade as the succulent it is. Water deeply, then let the mix dry out completely before watering again. In spring and summer that usually works out at every two to three weeks; in winter, once a month or less, especially in a cool room.

The leaves are the best gauge. Firm and plump means the plant is well watered; slightly soft and wrinkled means it is ready for a drink. Shrivelled, papery leaves mean it has been dry too long, and soft translucent ones mean it is far too wet.
Water the soil, not the foliage, and never leave the pot in a saucer of water. Humidity is irrelevant; jade is perfectly happy in dry indoor air and actually prefers it.
soil: Use a cactus or succulent mix, or two parts potting compost to one part coarse sand or perlite. The mix needs to drain fast and dry out fully between waterings.

Terracotta is strongly preferred. Jade grows top-heavy as it matures, and a heavy pot prevents tipping while the porous clay helps the root ball dry. Pick a pot that is wide rather than deep, since the roots are relatively shallow. Feed only two or three times across spring and summer with a half-strength succulent fertiliser, and not at all in winter.

propagation: Jade is among the most rewarding plants to propagate because both leaves and stem cuttings work, and the success rate is high. The key step that people skip is callusing.

For leaf propagation, gently twist a plump healthy leaf off the stem so it comes away cleanly with its base intact — a torn leaf will not root. For stem cuttings, take a three to four inch section with several leaves. Either way, leave the cutting on a dry surface out of direct sun for three to seven days until the cut end has dried and sealed. Then lay leaves flat on dry cactus mix, or insert stem cuttings an inch deep. Do not water for a week, then mist lightly or water sparingly every few days. Roots form in two to three weeks and a tiny plantlet follows at the base of a leaf after a month or more. Bright indirect light and warmth speed things up; damp soil at the callusing stage is the one thing that reliably causes failure.

problems.symptom: Leaves soft, translucent and dropping at a touch
problems.cause: Overwatering. Jade leaves become waterlogged and lose structure, and this is the most common way jades are killed.
problems.fix: Stop watering immediately and let the mix dry out completely. Check the roots and stem base for rot; cut away soft tissue and repot into dry gritty mix if found. Dropped leaves can be callused and rooted as insurance.

problems.symptom: Leaves wrinkled, thin and papery
problems.cause: Underwatering over an extended period.
problems.fix: Water thoroughly until it drains, then again a week later. Leaves plump back up over a week or two. Much easier to correct than overwatering.

problems.symptom: Stems long and leggy, leaves widely spaced
problems.cause: Not enough light. The plant is stretching, and the resulting growth is weak.
problems.fix: Move to the sunniest window available. Prune the stretched growth back to encourage branching — jade responds very well to pruning and the cuttings root easily.

problems.symptom: Leaf edges turning red or bronze
problems.cause: Sun stress, which in jade is normal and generally considered desirable. Occasionally it indicates underwatering.
problems.fix: No action needed if watering is adequate. If you prefer plain green foliage, move slightly out of the most direct sun.

problems.symptom: Black or brown soft patches at the base of the stem
problems.cause: Stem or root rot, usually from wet soil in cool conditions.
problems.fix: Take healthy cuttings from the upper stems immediately. Unpot, cut back to firm white tissue, let it dry for several days, and repot into dry mix. Advanced stem rot is often fatal, so the cuttings are your real insurance.

problems.symptom: White cottony spots in the leaf joints
problems.cause: Mealybugs, which favour the tight angles where leaves meet stems.
problems.fix: Dab each one with rubbing alcohol on a cotton bud, and inspect weekly for a month. Jade's compact growth gives them plenty of hiding places.

problems.symptom: Sudden loss of many leaves at once
problems.cause: A sharp change in conditions — a cold draught, a move, or a drastic swing in watering. Jade sheds leaves as a stress response.
problems.fix: Settle it in a stable bright position away from draughts and resume consistent care. New growth follows once conditions steady.

repotting: Jade grows slowly and likes being snug, so repot only every three to four years. The prompts are roots filling the pot entirely, a plant that has become unstable and top-heavy, or mix that has broken down and no longer drains.
Repot in spring into a pot one size larger — wide, heavy and shallow rather than tall. Stability matters: a mature jade is genuinely heavy and a light plastic pot will tip.

Use dry mix, handle the brittle branches carefully, and do not water for a week afterwards so any damaged roots can seal. Skip fertiliser for a couple of months. If the plant has grown lopsided, repotting is also the moment to prune it back into shape; jade tolerates hard pruning well and branches from just below each cut.
varieties: Crassula ovata is the standard jade, with rounded deep green leaves. 'Hobbit' and 'Gollum' have tubular, trumpet-shaped leaves and are popular for bonsai-style training. 'Tricolor' is variegated in cream, green and pink and needs strong light to hold the colour.

'Sunset' develops vivid red and yellow tones in bright light. Crassula arborescens, the silver jade, has blue-grey leaves with red margins and is a distinct species with the same care needs. All jade plants are toxic to cats and dogs, causing vomiting and lethargy if eaten — and because the leaves detach so easily, they are worth keeping well out of reach of a curious pet.

light: Chinese evergreen is one of the best genuinely low-light houseplants, and the darker green varieties tolerate conditions where almost nothing else will grow. It does equally well in medium and bright indirect light, where growth is noticeably faster.
