The variegation determines how much light a given plant needs. Dark green forms like 'Maria' cope with genuinely dim corners. Heavily patterned and pink or red cultivars such as 'Siam Aurora' need medium to bright indirect light to keep their colour and will fade toward green in shade. No variety tolerates direct sun, which scorches the leaves quickly.
water: Water when the top inch of mix has dried, then water thoroughly until it drains. In spring and summer that typically means every seven to ten days; in winter or in low light, every two to three weeks.

Chinese evergreen is noticeably more drought-tolerant than most tropical foliage plants and far more likely to be killed by overwatering than by neglect. The thick stems store some water, so a missed watering is not a crisis.

It prefers humidity above 50% but copes with average household air better than calatheas or ferns. Brown leaf tips usually indicate dry air, salt buildup or fluoride in tap water rather than a watering fault — try filtered water if tips keep browning despite a good routine.
soil: Use a standard well-draining potting mix with a handful of perlite. Aglaonema is not fussy, but it wants a medium that drains rather than staying saturated.

Feed monthly at half strength through spring and summer, stopping over winter. This is a slow, modest grower and over-fertilising causes leaf-tip burn. A pot with drainage holes matters more than the mix itself; the most frequent cause of failure is a decorative cachepot quietly collecting water underneath.

propagation: Division is the most reliable method. A mature Chinese evergreen forms a clump of several stems rising from a shared root mass, and these separate cleanly. In spring, slide the plant from its pot, shake off loose soil and identify sections that have their own stems and roots. Pull or cut them apart, giving each division at least a few leaves and a decent root share, and pot into fresh mix.

Stem cuttings also work. Cut a section of mature stem four to six inches long with a few leaves, remove the lowest leaf, and stand it in water or damp mix in a warm, bright spot. Roots take three to six weeks — slower than pothos or philodendron, so patience is needed. Older plants that have lost their lower leaves and developed a bare trunk can be cut back hard; the stump usually resprouts from the base, and the removed top roots as a cutting to make a second plant.

problems.symptom: Yellowing lower leaves
problems.cause: Overwatering if several yellow at once and the soil is wet; natural ageing if it is one old leaf at a time near the base.
problems.fix: Check the mix before watering and let the top inch dry. Confirm the pot drains and is not standing in water inside a cachepot.

problems.symptom: Brown, crispy leaf tips
problems.cause: Dry air, fluoride or chlorine in tap water, or fertiliser salt buildup.
problems.fix: Raise humidity, switch to filtered or rainwater, and flush the pot with plain water every few months. Trim tips at an angle.

problems.symptom: Pink or red variegation fading to green
problems.cause: Too little light for that cultivar. Coloured forms need more light than the plain green ones.
problems.fix: Move to brighter indirect light. The change shows on new growth; existing faded leaves stay as they are.

problems.symptom: Leaves curling inward
problems.cause: Underwatering, low humidity, or cold exposure. Aglaonema is sensitive to temperatures below about 15°C.
problems.fix: Check the soil and move the plant away from draughty windows and doors. Cold damage shows as greyish patches that do not recover.

problems.symptom: Drooping stems and mushy bases
problems.cause: Root rot from prolonged wet soil, often worse in winter when growth has slowed.
problems.fix: Unpot, cut away soft brown roots, and repot into fresh mix. Reduce watering substantially, especially in the colder months.

problems.symptom: Grey or greasy-looking patches on leaves
problems.cause: Cold damage from a draught or from being left near a window on a frosty night.
problems.fix: Move to a warmer spot away from glass. Damaged leaves will not recover; remove them and protect the plant through winter.

problems.symptom: Sticky residue and small brown bumps on stems
problems.cause: Scale insects, which favour the stems and leaf undersides.
problems.fix: Scrape them off with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol, wash away the honeydew, and treat with neem oil weekly for a month.

repotting: Chinese evergreen grows slowly and only needs repotting every two to three years. The prompts are roots circling the surface or emerging from the drainage holes, and water running straight through the pot.

Repot in spring into a container one size larger. Aglaonema prefers being slightly snug, and an oversized pot holding wet mix is a direct route to root rot in a plant that is already slow to use water.

Loosen the root ball, trim anything soft and brown, and set the plant at the same depth. This is the natural point to divide a crowded clump into two or three plants. Water thoroughly and wait six weeks before resuming fertiliser.
varieties: 'Maria' and 'Emerald Beauty' are the dark green, silver-marked forms and the most shade-tolerant. 'Silver Bay' has broad silver centres and is a reliable medium-light plant. 'Siam Aurora' and 'Red Valentine' carry pink or red midribs and margins and need noticeably more light to hold that colour.

'Cutlass' has narrow, lance-shaped leaves for a more architectural look. All Aglaonema are toxic to cats and dogs — the calcium oxalate crystals cause mouth and throat irritation if chewed — so despite their reputation as easy office plants, they are not a good choice within reach of a pet that nibbles.

light: Calathea medallion grows on the forest floor in Brazilian rainforest, in light that has already been filtered through a canopy. Indoors it wants medium to bright indirect light and absolutely no direct sun, which bleaches the patterning and scorches the thin leaves within days.

A north-facing window is often ideal. An east window works if the plant sits back from the glass. In light that is too low the leaves lose contrast and the purple undersides dull, and the plant stops producing new growth — but low light is a far less common cause of calathea problems than water quality.
water: Keep the mix evenly moist — never soggy, never dried out. Water when the top half-inch feels dry, which in spring and summer is usually every five to seven days. Reduce to every ten days or so in winter, but do not let the root ball dry out completely at any point.

Water quality matters more for calatheas than for almost any other houseplant. They are highly sensitive to fluoride, chlorine and dissolved salts, and hard tap water produces the crispy brown edges this genus is notorious for. Use filtered, distilled or rainwater, and the single most common calathea complaint largely disappears.

Humidity is the other non-negotiable. Calathea medallion wants 60% or more. A humidifier is the reliable answer; pebble trays and grouping help at the margins. Misting raises humidity for only minutes and wet leaves in still air invite fungal spotting, so it is not a substitute.
soil: Use a moisture-retentive but airy mix: roughly two parts peat or coir-based compost to one part perlite, with a little orchid bark. The aim is a medium that stays damp without compacting into a waterlogged block.

Plastic or glazed ceramic pots suit calatheas better than terracotta, which dries the root ball too quickly for a plant that wants consistent moisture. Drainage holes are still essential. Feed at quarter to half strength monthly through spring and summer only — calatheas are sensitive to fertiliser salts, and flushing the pot with clean water every couple of months prevents buildup.

propagation: Calathea medallion is propagated by division only. Stem and leaf cuttings will not root, because the plant grows from a clumping rhizome rather than from nodes along a stem — a cut leaf simply rots.

Divide in spring, ideally while repotting, and only once the plant has formed a decent clump. Slide it from the pot and gently wash or tease the soil away so you can see where the rhizomes separate naturally. Pull the clump apart with your hands where possible, using a clean knife only where roots are too dense. Each division needs its own roots and at least two or three leaves; smaller pieces rarely establish. Pot each into fresh moisture-retentive mix, water with filtered water, and keep them warm, shaded and humid for the first three to four weeks — a clear bag loosely over the pot helps enormously. Expect the divisions to sulk and possibly drop a leaf before new growth begins.

problems.symptom: Brown, crispy leaf edges
problems.cause: The classic calathea complaint. Usually minerals in tap water, low humidity, or both. Fertiliser salt buildup contributes.
problems.fix: Switch to filtered, distilled or rainwater, raise humidity to 60% with a humidifier, and flush the pot with clean water every couple of months. Trim damaged edges following the leaf's natural shape.

problems.symptom: Leaves curling inward along the midrib
problems.cause: Underwatering, low humidity, or the plant reacting to too much light. Some curling at night is normal — calatheas fold their leaves up in darkness, which is where the name prayer plant comes from.
problems.fix: Check the soil first. If dry, water. If moist and the curl persists during the day, raise humidity and move out of any direct light.

problems.symptom: Yellowing leaves, soil constantly wet
problems.cause: Overwatering and the beginnings of root rot.
problems.fix: Confirm the pot drains freely and is not sitting in water. Let the top half-inch dry before watering. If roots are brown and soft rather than firm, trim and repot into fresh mix.

problems.symptom: Faded, washed-out patterning
problems.cause: Too much light. Direct sun bleaches the markings and flattens the contrast that makes this plant worth growing.
problems.fix: Move to a shadier position with indirect light only. Faded leaves will not recover their pattern, but new growth will come in correctly marked.

problems.symptom: Fine webbing and stippled, dull leaves
problems.cause: Spider mites, which are the single most common calathea pest precisely because they thrive in the dry air that also causes brown edges.
problems.fix: Rinse the plant thoroughly, paying attention to leaf undersides, then treat with insecticidal soap every five days for three cycles. Fixing the humidity is what stops them returning.

problems.symptom: Leaves drooping dramatically
problems.cause: Either thirst or root rot — the symptom looks the same both ways, which catches people out.
problems.fix: Feel the soil before doing anything. Dry means water; wet means stop watering and check the roots immediately.

problems.symptom: Brown or black spots with yellow halos
problems.cause: Fungal leaf spot, usually after misting or water sitting on foliage in cool, still air.
problems.fix: Remove affected leaves, improve air circulation, stop misting, and water the soil rather than the leaves.

repotting: Calatheas dislike root disturbance and are best repotted only every two years, or when roots fill the pot entirely and the plant dries out much faster than it used to. Spring is the right time, when the plant has the growing season ahead to recover.

Move up one size only, into a plastic or glazed pot that will hold moisture. Disturb the root ball as little as possible — loosen the outer roots and leave the core intact rather than washing the soil away, unless you are dividing.

Water with filtered water afterwards, keep humidity high, and expect a period of sulking. Do not fertilise for six to eight weeks. If your calathea is otherwise healthy, leaving it alone is usually better than repotting on schedule; this is not a plant that appreciates routine disturbance.
varieties: Calathea veitchiana 'Medallion' has large rounded leaves with feathered green patterning and deep burgundy undersides. Calathea orbifolia is bigger, with broad silver-striped leaves and a reputation for being fussier still. Calathea lancifolia, the rattlesnake plant, has wavy lance-shaped leaves with dark blotches and is among the most forgiving in the genus.

Calathea 'White Fusion' is the most demanding of the commonly sold forms, with white variegation that browns readily if humidity drops. Note that many calatheas have been reclassified as Goeppertia, so you may see either name on a label. All calatheas are non-toxic to cats and dogs, which makes them a popular pet-household choice despite the care demands.

light: Parlor palm is the classic Victorian parlour plant precisely because it copes with the dim interiors of the period. It handles low light better than almost any other palm and does well in medium indirect light, where growth is faster and fuller.

Keep it out of direct sun, which yellows and scorches the delicate fronds. An east or north window suits it, or a position a few feet back from a brighter one. In very low light expect slow growth and a somewhat sparse plant, but it will not decline the way most palms do in shade.
water: Water when the top inch of mix has dried, then water thoroughly until it drains. In spring and summer that is usually every seven to ten days; in winter, every two weeks or so.

Parlor palms are more sensitive to overwatering than underwatering. The root system is fine and relatively small for the size of the plant, and it rots readily in soil that stays saturated. Empty the saucer after every watering.

They prefer humidity above 50% and show dry air as browning frond tips, which is the most common complaint. A pebble tray, a humidifier or grouping with other plants all help. They are also sensitive to fluoride in tap water, so filtered or rainwater is worth trying if tips keep browning.
soil: A standard peat-based potting mix with a handful of perlite works well. The mix should hold some moisture while draining freely — palms dislike both drought and waterlogging.

Note that parlor palms are almost always sold as several seedlings planted together in one pot to look full. That is normal and they should be left that way; separating them produces thin, sparse individual plants. Feed every six to eight weeks at half strength through spring and summer only, since palms are light feeders and prone to tip burn from excess fertiliser salts.

propagation: Parlor palm cannot be propagated from cuttings. It grows from a single growing point at the top of each stem, so a cut stem will not regrow and a severed frond will not root. This is true of most palms and is the thing most people get wrong.

The only genuine method is from seed, which is slow and difficult at home — germination takes months and requires consistent warmth and humidity, which is why almost all parlor palms are commercially grown. What you can do is separate the clump: since a shop plant is usually several individual seedlings potted together, you can carefully divide the root mass into two or three smaller clumps in spring. Keep at least three or four stems per division so the result still looks full, disturb the roots as little as possible, and keep the new pots warm and humid for a month. This multiplies your pots but does not produce new plants, and each division will be noticeably thinner than the original.

problems.symptom: Brown frond tips
problems.cause: The most common parlor palm complaint. Dry air, fluoride or salts in tap water, or inconsistent watering.
problems.fix: Raise humidity, switch to filtered or rainwater, and flush the pot with plain water every few months. Trim the brown tip only, following the frond's natural taper, and leave the green tissue intact.

problems.symptom: Whole fronds yellowing from the bottom up
problems.cause: Overwatering if the mix is wet, or natural ageing if it is only the oldest lower fronds one at a time.
problems.fix: Check the soil. Let the top inch dry before watering and confirm drainage. Cut spent fronds off at the base — they will not green up again.

problems.symptom: Fronds pale and washed-out
problems.cause: Too much light, or a nutrient shortage in a plant that has not been fed or repotted for several years.
problems.fix: Move out of direct sun. If light is already indirect, feed at half strength through the growing season and refresh the potting mix in spring.

problems.symptom: Fine webbing between fronds, stippled grey foliage
problems.cause: Spider mites, which are the signature parlor palm pest and thrive in dry indoor air.
problems.fix: Rinse the whole plant in the shower, including frond undersides, then treat with insecticidal soap every five days for three cycles. Raising humidity is what prevents recurrence.

problems.symptom: Stems browning at soil level, plant collapsing
problems.cause: Root rot from prolonged wet soil.
problems.fix: Unpot, cut away soft brown roots and any collapsed stems at the base, and repot into fresh free-draining mix. Water sparingly until new growth appears. Individual stems that have rotted will not recover.

problems.symptom: No new growth for a long period
problems.cause: Low light, cold, or an exhausted potting mix. Parlor palms are naturally slow, so some patience is warranted.
problems.fix: Move somewhere a little brighter and warmer, feed lightly through spring and summer, and repot every two to three years to refresh the mix.

problems.symptom: Small brown bumps on stems and frond undersides
problems.cause: Scale insects, which hide along the thin stems where they are easily missed.
problems.fix: Wipe them off with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol and follow with neem oil weekly for a month.

repotting: Parlor palms grow slowly and dislike root disturbance, so repot only every two to three years, or when roots are clearly emerging from the drainage holes. Spring is the best time.

Move up one pot size only. Keep the clump intact rather than separating the stems — the full appearance depends on them growing together. Handle the root ball gently; palm roots are brittle and damaged roots are slow to replace.

Set the plant at the same depth, water thoroughly, and keep it out of direct light and in decent humidity for a few weeks. Do not feed for six weeks. If the plant is large and repotting is impractical, top-dress instead by replacing the top two inches of mix each spring.
varieties: Chamaedorea elegans is the species sold as parlor palm and there are few named cultivars — 'Bella' is a compact form sometimes offered. Related species are worth knowing: Chamaedorea seifrizii is the bamboo palm, taller with narrower canes, and Chamaedorea metallica has broad blue-green leaves with a metallic sheen.

For a similar look with more height, the cat palm and kentia palm are both good choices, though kentia needs more light. Parlor palm is non-toxic to cats and dogs and appears on most pet-safe lists, which together with its shade tolerance makes it one of the most practical palms for an ordinary home.

light: String of pearls needs bright light — more than most people give it. Several hours of direct morning sun plus bright indirect light for the rest of the day is close to ideal. A south or east-facing window is usually right.

In insufficient light the strands stretch, the pearls space out widely along bare stems, and the plant looks sparse rather than dense. This is the single most common reason string of pearls disappoints. Harsh afternoon sun through glass can scorch the beads, so filter the strongest midday light in summer while keeping overall levels high.
water: Treat it as the succulent it is. Water thoroughly, then let the mix dry out almost completely before watering again — typically every two to three weeks in spring and summer, and once a month or less in winter.

The pearls themselves are the gauge. Plump and firm means well watered; slightly flattened or shrivelled means it is time. Mushy, translucent pearls that burst at a touch mean serious overwatering, and by then root rot is usually established.

Water at the soil surface rather than over the strands, and drain completely. The shallow root system sits near the surface, so a deep soak followed by a long dry period suits it far better than frequent light watering. Humidity is irrelevant; dry household air is fine.
soil: Use a gritty cactus or succulent mix, or two parts succulent compost to one part perlite or coarse sand. Fast drainage is essential — this plant rots faster than almost any other common houseplant in soil that stays damp.

String of pearls has a shallow, fine root system, so a wide shallow pot suits it much better than a deep one, which holds a reservoir of wet soil below the roots. Terracotta helps. Feed sparingly: a half-strength succulent fertiliser twice during the growing season is ample, none in winter.

propagation: String of pearls is very easy to propagate, which is fortunate because plants tend to thin at the crown over time and benefit from being refreshed with new cuttings.

Take a strand four to six inches long and remove the pearls from the last inch or two to expose the bare stem. You can then either lay the strand flat on the surface of damp cactus mix and press the bare section lightly into contact — roots form at each node where stem touches soil — or insert the bare end an inch into the mix. The laying method is more productive, because a single strand roots at multiple points and produces a fuller plant. Let cut ends callus for a day first. Keep the mix barely moist, not wet, and in bright indirect light; roots take two to three weeks. Planting several rooted cuttings around the edge of the parent pot is the standard way to thicken a plant that has gone bare in the middle. Avoid water propagation, which works poorly and often rots the strands.

problems.symptom: Pearls shrivelling and going flat
problems.cause: Underwatering, or occasionally root rot preventing water uptake despite damp soil.
problems.fix: Check the soil. If dry, water thoroughly and the pearls plump up within days. If the soil is wet and the pearls are still shrivelled, the roots have failed — take healthy cuttings and restart.

problems.symptom: Pearls turning mushy and bursting
problems.cause: Overwatering. The pearls take up more water than they can hold and the cells rupture.
problems.fix: Stop watering and let the mix dry out completely. Check for rot at the crown and take cuttings from healthy strands as insurance. Repot into grittier mix if the soil holds water too long.

problems.symptom: Bare stems with pearls far apart
problems.cause: Not enough light. The strands stretch toward the light source instead of producing dense growth.
problems.fix: Move to a much brighter position. Stretched sections will not fill in, so trim them and use the cuttings to replant into the same pot.

problems.symptom: Plant thinning and dying back in the middle
problems.cause: Natural ageing of the crown, worsened by water collecting among the strands at the centre.
problems.fix: This is normal for mature plants. Take cuttings from the healthy outer strands and replant them around the crown, or start a fresh pot. Water at the soil edge rather than over the centre.

problems.symptom: Brown or scorched patches on individual pearls
problems.cause: Sunburn from intense direct afternoon sun, especially through glass.
problems.fix: Filter the strongest midday light while keeping overall brightness high. Damaged pearls do not recover and can be trimmed away.

problems.symptom: White cottony clusters among the strands
problems.cause: Mealybugs, which hide among the dense pearls and are hard to spot until numerous.
problems.fix: Dab each cluster with rubbing alcohol on a cotton bud. Check thoroughly every week for a month — the tangled strands give them excellent cover.

problems.symptom: Whole strands going brown and dry from the base
problems.cause: Crown or stem rot at soil level, usually from overwatering or water sitting against the stems.
problems.fix: Cut away affected strands entirely, let the soil dry, and salvage healthy strands as cuttings. Improve drainage and water only at the pot edge.

repotting: String of pearls has a small, shallow root system and is happy pot-bound, so repot only every two to three years, or when the mix has broken down and stopped draining.
Choose a wide, shallow pot rather than a deep one — excess soil below the shallow roots simply stays wet. Terracotta or another breathable material helps. Spring is the right time.

Handle the strands carefully; they detach easily and every broken strand is a cutting worth saving. Use dry mix, wait a week before the first watering, and skip fertiliser for a couple of months. Repotting is a good moment to tuck rooted cuttings into any bare areas of the pot.
varieties: Curio rowleyanus, formerly Senecio rowleyanus, is the true string of pearls with spherical beads. A variegated form with cream-marbled pearls exists and is slower, more delicate and needs strong light.

Close relatives with identical care include string of bananas, with crescent-shaped leaves and a reputation for being noticeably tougher, string of dolphins, whose leaves curve into little dolphin shapes, and string of tears, with more teardrop-shaped beads. All of these Curio species are toxic to cats and dogs, and because the trailing strands are so attractive to a playful cat, a high shelf or hanging position well out of reach is genuinely important.

light: English ivy prefers bright indirect light and tolerates medium light, though variegated forms lose their cream and white markings in anything too dim. It handles more shade than most variegated plants but at the cost of leaf colour and density.

Keep it out of hot direct sun, which scorches the leaves and dries the plant out quickly. An east or north window is well suited. If a variegated ivy is reverting to plain green, insufficient light is the cause — move it brighter and trim out the green shoots.
water: Water when the top inch of mix has dried, keeping the soil lightly moist but never saturated. In spring and summer that is usually every five to seven days; in winter, every ten to fourteen days.

Ivy dislikes both extremes. Dry soil causes crisp brown leaves that drop, while soggy soil leads to root rot and the sudden collapse of whole stems. The plant also prefers cooler conditions than most houseplants — around 15 to 21°C — and struggles in hot, dry rooms.

Humidity above 40% helps considerably, and low humidity is the primary reason indoor ivy attracts spider mites. This is the pest that kills more indoor ivy than any cultural problem, and it is essentially a symptom of dry air.
soil: A standard well-draining potting mix with added perlite works well. Ivy is not fussy about medium but does want drainage; it grows in ordinary garden soil outdoors but rots in a pot that stays wet.

Feed monthly at half strength through spring and summer, stopping in winter. Ivy is a vigorous grower and responds well to feeding during the growing season, but over-fertilising produces soft growth that is more attractive to pests. Flush the pot with plain water occasionally to clear accumulated salts.

propagation: English ivy roots very readily from stem cuttings, and spring or summer cuttings establish fastest. Take a four to six inch section from a healthy vine, cutting just below a node, and strip the leaves from the lowest inch or two.

Stand the cuttings in water with the bare nodes submerged, in bright indirect light, changing the water weekly. Roots usually appear within two to three weeks. Alternatively, push cuttings directly into damp potting mix — dipping the cut end in rooting hormone first improves the strike rate for soil propagation, though it is not essential. Pot several rooted cuttings together for a full plant rather than growing them on singly. Ivy also layers naturally: pin a trailing stem down onto the surface of an adjacent pot and it will root where the nodes touch damp soil, after which you can sever it from the parent. Keep new cuttings out of direct sun and lightly moist until growth resumes.

problems.symptom: Fine webbing, stippled and dusty-looking leaves
problems.cause: Spider mites. This is by far the most common problem with indoor English ivy and is driven by dry, warm air.
problems.fix: Rinse the entire plant thoroughly in the shower, paying particular attention to leaf undersides, then treat with insecticidal soap or neem every five days for at least three cycles. Raise humidity and lower the temperature if you can — without that, they come straight back.

problems.symptom: Brown, crispy leaves, especially at the edges
problems.cause: Dry air, underwatering, or a position too close to a radiator.
problems.fix: Water more consistently, raise humidity, and move it to a cooler spot. Ivy is happier at 15-21°C than in a warm living room.

problems.symptom: Yellowing leaves, soil wet
problems.cause: Overwatering and poor drainage, leading to root rot.
problems.fix: Let the top inch dry properly between waterings and confirm the pot drains. Trim any soft brown roots and repot into fresh mix if rot has set in.

problems.symptom: Variegated leaves turning plain green
problems.cause: Too little light. The plant favours chlorophyll-rich tissue when energy is short.
problems.fix: Move to brighter indirect light and prune out fully green shoots to encourage variegated growth.

problems.symptom: Long bare vines with leaves only at the tips
problems.cause: Low light combined with a lack of pruning. Ivy naturally runs rather than branching unless cut back.
problems.fix: Prune the vines back hard in spring — ivy tolerates this well and branches from the cut nodes. Root the removed sections and add them to the pot to thicken the plant.

problems.symptom: Sudden collapse of a whole stem
problems.cause: Stem or root rot at soil level, usually from overwatering.
problems.fix: Cut the affected stem back to healthy tissue, let the mix dry out, and take cuttings from unaffected vines as insurance.

problems.symptom: Small brown bumps along stems and leaf veins
problems.cause: Scale insects, which are common on ivy and easy to miss against the woody stems.
problems.fix: Scrape them off with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol and follow with neem oil weekly for a month.

repotting: English ivy grows vigorously and usually needs repotting every one to two years, in spring. The signs are roots emerging from the drainage holes, water running straight through, and rapid drying between waterings.
Move up one pot size. Ivy suits hanging baskets and shelf positions where the vines can trail, so consider weight and balance when choosing a container. Loosen circling roots before replanting.

This is the right moment to prune hard if the plant has gone bare and leggy, and to root the trimmings back into the same pot. Water thoroughly afterwards and hold off fertiliser for a month. A congested root ball can also be divided into two plants at this stage.
varieties: Hedera helix has hundreds of named cultivars. 'Glacier' has grey-green leaves with white margins, 'Gold Child' carries yellow edging, and 'Needlepoint' has narrow, sharply lobed leaves. 'Duckfoot' and 'Teardrop' are small-leaved forms well suited to pots and terrariums.

Hedera canariensis, Algerian ivy, has larger leaves and is a related species with the same care needs. Two practical warnings: English ivy is toxic to cats and dogs, causing vomiting and drooling if eaten, and the sap irritates human skin for some people — gloves are sensible when pruning. It is also highly invasive outdoors in much of North America, so dispose of trimmings in household waste rather than composting them or planting them out.

light: Bird of paradise is a full-sun plant in its native South Africa and needs the brightest position you can offer indoors. Several hours of direct sun daily, ideally from a south or west-facing window, is what produces strong upright growth and the large paddle leaves.

This is not a low-light plant, despite sometimes being sold as one. In insufficient light it produces small leaves on long weak stems and will never flower. Indoor flowering requires a mature plant — typically four to five years old — in excellent light, and many indoor specimens never bloom at all, which is worth knowing before you buy one for the flowers.
water: Water thoroughly when the top two inches of mix have dried, letting water run from the drainage holes. In spring and summer, in a bright spot, that is usually every seven to ten days. These are large plants that transpire a lot of water in good light.

Reduce substantially in autumn and winter, to every two to three weeks. The combination of lower light and cooler temperatures means the mix stays wet far longer, and winter overwatering is the most common cause of root problems.

Bird of paradise appreciates humidity above 50% and shows dry air as browning leaf edges. It is also sensitive to salts and fluoride in tap water, which contribute to the same symptom, so filtered or rainwater is worth trying if edges keep browning despite good humidity.
soil: Use a rich, well-draining mix: roughly two parts quality potting compost to one part perlite and one part bark. The plant is a heavy feeder with vigorous thick roots and wants a medium with both substance and drainage.

Choose a sturdy, heavy pot — a mature bird of paradise is tall and top-heavy, and the root system is powerful enough to crack thin plastic. Feed every two to four weeks through spring and summer with a balanced fertiliser; this is one of the hungrier houseplants and responds visibly to regular feeding. Stop over winter.

propagation: Bird of paradise is propagated by division, which is the only practical home method. Seed is possible but germination is slow and erratic, and a seed-grown plant takes four to five years to reach flowering size.

Divide in spring, ideally while repotting a mature clump. Slide the plant out and look for natural divisions where a fan of leaves has its own rhizome and root mass. The roots are thick, fleshy and densely packed, so a clean sharp knife or even a saw is usually needed rather than teasing them apart. Each division needs at least a fan or two of leaves and a substantial share of roots. Pot into fresh rich mix, water well, and keep in bright indirect light rather than full sun for the first month while the cut roots heal. Expect the division to sulk for several weeks and possibly lose a leaf. Note that dividing sets back flowering considerably, so if your plant blooms, think twice before splitting it.

problems.symptom: Leaves splitting along their length
problems.cause: Entirely normal. The splits are an adaptation that lets wind pass through the large leaves in the wild, and indoor plants split as the leaves mature and are brushed against.
problems.fix: No action needed. Excessive splitting on young leaves can indicate low humidity or a plant in a high-traffic spot, so move it somewhere less brushed past if it bothers you.

problems.symptom: Brown, crispy leaf edges
problems.cause: Low humidity, salts and fluoride in tap water, or inconsistent watering.
problems.fix: Raise humidity, switch to filtered or rainwater, and flush the pot with plain water every few months. Water on a more regular schedule.

problems.symptom: Yellowing lower leaves
problems.cause: Overwatering if widespread and the mix is wet; normal ageing if it is the oldest leaf one at a time.
problems.fix: Let the top two inches dry between waterings, particularly in winter. Cut spent leaves off at the base.

problems.symptom: No flowers on a mature plant
problems.cause: Insufficient light is the usual reason, followed by insufficient feeding, too large a pot, or a plant that is simply not old enough.
problems.fix: Move it to the brightest available position and feed regularly through the growing season. Keep it slightly pot-bound, which encourages flowering. Be realistic: many indoor plants never flower.

problems.symptom: New leaves emerging small and pale
problems.cause: Too little light, a shortage of nutrients, or a root system that has outgrown its pot.
problems.fix: Increase light, feed through spring and summer, and repot if roots have filled the container.

problems.symptom: Fine webbing under leaves, stippled surfaces
problems.cause: Spider mites, which colonise the broad undersides where they go unnoticed for weeks.
problems.fix: Wipe both sides of every leaf, rinse the plant, and treat with insecticidal soap every five days for three cycles. Raising humidity discourages them.

problems.symptom: Leaves curling and drooping with wet soil
problems.cause: Root rot from overwatering, which prevents the roots taking up water even though the mix is saturated.
problems.fix: Unpot and inspect. Trim every soft brown root, repot into fresh free-draining mix, and water sparingly until new growth appears.

repotting: Repot every two to three years while the plant is building size, then less often. Bird of paradise has thick, vigorous roots that will visibly deform or split a plastic pot when it is genuinely ready.
Repot in spring into a pot one size larger, choosing something heavy and stable — a large specimen is top-heavy and a light pot will tip. Ceramic or a weighted planter is worth the investment.

There is a trade-off worth understanding: this plant flowers best when slightly pot-bound, so if flowering is your goal, resist moving it up too eagerly and top-dress with fresh compost instead. Water well after repotting and wait six weeks before feeding. For very large plants, replacing the top few inches of mix each spring is more practical than repotting at all.
varieties: Strelitzia reginae is the orange bird of paradise, reaching four to six feet indoors with the familiar orange and blue flowers. Strelitzia nicolai, the giant white bird of paradise, is much larger — easily reaching the ceiling — with white and blue flowers and broader leaves; it is the one most often sold as a large architectural houseplant and it very rarely flowers indoors.

Strelitzia juncea has narrow, almost reed-like leaves and a sculptural habit. All Strelitzia are toxic to cats and dogs, with the flowers and seeds being the most hazardous parts. Given the size these plants reach, the practical constraint indoors is usually ceiling height and light, not care difficulty.

light: Dracaena marginata tolerates medium light and grows best in bright indirect light. It is one of the more shade-tolerant tall houseplants, which is why it appears so often in offices, but growth in dim conditions is slow and the stems stretch toward the window.

Keep it out of direct sun, which bleaches the narrow leaves and produces dry brown patches. The red-edged varieties hold their colour better in bright light; in shade the margins dull toward green. Rotate the pot every few weeks, because this plant leans noticeably toward its light source and develops a permanent bend if left facing one way.
water: Let the top two inches of mix dry out before watering. In spring and summer that usually means every ten to fourteen days, which is less often than most people expect from a plant this size. Dracaenas store water in their thick canes and are considerably more drought-tolerant than they look.
In winter, extend to every three to four weeks. Overwatering is the dominant cause of failure, showing first as yellowing lower leaves and soft stem bases.

Water quality is the other critical factor. Dracaenas are among the most fluoride-sensitive houseplants, and fluoridated tap water produces the dead brown leaf tips that almost every specimen eventually develops. Use filtered, distilled or rainwater and the problem largely disappears. Average humidity is fine, though above 40% is preferred.
soil: A standard well-draining potting mix with added perlite suits it. Avoid anything heavy or peat-dense that holds water around the roots, and avoid mixes containing superphosphate, which is a fluoride source.

Feed only every two months at half strength through spring and summer, and not at all in winter. Dracaenas are light feeders and sensitive to salt accumulation, which compounds the tip-burn problem. Flush the pot thoroughly with clean water two or three times a year to wash out what does build up.

propagation: Dracaena marginata propagates easily from cane cuttings, and this doubles as the way to deal with a plant that has grown too tall and bare. The plant regrows from the cut stump, so pruning and propagating are the same operation.

In spring, cut the cane wherever you want the plant to branch, using clean sharp secateurs. The stump will sprout two or three new shoots from just below the cut within a few weeks, making the parent bushier. The section you removed can be cut into pieces four to six inches long — keep track of which end was up, because a cutting planted upside down will not root. Stand the top cutting with its leaf rosette in water or damp mix; bare cane sections can be laid horizontally on damp mix or stood upright. Roots take three to six weeks in warmth and bright indirect light. Sealing the cut end of the parent with wax is sometimes recommended but is not necessary indoors.

problems.symptom: Brown, dry leaf tips on almost every leaf
problems.cause: Fluoride in tap water is the classic cause for this genus, with salt buildup and dry air contributing.
problems.fix: Switch to filtered, distilled or rainwater and flush the pot with clean water a few times a year. Trim the brown section at an angle, leaving a thin margin of dead tissue so you do not cut into living leaf.

problems.symptom: Yellowing lower leaves dropping steadily
problems.cause: Overwatering if widespread and the mix is damp. Losing the occasional lowest leaf as the cane grows taller is entirely normal for this species.
problems.fix: Extend the watering interval and check the pot drains. A bare lower cane with a tuft of leaves on top is the natural habit, not a fault.

problems.symptom: Soft, mushy cane at soil level
problems.cause: Stem rot from waterlogged soil, often after a winter of unchanged watering.
problems.fix: Cut the cane back above the rot into firm white tissue and root the healthy top as a cutting. The lower section is rarely salvageable once soft. Repot into fresh, faster-draining mix.

problems.symptom: Pale or bleached patches on the leaves
problems.cause: Direct sun through glass.
problems.fix: Move back from the window or filter the light. Scorched tissue does not recover; remove the worst leaves as new growth replaces them.

problems.symptom: Canes leaning heavily to one side
problems.cause: Phototropism — the plant is growing toward its light source — combined with not being rotated.
problems.fix: Rotate the pot a quarter turn every couple of weeks. An established bend will not straighten, but you can prune the cane and let it regrow upright.

problems.symptom: Fine webbing between leaves in the crown
problems.cause: Spider mites, which favour the tight rosette at the top of each cane.
problems.fix: Rinse the crown thoroughly in the shower and treat with insecticidal soap every five days for three cycles.

problems.symptom: Small brown bumps along canes and leaf undersides
problems.cause: Scale insects, well camouflaged against the woody cane.
problems.fix: Scrape them off with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol and follow with neem oil weekly for a month.

repotting: Dracaenas grow slowly and are happy pot-bound, so repot only every two to three years. The signals are roots circling the surface or through the drainage holes, and water running straight through without wetting the mix.
Repot in spring into a pot one size larger, choosing something heavy — a tall dracaena is top-heavy and light plastic tips easily. Loosen circling roots and trim any that are soft and brown.

For a large specimen that has outgrown practical repotting, top-dress instead: scrape off the top two or three inches of mix and replace with fresh compost each spring. Water well after repotting and hold off on fertiliser for two months.
varieties: Dracaena marginata has narrow green leaves with thin red margins. 'Tricolor' adds a cream stripe for a green, cream and pink effect and needs brighter light. 'Colorama' is dominated by broad red margins, is the most light-hungry of the three, and reverts toward green in shade.

'Bicolor' sits between the plain species and Tricolor. Related dracaenas worth knowing include the corn plant, with broad strappy leaves on thick canes, and 'Janet Craig', a solid deep green. All Dracaena species are toxic to cats and dogs, and cats in particular are attracted to the thin arching leaves — ingestion causes vomiting, drooling and dilated pupils in cats specifically.

light: Croton needs a lot of light — this is the entire basis of its reputation for difficulty. The vivid red, orange and yellow colouring only develops and persists in bright light, including several hours of direct sun. A south or west-facing window is usually required.

In insufficient light the plant does not die; it simply turns green. New leaves emerge without the colour that made you buy it, and the plant becomes leggy. If your croton is greening up, light is the answer and nothing else will fix it. Introduce strong sun gradually to a plant that has been in dimmer conditions, since abrupt changes cause leaf drop.
water: Keep the mix evenly moist through spring and summer, watering when the top inch is dry — usually every five to seven days. Croton dislikes drying out completely and responds to drought by dropping leaves, often dramatically.

Reduce to every ten to fourteen days in winter, but still do not let the root ball go bone dry. The balance to strike is consistently moist without being soggy; both extremes cause the same symptom of leaf drop.

Humidity above 50% is important. Croton is a tropical shrub and dry indoor air, particularly in winter, is the main trigger for both leaf drop and spider mites. A humidifier makes a visible difference. Keep it away from draughts and cold windows — it resents temperatures below about 15°C.
soil: Use a rich, well-draining potting mix with added perlite — roughly three parts compost to one part perlite. The plant wants moisture retention with free drainage.

Feed every two to four weeks through spring and summer with a balanced fertiliser at half strength. Crotons are moderately hungry and good feeding supports the strong colouring. Stop completely in autumn and winter. Make sure the pot drains; croton roots rot in standing water.

propagation: Croton propagates from stem cuttings taken in spring or early summer, and warmth is the deciding factor in whether they root. Take a tip cutting four to six inches long with three or four leaves, cutting just below a node.

The cut bleeds a milky latex that irritates skin — wear gloves and rinse the cut end until it stops before potting. Remove the lowest leaves, dip the end in rooting hormone, and insert into damp, free-draining mix. Cover with a clear bag or propagator to hold humidity, and keep it somewhere genuinely warm; croton cuttings root poorly below about 21°C. Bright indirect light rather than direct sun while rooting. Expect four to eight weeks. Air layering is the more reliable option for a tall, leggy plant and produces a large plant immediately: wound the stem, pack damp sphagnum moss around it inside a plastic sleeve, and cut below the roots once they fill the moss.

problems.symptom: Sudden dropping of many leaves
problems.cause: The signature croton behaviour. Triggered by any abrupt change — being brought home from the shop, a move, a cold draught, or the soil drying out completely.
problems.fix: Settle it in one bright, warm, draught-free position and keep watering consistent. Some drop after purchase is normal and the plant usually recovers. Resist moving it again while it adjusts.

problems.symptom: New leaves coming in plain green
problems.cause: Not enough light. Colour production requires high light levels.
problems.fix: Move to the brightest window available, increasing exposure gradually. Existing green leaves will not colour up, but new growth will come in correctly.

problems.symptom: Fine webbing, stippled dull leaves
problems.cause: Spider mites, the most common croton pest, driven by dry air.
problems.fix: Rinse the whole plant thoroughly including leaf undersides, treat with insecticidal soap every five days for three cycles, and fix the humidity — otherwise they return immediately.

problems.symptom: Brown, crispy leaf edges and tips
problems.cause: Low humidity or underwatering, often combined with a position near a radiator.
problems.fix: Raise humidity, water more consistently, and move away from heat sources.

problems.symptom: Leaves wilting despite damp soil
problems.cause: Root rot from overwatering or poor drainage.
problems.fix: Check the roots, trim anything soft and brown, and repot into fresh free-draining mix. Water sparingly until new growth resumes.

problems.symptom: Leggy stems with leaves only at the tips
problems.cause: Insufficient light combined with no pruning.
problems.fix: Increase light and prune back by a third in spring. Croton branches readily from below the cut, and the removed sections can be rooted or air-layered.

problems.symptom: Pale, washed-out or scorched leaf patches
problems.cause: Sunburn after an abrupt move into strong direct sun.
problems.fix: Increase sun exposure gradually over two to three weeks rather than all at once. Remove badly scorched leaves.

repotting: Repot every one to two years in spring while the plant is growing, then less often. Signs are roots through the drainage holes and water running straight through the pot.
Move up one size only. Croton dislikes root disturbance and often drops leaves after repotting, so handle the root ball gently and keep disturbance minimal. Expect a sulk regardless.

Water thoroughly afterwards, keep humidity high and the plant out of direct sun for a couple of weeks while it recovers, then return it to full light. Do not fertilise for six weeks. If it starts shedding after repotting, hold your nerve and keep conditions stable rather than intervening further.
varieties: Codiaeum variegatum has dozens of named forms distinguished mainly by leaf shape. 'Petra' is the common one, with broad oval leaves veined in yellow, orange and red. 'Mammy' has narrow twisting leaves in deep reds and purples. 'Gold Dust' is green speckled with yellow and is among the more shade-tolerant.

'Zanzibar' has very narrow, almost grassy leaves in mixed colours. All crotons are toxic to cats and dogs, and the milky sap irritates human skin and can stain — gloves are worth wearing for pruning. The sap is also the reason this plant should be kept away from children who might break a leaf.

light: Ponytail palm wants bright light, including several hours of direct sun. It is not a palm at all but a succulent from the semi-desert of eastern Mexico, and it is adapted to open, exposed conditions. A south or west-facing window is the right position.

It tolerates medium light, where it simply grows very slowly and produces fewer new leaves. It will not thrive in a dim corner despite occasionally being sold as low-light tolerant. In good light the caudex — the swollen bulb at the base — thickens faster, which is the feature most people grow it for.
water: This is the most drought-tolerant plant most people will own. The caudex is a water store, and a mature ponytail palm can go a month or more without water. Water deeply, then let the mix dry out completely — all the way through — before watering again.
In spring and summer that is typically every three to four weeks. In winter, every six to eight weeks is often sufficient, and in a cool room it can go longer still.

Overwatering is essentially the only way to kill this plant. A soft, squashy caudex means rot and is usually terminal by the time it is noticeable. When in doubt, do not water. Humidity is irrelevant; dry household air is exactly right.
soil: Use a cactus or succulent mix, or two parts potting compost to one part coarse sand and grit. It must drain fast and dry out fully between waterings.

Terracotta is strongly preferable, and the pot should be wide rather than deep, since the roots are shallow relative to the size of the caudex. Choose a snug pot: ponytail palms genuinely prefer being tight, and excess soil around a small root system stays wet. Feed at most two or three times across spring and summer with a half-strength succulent feed, and never in winter.

propagation: Ponytail palm is propagated from offsets, and only from offsets — there is no way to root a cutting of the leaves or the caudex. Mature plants occasionally produce pups around the base of the trunk, though many never do, and a plant that has never offset cannot be forced.

When a pup is at least four inches tall and has begun developing its own roots, you can separate it. In spring, unpot the parent, brush the soil away and locate the join. Cut the pup away with a clean sharp knife, taking as much of its own root as possible, and let the cut surfaces dry and callus for several days in a shaded spot — this step is essential, and potting a fresh wound into soil reliably causes rot. Then plant in dry cactus mix and wait a week or more before the first light watering. Keep the pup in bright indirect light rather than full sun until it is established. Growth is slow: expect years, not months, for a pup to develop a noticeable caudex.

problems.symptom: Caudex soft or squashy to the touch
problems.cause: Rot from overwatering. This is the one serious problem this plant has, and it is almost always advanced by the time it is felt.
problems.fix: Unpot immediately, cut away all soft tissue back to firm material, dust with sulphur if you have it, and let it dry for several days before repotting in dry gritty mix. Recovery depends entirely on how much firm caudex remains.

problems.symptom: Brown, crispy leaf tips
problems.cause: Normal on older leaves, but widespread browning indicates dry air, fluoride in tap water, or a long drought.
problems.fix: Trim the brown tips at an angle for appearance. Water more regularly if the mix has been dry for months, and try filtered water if tips keep browning.

problems.symptom: Leaves yellowing and drooping from the base
problems.cause: Overwatering if the mix is damp, or natural shedding of the oldest leaves as the plant grows.
problems.fix: Check the soil and extend the watering interval. Pull off spent lower leaves; a slightly bare stem below the ponytail is the natural habit.

problems.symptom: Very little new growth for a year or more
problems.cause: Low light, or simply the plant's natural pace. Ponytail palms are slow even in ideal conditions.
problems.fix: Move to the brightest position available and feed lightly in summer. Do not respond by watering more, which is the common and damaging mistake.

problems.symptom: Leaves pale and washed-out
problems.cause: Either too little light over a long period, or scorching from an abrupt move into intense sun.
problems.fix: Adjust position accordingly, increasing light gradually if moving it into a sunnier spot.

problems.symptom: White cottony clusters where leaves meet the trunk
problems.cause: Mealybugs, which shelter in the dense crown and among the leaf bases.
problems.fix: Dab with rubbing alcohol on a cotton bud and inspect weekly for a month. The crown gives them good cover, so be thorough.

problems.symptom: Small flies around the pot
problems.cause: Fungus gnats, which indicate the mix is being kept far too damp for this species.
problems.fix: Let the soil dry out completely and extend the watering interval substantially. A gritty top dressing discourages them.

repotting: Ponytail palms need repotting rarely — every three to five years at most. They actively prefer being pot-bound, and a snug pot helps keep the mix dry. The usual prompt is the caudex physically filling the container.
Repot in spring into a pot only slightly larger, wide rather than deep, and heavy enough to balance a top-heavy plant. Terracotta suits it well.

Plant at the same depth — burying the caudex deeper than it was growing is a common mistake and leads directly to rot. Use dry mix and wait at least a week before watering. Skip fertiliser for a couple of months afterwards.
varieties: Beaucarnea recurvata is the species, and there are no widely sold cultivars. What varies is form: single-trunk plants are the most common, while multi-headed specimens with two or three ponytails from one caudex are sold as a premium.

Beaucarnea guatemalensis is a close relative with a reddish tint to new growth. The plant is also sold as elephant's foot palm or bottle palm, and is sometimes mislabelled as Nolina recurvata, an older synonym. Ponytail palm is non-toxic to cats and dogs, which along with its extreme drought tolerance makes it one of the most practical plants for a pet household or for someone who travels frequently.

light: Prayer plant grows on the rainforest floor in Brazil and wants medium indirect light, well away from direct sun. Morning light from an east window is ideal; a north window works too. Direct sun bleaches the markings and scorches the thin leaves quickly.

In light that is too low the plant survives but the leaf patterning loses contrast and growth slows to nothing. The nightly folding movement that gives the plant its name — leaves rising and closing at dusk, opening flat again by morning — is driven by light cycles, so a plant in a room with lights on late may fold less predictably.
water: Keep the mix evenly moist at all times, watering when the top half-inch feels dry. Through spring and summer that is usually every four to six days. Prayer plant will not tolerate drying out completely and responds to drought with crisping edges and curled leaves.
Reduce slightly in winter to every seven to ten days, but never let the root ball go dry. Equally, do not leave it soggy — the aim is consistent light moisture.

Like its calathea relatives, Maranta is sensitive to fluoride, chlorine and dissolved salts. Hard tap water produces brown leaf edges that no amount of humidity will fix. Use filtered, distilled or rainwater, and use lukewarm rather than cold water, which this plant dislikes. Humidity above 50% is genuinely needed.
soil: Use a moisture-retentive but airy mix — two parts peat or coir-based compost to one part perlite. The roots are shallow and fine, and want consistent dampness without compaction.

A shallow, wide pot suits the root system better than a deep one. Plastic or glazed ceramic holds moisture better than terracotta, which dries too fast for this plant. Feed at quarter to half strength every three to four weeks through spring and summer only, and flush the pot with clean water every couple of months to prevent salt buildup.

propagation: Prayer plant propagates readily by division and by stem cuttings, which makes it considerably easier than calathea despite the similar appearance.

For division, unpot in spring and separate the clump where natural sections with their own roots and stems come apart. Each division needs several leaves and a decent root share. Pot into fresh moist mix and keep warm, shaded and humid for a few weeks. For cuttings, take a section of stem just below a node — Maranta, unlike Calathea, does have true nodes along trailing stems — with two or three leaves attached. Root in water, changing it weekly, or straight into damp mix under a clear bag. Roots appear in two to four weeks. Potting several rooted cuttings together produces a full plant much faster than growing one on alone. Warmth and humidity are what determine success.

problems.symptom: Brown, crispy leaf edges
problems.cause: Minerals in tap water, low humidity, or salt buildup from fertiliser — usually a combination.
problems.fix: Switch to filtered, distilled or rainwater, raise humidity above 50%, and flush the pot with clean water every couple of months. Trim damaged edges following the leaf shape.

problems.symptom: Leaves curling and not opening flat
problems.cause: Underwatering or low humidity. A prayer plant that stays closed during the day is stressed rather than resting.
problems.fix: Check the soil and water if the top half-inch is dry. Raise humidity. Leaves usually resume their normal daily rhythm within a week of conditions improving.

problems.symptom: Yellowing leaves with wet soil
problems.cause: Overwatering leading to root rot in the fine shallow root system.
problems.fix: Confirm the pot drains and is not standing in water. Let the top half-inch dry before each watering. Trim soft brown roots and repot if rot is present.

problems.symptom: Faded patterning and washed-out colour
problems.cause: Too much light, usually direct sun.
problems.fix: Move to a shadier position. Existing faded leaves stay as they are, but new growth comes in properly marked.

problems.symptom: Leggy stems with bare stretches
problems.cause: Too little light, or simply a mature plant that has not been pruned.
problems.fix: Increase light moderately and pinch back the trailing stems, which encourages branching at the nodes. The trimmings root easily and can go back into the same pot.

problems.symptom: Fine webbing under the leaves
problems.cause: Spider mites, drawn by dry air — the most common prayer plant pest.
problems.fix: Rinse thoroughly, treat with insecticidal soap every five days for three cycles, and address the humidity, which is the underlying cause.

problems.symptom: Leaf tips brown despite good humidity and filtered water
problems.cause: Cold water or cold draughts. Maranta is sensitive to temperature shocks.
problems.fix: Water with room-temperature or lukewarm water and move the plant away from draughty windows and doors.

repotting: Repot every one to two years in spring. Prayer plant has a shallow, spreading root system that fills a pot sideways rather than downwards, so look for roots at the surface rather than through the drainage holes.
Choose a wide, shallow pot one size larger, in plastic or glazed ceramic to retain moisture. Disturb the fine roots as little as possible; loosen the outer edge and leave the core intact.

Water with filtered water at room temperature, keep humidity high for a few weeks, and do not feed for six weeks. This is the natural moment to divide a crowded clump, which also rejuvenates a plant that has become bare in the centre.
varieties: Maranta leuconeura 'Erythroneura', the herringbone plant, has deep green leaves with bright red veins and a pale central band — the most widely sold form. 'Kerchoveana', sometimes called rabbit's foot, has pale green leaves with dark brown blotches that fade with age.

'Massangeana' has silver-grey central markings and darker foliage. Prayer plant is often confused with calathea and stromanthe, all in the same family; the practical difference is that Maranta trails and roots from nodes, while Calathea grows upright from a rhizome and cannot be propagated by cuttings. All Maranta are non-toxic to cats and dogs, which makes them a good pet-safe alternative to the many toxic trailing plants.

light: Cast iron plant earns its name. It tolerates deeper shade than virtually any other houseplant, including north-facing rooms, dim hallways and corners several metres from a window. Low light is where it is genuinely useful rather than merely surviving.

It prefers medium indirect light, where growth is faster, but the difference is modest. What it will not tolerate is direct sun, which scorches and bleaches the broad leaves within days — an unusual sensitivity for such a tough plant. Keep it well away from south-facing glass.
water: Water when the top inch or two of mix has dried, which in spring and summer typically means every ten to fourteen days. In low light and in winter, every three to four weeks is often enough.

This is a slow-growing plant that uses water slowly, and overwatering is the main way it is killed. It tolerates drought far better — a forgotten cast iron plant recovers from weeks of dryness without complaint.

Average household humidity is fine. The plant is not sensitive to dry air in the way ferns and calatheas are. It does show fluoride and salt damage as brown leaf tips over time, so flushing the pot occasionally and using filtered water is worthwhile if your supply is hard.
soil: Any decent well-draining potting mix works. Add a handful of perlite for insurance against overwatering. Aspidistra is not fussy about medium — it is the drainage that matters.

Feed only two or three times across spring and summer at half strength. This is a genuinely slow grower and cannot use much fertiliser; excess accumulates as salts and burns the leaf tips. No feeding at all in autumn and winter. Make sure the pot has working drainage holes and is not sitting inside a cachepot collecting water.

propagation: Cast iron plant is propagated by division only. It grows from a slowly creeping underground rhizome that sends up individual leaves, so there is no stem to cut and a detached leaf will not root.

Divide in spring. Slide the plant out of its pot and examine the rhizome: it looks like a knobbly horizontal root running through the soil, with leaves emerging at intervals. Cut it into sections with a clean sharp knife, making sure each piece has at least two or three leaves and a good share of roots. Smaller pieces will survive but take years to look like anything. Pot each division into fresh mix at the same depth, water lightly, and put them somewhere shaded and warm. Expect very slow establishment — new growth may not appear for several months, which is normal for this species and not a sign of failure. Patience is the whole technique.

problems.symptom: Brown, scorched patches on leaves
problems.cause: Direct sunlight. Despite its toughness in every other respect, Aspidistra burns readily in sun.
problems.fix: Move it out of direct light entirely. Damaged leaves will not recover; cut them off at the base as new growth replaces them.

problems.symptom: Yellowing leaves
problems.cause: Overwatering in most cases, particularly in low light or winter when the plant is using very little.
problems.fix: Extend the watering interval substantially and confirm the pot drains. One older leaf yellowing occasionally is normal.

problems.symptom: Brown leaf tips
problems.cause: Fluoride or salts in tap water, or fertiliser buildup in a plant that has been fed too generously.
problems.fix: Flush the pot with clean water, reduce feeding to two or three times a year, and try filtered water. Trim tips at an angle.

problems.symptom: No new growth for a long time
problems.cause: Usually just the plant's pace — cast iron plant is one of the slowest houseplants and may produce only a handful of new leaves a year. Deep shade slows it further.
problems.fix: Move somewhere with a little more indirect light and feed lightly in spring. Otherwise accept the pace; this is not a plant for people who want visible progress.

problems.symptom: Soft, mushy leaf bases at soil level
problems.cause: Rhizome rot from prolonged wet soil.
problems.fix: Unpot, cut away soft sections of rhizome back to firm tissue, and repot healthy pieces into fresh mix. Water sparingly afterwards.

problems.symptom: Small brown bumps on leaves and stems
problems.cause: Scale insects, which are the most common pest on this otherwise trouble-free plant.
problems.fix: Scrape them off with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol, then treat with neem oil weekly for a month.

problems.symptom: Dusty, dull-looking leaves
problems.cause: Dust accumulation on the broad leaf surfaces, which in a low-light position measurably reduces the light reaching the plant.
problems.fix: Wipe both sides with a damp cloth every few weeks. For a plant in deep shade this genuinely matters rather than being merely cosmetic.

repotting: Cast iron plant is slow and resents disturbance, so repot only every three to five years, or when the rhizomes have completely filled the pot and are pushing the plant upward.

Repot in spring into a pot one size larger. This plant flowers and grows best when slightly crowded, so there is no advantage in moving it up early. Handle the rhizomes carefully and set them at the same depth.

Water lightly afterwards and expect a long pause before new growth appears — six months is not unusual. Do not fertilise for a couple of months. Division is best done at this point if the clump has become dense.
varieties: Aspidistra elatior is the standard, with plain deep green strappy leaves. 'Variegata' carries irregular cream stripes and needs a little more light than the plain form to hold them. 'Milky Way' is speckled with small white dots and is one of the more decorative forms.

'Asahi' produces leaves that emerge green and develop white tips as they mature. Cast iron plant is non-toxic to cats and dogs, and combined with its tolerance of deep shade, neglect and irregular watering, it is arguably the single most practical plant for a dark pet household — provided you accept how slowly it grows.

light: Peperomia Hope wants bright indirect light. The small round leaves are semi-succulent and hold up well in a bright spot, but direct afternoon sun scorches them and fades the subtle striping. An east window, or a position near a south or west window behind a sheer curtain, suits it well.

In low light the trailing stems stretch, leaves space out along bare stem, and the plant loses the dense, compact look that makes it attractive. This is the commonest reason a Peperomia Hope disappoints — it is not dying, it is simply reaching for light.
water: The thick leaves store water, so treat this as a semi-succulent rather than a typical tropical. Let the top inch or two dry out before watering, then water thoroughly and drain completely. In spring and summer that is usually every ten to fourteen days.

Reduce to every three weeks or so in winter. Overwatering is by far the most common cause of failure and shows as sudden stem collapse rather than gradual decline — by the time you notice, the base is often already rotten.

Peperomias have small, fine root systems relative to their foliage, which is why they rot so readily in soil that stays wet. Average household humidity is fine; they do not need the 60% that calatheas demand, though they appreciate a little extra.
soil: Use a light, airy mix that drains fast — two parts standard potting compost to one part perlite, with a little orchid bark. Many growers use a chunky aroid-style mix successfully.

Choose a small pot. The root system is modest and an oversized pot holds a reservoir of wet soil the plant cannot use, which is the direct route to rot. Terracotta helps. Feed monthly at half strength through spring and summer only; peperomias are light feeders and over-fertilising causes leaf drop.

propagation: Peperomia Hope is very easy to propagate from stem cuttings, and this is the standard way to refill a plant that has gone leggy.

Take a stem cutting three to four inches long with two or three whorls of leaves, cutting just below a node. Strip the lowest whorl so the node is bare. Root either in water, keeping the node submerged and changing the water weekly, or directly in damp mix. Roots appear within two to three weeks. Because the stems are somewhat brittle and prone to rotting in water if left too long, soil propagation is often the more reliable route for this species. Single leaf cuttings also work: take a leaf with a short piece of petiole attached and insert the petiole into damp mix — a plantlet forms at the base after a month or two, though this is slower than stem cuttings. Pot several rooted cuttings together for a full plant, and tuck extras back into the parent pot to thicken it.

problems.symptom: Stems suddenly collapsing at the base
problems.cause: Stem rot from overwatering. Peperomias fail abruptly rather than gradually, and this is the classic presentation.
problems.fix: Take healthy cuttings from the upper stems immediately as insurance. Unpot, cut away all soft tissue, and repot healthy sections into fresh airy mix in a smaller pot. Water far less often afterwards.

problems.symptom: Leaves dropping at a touch
problems.cause: Overwatering most commonly, occasionally severe drought or a sudden cold draught.
problems.fix: Check the soil. Wet means stop watering and inspect the roots; bone dry means water thoroughly and the shedding should stop.

problems.symptom: Leaves wrinkled and soft
problems.cause: Underwatering — the plant is drawing on the water stored in its leaves.
problems.fix: Water thoroughly until it drains. Leaves firm up within a few days. Easier to correct than the opposite problem.

problems.symptom: Long bare stems with widely spaced leaves
problems.cause: Insufficient light. The stems stretch toward the window.
problems.fix: Move to brighter indirect light and pinch the stems back. Peperomia branches from the cut, and the trimmings root easily to fill the pot.

problems.symptom: Pale or bleached leaves
problems.cause: Too much direct sun, which the semi-succulent leaves scorch under.
problems.fix: Move back from the glass or filter the light. Damaged leaves do not recover.

problems.symptom: Small flies around the pot
problems.cause: Fungus gnats in soil kept too damp — a strong sign the watering routine is wrong for this plant.
problems.fix: Let the mix dry out properly between waterings, use sticky traps, and consider repotting into a grittier mix and a smaller pot.

problems.symptom: Corky brown bumps on leaf undersides
problems.cause: Oedema — cells rupturing after the plant took up water faster than it could use it, typically from heavy watering in low light.
problems.fix: Water less and increase light. The marks are permanent on affected leaves but harmless, and new growth comes in clean.

repotting: Peperomias have small root systems and like being snug, so repot only every two to three years, or when roots have genuinely filled the pot.

Move up one small size — and resist going larger. Overpotting is the single most common mistake with this genus, because the excess soil stays wet and the fine roots rot. Terracotta in a small size is ideal.

Repot in spring into fresh airy mix, handle the brittle stems carefully, and water lightly afterwards. Wait six weeks before feeding. This is a good moment to tuck rooted cuttings into the pot to thicken a plant that has grown sparse.
varieties: Peperomia 'Hope' is a hybrid of P. deppeana and P. quadrifolia, with round leaves in whorls of three or four along trailing stems. Peperomia rotundifolia is similar but with smaller, thinner leaves and finer stems.

Related peperomias worth knowing include the watermelon peperomia, with striped teardrop leaves on red stems, the baby rubber plant with thick glossy oval leaves, and 'Rosso' with dark leaves and deep red undersides. The genus is large and care is broadly consistent across it. All peperomias are non-toxic to cats and dogs, which makes them one of the safest and most varied groups for a pet household.

light: Phalaenopsis wants bright indirect light and no direct sun. An east-facing window is close to ideal, giving gentle morning light. A north window works. South and west windows need a sheer curtain or the plant set well back.

The leaves are the best guide to whether light is right. A healthy Phalaenopsis has mid-green, slightly leathery leaves. Very dark green leaves mean too little light — the commonest reason an orchid never reflowers. Yellowish or reddish-tinged leaves mean too much. Adjusting light on that basis is more reliable than any rule about window direction.
water: This is where most Phalaenopsis are lost. They are epiphytes that grow on tree branches with their roots exposed to air, not in soil. Water thoroughly about once a week, letting water run right through the bark, then let the roots approach dryness before watering again.

The roots tell you when. Plump silvery-green roots are hydrated; silvery-white, slightly shrivelled roots need water. This is far more reliable than a schedule. In winter, watering every ten to fourteen days is usually right.

Never let the pot stand in water, and never leave water sitting in the crown between the leaves, which causes crown rot and kills the plant outright. The old advice about an ice cube a week is poor practice — it delivers too little water and chills tropical roots. Humidity of 50-70% is preferred, and a bathroom windowsill often suits them well.
soil: Phalaenopsis must not be grown in potting compost, which suffocates and rots the roots. Use a coarse orchid bark mix, optionally with some sphagnum moss, perlite or charcoal. The medium exists to anchor the plant and hold brief moisture, not to feed it.

Clear plastic orchid pots are genuinely useful: they let you see root colour and condition, and the roots themselves photosynthesise. Drainage and airflow are everything. Feed weakly and often — a quarter-strength balanced orchid fertiliser with every second watering during growth — and flush with plain water monthly to clear salts.

propagation: Phalaenopsis cannot be propagated by cuttings or division in the way most houseplants can, because it is a monopodial orchid: it grows from a single point and has no rhizome to split.

The practical home method is via keikis — baby plants that sometimes form on a flower spike node. A keiki appears as a small plantlet with its own leaves, then produces roots. Leave it attached until it has two or three roots at least two inches long, which usually takes several months. Then cut the spike an inch either side of the keiki with sterile scissors and pot it in fine bark, keeping humidity high while it establishes. Keikis are not guaranteed — many plants never produce one, and they are sometimes a stress response. Keiki paste applied to a node can induce one, though it diverts energy from flowering. Commercial propagation is by tissue culture, which is not practical at home.

problems.symptom: Leaves limp, wrinkled and leathery
problems.cause: Almost always root loss from overwatering rather than thirst. Dead roots cannot take up water, so the leaves dehydrate even in a damp pot.
problems.fix: Unpot and inspect. Healthy roots are firm and green or silver; dead ones are brown, hollow and squash flat. Trim all dead roots, repot into fresh bark, and water carefully. Recovery takes months.

problems.symptom: Flowers dropping soon after purchase
problems.cause: Normal if the blooms were already mature, or shock from the change in light, temperature and humidity between shop and home.
problems.fix: Settle it in a stable bright spot. A Phalaenopsis typically blooms for two to four months; once done, the flowers drop naturally and this is not a fault.

problems.symptom: No reflowering after a year
problems.cause: Insufficient light most often, or no temperature drop to trigger a spike.
problems.fix: Move somewhere brighter but still out of direct sun. Phalaenopsis need a period of cooler nights — around 15-18°C for a few weeks in autumn — to initiate a flower spike. A cooler room or a windowsill at night usually does it.

problems.symptom: Soft, brown, mushy centre where new leaves emerge
problems.cause: Crown rot from water sitting between the leaves.
problems.fix: This is often fatal. Tip the plant to drain any water immediately, dry the crown with kitchen paper, and keep it dry. Water into the bark only, never over the plant, and avoid watering in the evening.

problems.symptom: Yellowing lowest leaf
problems.cause: Normal. Phalaenopsis shed their oldest leaf periodically as they produce new ones from the top.
