problems.fix: Let the top inch dry between waterings and confirm drainage. Repot into a chunkier mix if the medium stays soggy.

problems.symptom: Leaves drooping though the soil is damp
problems.cause: Root rot preventing water uptake.
problems.fix: Take cuttings immediately as insurance, then unpot, trim soft roots, and repot into fresh airy mix.

problems.symptom: New growth pale or deformed
problems.cause: Nutrient shortage in a fast-growing plant, or a pot-bound root system.
problems.fix: Feed regularly through the growing season and repot if roots have filled the container. This plant grows fast enough to exhaust its mix within a year.

problems.symptom: Fine webbing under the leaves
problems.cause: Spider mites, encouraged by dry air.
problems.fix: Rinse thoroughly, treat with insecticidal soap every five days for three cycles, and raise humidity.

repotting: Repot every year in spring while the plant is young, then every two years. Tetrasperma grows fast enough that it commonly outgrows its pot within a single season.
Move up one pot size into fresh chunky aroid mix. Add or replace the moss pole at this point while the root ball is out — a taller pole is often the real reason to repot.

Guide the aerial roots onto the pole rather than trimming them. Water thoroughly, keep humidity up, and wait a month before feeding. This is also the moment to prune the vine back and replant cuttings to keep the pot dense.
varieties: Rhaphidophora tetrasperma is sold under several misleading names — mini monstera, Monstera minima, Philodendron Ginny — none of which are correct. It is neither a Monstera nor a Philodendron, though it belongs to the same aroid family and looks like a miniature Monstera deliciosa.

A variegated form with cream and white sections exists and is slow, expensive and more demanding. Related Rhaphidophora species include R. decursiva, with much larger deeply divided leaves, and R. hayi, a shingling plant that presses flat against surfaces. All Rhaphidophora are toxic to cats and dogs due to calcium oxalate crystals.

light: Money tree wants bright indirect light and tolerates medium light, where growth slows considerably. In its native Central American wetlands it grows as an understorey tree, so filtered light rather than full sun is what it expects.

An east window, or a few feet back from a south or west window, suits it well. Direct afternoon sun scorches the leaflets. Rotate the pot every few weeks — money trees lean toward light quite strongly, and since most are sold as braided trunks with a formal shape, an uneven crown spoils the look. Sudden changes in light cause leaf drop, so move it gradually if relocating.
water: Water thoroughly when the top two inches of mix are dry, letting water run from the drainage holes, then let it dry down again. In spring and summer that is usually every seven to ten days; in winter, every two to three weeks.
Money tree stores water in its swollen trunk base and is more tolerant of drought than of saturation. Overwatering is the main cause of failure and shows as yellowing leaves and a soft trunk.

Humidity above 50% is preferred and dry air shows as browning leaflet tips. A pebble tray helps. This plant is often sold in a decorative outer pot with no drainage — check, because water collecting invisibly at the bottom is the single most common reason money trees die.
soil: Use a well-draining potting mix with added perlite and a little sand — something closer to a cactus blend than a moisture-retentive compost. The trunk stores water, so the roots do not need the soil to.

Drainage holes are essential. Feed every four to six weeks at half strength through spring and summer, stopping in winter. Money trees are light feeders and over-fertilising causes leaf drop. A pot that is snug rather than roomy suits them; excess wet soil around the roots is the main risk.

propagation: Money tree propagates from stem cuttings, though with lower success rates than most houseplants and with one important caveat about appearance.

Take a cutting six inches long with several leaves, from a healthy stem, cutting just below a node in spring or early summer. Remove the lower leaves, dip the cut end in rooting hormone, and insert into damp free-draining mix. Cover with a clear bag to maintain humidity and keep warm in bright indirect light. Roots take four to eight weeks and not every cutting succeeds.

The caveat: a cutting grows as a single straight stem and will never develop the swollen trunk base or the braided form of a shop-bought plant. Braiding is done by growers who plant several young seedlings together and weave the flexible green stems while they are still pliable, tightening the braid as they grow. You can braid your own if you have several young plants with green stems, but once the trunks lignify the shape is fixed. Seed propagation produces the characteristic swollen base but seed is rarely available.

problems.symptom: Yellowing leaves dropping steadily
problems.cause: Overwatering most commonly, particularly if the plant sits in a decorative pot with no drainage.
problems.fix: Check for standing water in the outer pot immediately. Let the top two inches dry before watering and make sure water can escape. This alone fixes most struggling money trees.

problems.symptom: Sudden leaf drop after being moved
problems.cause: Shock from a change in light or temperature. Money trees are sensitive to relocation.
problems.fix: Settle it in one position away from draughts and keep care consistent. Recovery usually takes a few weeks. Avoid making further changes while it adjusts.

problems.symptom: Trunk soft or squashy
problems.cause: Trunk rot from chronic overwatering. Serious, and often advanced by the time it is noticeable.
problems.fix: Unpot immediately, cut away soft tissue to firm material, let it dry for several days, and repot in dry free-draining mix. Take stem cuttings as insurance. If several braided trunks are affected, the others may still be saved.

problems.symptom: Brown crispy leaflet tips
problems.cause: Low humidity, underwatering, or salts in tap water.
problems.fix: Raise humidity, water more consistently, and flush the pot with plain water every few months.

problems.symptom: Leggy stems with leaves only at the top
problems.cause: Insufficient light combined with no pruning.
problems.fix: Increase light and prune the crown back in spring. Money tree branches readily from below a cut, which is how the rounded canopy is maintained.

problems.symptom: One trunk in the braid dying while others are fine
problems.cause: Normal in braided specimens — the trunks compete and the weakest sometimes fails. Also a sign of localised rot.
problems.fix: Cut the dead trunk out at the base. The remaining trunks continue and the braid usually still looks acceptable. Check drainage in case rot is the cause.

problems.symptom: Fine webbing or cottony white spots
problems.cause: Spider mites or mealybugs, both drawn to the dense canopy and dry air.
problems.fix: Rinse the plant, wipe leaflets on both sides, and treat with insecticidal soap weekly for a month.

repotting: Repot every two to three years in spring. Money trees are moderate growers and prefer being slightly snug, so there is no benefit to frequent repotting.

Move up one pot size only into free-draining mix. A pot that is too large holds wet soil around the roots, which is the main hazard for this species. Make sure the new pot drains, and if you use a decorative outer pot, either drill it or remove the inner pot to water.
Handle the braided trunks carefully and set the plant at the same depth. Water thoroughly and wait six weeks before feeding. Expect some leaf drop after repotting as a stress response.
varieties: Pachira aquatica is the species, sold as money tree or Malabar chestnut. What varies commercially is the form: single-trunk plants, braided multi-stem specimens, and small bonsai-style plants with a pronounced swollen base.

A variegated form with cream-splashed leaflets exists and needs brighter light. The plant is closely associated with feng shui, where the five leaflets per stem and the braided trunk are said to be auspicious, which is why it is so commonly given as a gift. Pachira aquatica is non-toxic to cats and dogs, which together with its sculptural form makes it one of the better large statement plants for a pet household.

light: Lucky bamboo is not bamboo at all — it is Dracaena sanderiana, and it wants the same conditions as other dracaenas: bright indirect light, never direct sun.

It tolerates quite low light, which is why it survives on office desks, though growth slows and the leaves lose colour. Direct sun scorches the leaves and turns them yellow quickly. If your stalks are pale and the leaves yellowing at the tips, check for sun exposure before assuming it is a water problem. Rotate the container so the stalks grow straight rather than curving toward one side.
water: Lucky bamboo is usually grown in water rather than soil, and the water is where almost every problem starts. Keep the roots covered by one to two inches of water — no more — and change it completely every one to two weeks. Stale water is what turns stalks yellow and causes the slimy root rot this plant is prone to.

The critical point is water quality. Dracaena sanderiana is highly sensitive to chlorine and especially fluoride, and ordinary tap water causes brown, burnt leaf tips within weeks. Use filtered, distilled or rainwater, or leave tap water standing uncovered for 24 hours to let chlorine dissipate — though this does not remove fluoride.

If grown in soil, keep the mix consistently moist but not waterlogged, watering when the surface feels barely dry. Soil-grown plants are generally longer-lived and more robust than water-grown ones. Humidity above 40% is appreciated.
soil: In water culture, use clean pebbles or glass beads to hold the stalks upright, filling the container so the roots are submerged and the stalks are not. Rinse the pebbles when you change the water.

If growing in soil, use a well-draining potting mix with added perlite. Soil culture suits the plant better long term and produces stronger growth. Feed very sparingly either way — a single drop of liquid fertiliser diluted in the water every couple of months is plenty for water-grown plants, and a half-strength feed every two months for soil-grown ones. Over-feeding causes yellowing and algae.

propagation: Lucky bamboo propagates readily from stem cuttings, and the technique differs slightly from other dracaenas because of how the stalks are grown.

Look for an offshoot — a side shoot growing from the main stalk. Cut it off where it joins, leaving a short stub, and stand it in clean water. Roots appear within three to five weeks. Alternatively, cut a main stalk into sections, each with at least one node, keeping track of which end was up; a section planted upside down will not root.

Seal the top cut of the parent stalk with wax or a little paraffin to prevent rot and moisture loss — this is standard practice with lucky bamboo and worth doing. Keep new cuttings in filtered water in bright indirect light, changing it weekly. Once roots are two inches long, the cutting can continue in water or be potted into soil. Note that the spiral shapes sold commercially are produced by rotating the plant beside a light source over months, not by any genetic trait, so cuttings grow straight.

problems.symptom: Brown, burnt leaf tips
problems.cause: Fluoride and chlorine in tap water. This is the single most common lucky bamboo complaint.
problems.fix: Switch to filtered, distilled or rainwater immediately and change the water every one to two weeks. Trim the brown tips at an angle. New growth will be clean.

problems.symptom: Stalk turning yellow from the bottom up
problems.cause: Stale water, too much fertiliser, or direct sun. Yellowing that starts at the base usually means rot.
problems.fix: Remove the affected stalk from the arrangement so it does not contaminate the others. If only the lower portion is yellow, cut above it into green tissue and re-root the healthy top.

problems.symptom: Slimy roots and cloudy, smelly water
problems.cause: Bacterial rot from water left too long without changing.
problems.fix: Rinse the roots and pebbles thoroughly, trim any mushy roots, and refill with fresh filtered water. Change water every week thereafter. Discard badly affected stalks.

problems.symptom: Yellow leaves while the stalk stays green
problems.cause: Over-fertilising, too much light, or fluoride in the water.
problems.fix: Stop feeding, move out of direct sun, and switch to filtered water. Remove yellow leaves cleanly.

problems.symptom: Algae growing on the pebbles and container walls
problems.cause: Light reaching the water in a clear glass container, combined with nutrients from fertiliser.
problems.fix: Clean the container and pebbles thoroughly, reduce feeding, and consider an opaque container or one that keeps light off the water.

problems.symptom: No new growth for a long period
problems.cause: Low light, or a plant grown in water for years that has exhausted what water culture can provide.
problems.fix: Move somewhere brighter and feed very lightly. Potting into soil often revitalises a plant that has stalled in water after several years.

problems.symptom: Stalk soft and mushy
problems.cause: Rot, usually from stale water or from the stalk being submerged rather than just the roots.
problems.fix: Remove that stalk immediately. Keep water level below the stalk bases — only the roots should be submerged. Salvage healthy tops as cuttings.

repotting: For water-grown plants, there is no repotting as such, but the container should be emptied, rinsed and refilled with fresh water every one to two weeks, and the pebbles washed occasionally. This is the maintenance that keeps the plant alive.

Move a water-grown plant into soil every few years if it has stalled — many lucky bamboos decline after two or three years in water alone, and potting into a well-draining mix often revives them. Do this in spring, keeping the soil consistently moist for the first month while the water roots adapt.
For soil-grown plants, repot every two to three years into a pot one size larger, handling the roots gently and setting the stalks at the same depth.
varieties: Dracaena sanderiana is the species. What varies commercially is the arrangement rather than the plant: straight stalks, spirals, woven lattices and tiered towers are all produced by manipulating the growing plant next to a light source over months.

'Victory' has broader variegated leaves and 'Golden' has yellow-striped foliage. The number of stalks carries meaning in feng shui tradition — three for happiness, five for wealth, eight for growth — with four generally avoided. Important safety note: despite the name and its reputation as a gift plant, Dracaena sanderiana is toxic to cats and dogs, and cats are particularly affected. It is frequently assumed to be safe because true bamboo is; it is not.

light: Alocasia Polly wants bright indirect light. It grows under rainforest canopy in Southeast Asia, so it is adapted to filtered brightness rather than either deep shade or full sun.

An east window is ideal, or a position near a south or west window behind a sheer curtain. Direct sun scorches the thin, glossy leaves within days, leaving brown papery patches that do not heal. In light that is too low the plant produces fewer, smaller leaves and is far more likely to go dormant. Rotate the pot every couple of weeks, since the leaves orient toward light.
water: Keep the mix lightly and evenly moist, watering when the top inch is dry — usually every five to seven days in spring and summer. Alocasia wants consistent moisture but is very prone to root rot, so the balance is narrower than with most aroids.

Reduce substantially in autumn and winter. This is the critical seasonal point: alocasias naturally go dormant in winter, dropping some or even all of their leaves. A dormant plant uses almost no water, and continuing to water on a summer schedule rots the tuber. Water sparingly, keep the tuber just barely damp, and wait.

Humidity above 60% is genuinely required. Dry air produces brown crispy edges and is the main trigger for spider mites, which are the signature Alocasia pest. A humidifier is close to essential for good growth.
soil: Use a very chunky, free-draining aroid mix — equal parts orchid bark, perlite and coco coir, with little or no ordinary compost. Alocasia roots need air more than most aroids and rot quickly in dense wet soil.

The pot should be snug; these plants grow from a tuber with a modest root system, and an oversized pot holds wet mix. Drainage holes are essential. Feed monthly at half strength through spring and summer only, and stop entirely once growth slows in autumn. Feeding a dormant plant does nothing useful and contributes to salt buildup.

propagation: Alocasia Polly propagates by division of the tuber and by separating offsets, not by leaf or stem cuttings. A cut leaf will not root, because the growth points are all in the underground corm.

In spring, unpot the plant and wash the mix away from the roots so you can see what you are working with. You will find a main tuber with smaller offset corms attached — firm, brown, bulb-like structures, sometimes with their own small roots and shoots. Twist or cut these away cleanly.

Pot each offset just below the surface of damp chunky mix, or root them in damp sphagnum moss in a covered container, which many growers find more reliable. Keep warm — 24°C or above — and humid. Corms can take several weeks to months to sprout, and patience is required; a corm that has not sprouted is usually still viable as long as it is firm. Spring division is far more successful than autumn, when the plant is heading into dormancy.

problems.symptom: All leaves dying back in autumn or winter
problems.cause: Dormancy, which is normal for Alocasia and alarms most owners into over-caring for the plant.
problems.fix: Reduce watering to barely damp and stop feeding. Keep the pot somewhere warm and leave it alone. The tuber is alive and will resprout in spring. Do not discard the plant.

problems.symptom: Fine webbing, stippled and dull leaves
problems.cause: Spider mites, the signature Alocasia pest, driven by dry air.
problems.fix: Rinse the plant thoroughly including leaf undersides, then treat with insecticidal soap every five days for at least three cycles. Raise humidity above 60% — without that they return immediately.

problems.symptom: Yellowing leaves with wet soil
problems.cause: Overwatering and tuber rot, which is the main way Alocasia are killed.
problems.fix: Unpot and inspect the tuber. Firm and brown is healthy; soft and mushy is rot. Cut away rotten tissue, let it dry a day, and repot into fresh chunky mix. Water far more sparingly.

problems.symptom: Brown crispy leaf edges
problems.cause: Low humidity, or salts and chlorine in tap water.
problems.fix: Raise humidity, switch to filtered or rainwater, and flush the pot with clean water every couple of months.

problems.symptom: Water droplets forming at the leaf tips
problems.cause: Guttation — the plant releasing excess water through pores. Entirely normal, and often a sign of healthy root pressure, though it can indicate slight overwatering.
problems.fix: No action needed. If it happens constantly, ease back slightly on watering.

problems.symptom: New leaf emerges then an old one dies
problems.cause: Normal for Alocasia, which maintains a limited number of leaves and sheds an old one for each new one, especially when conditions are less than ideal.
problems.fix: Improve light, humidity and feeding to encourage the plant to hold more leaves at once. A well-grown Polly carries five or six.

problems.symptom: Brown papery patches on leaves
problems.cause: Sunburn from direct sun through glass.
problems.fix: Move out of direct light into filtered brightness. Damaged tissue does not recover.

repotting: Repot every one to two years in spring, as the plant comes out of dormancy and before active growth begins. Never repot a dormant plant in autumn.
Move up one small size only into fresh chunky aroid mix. Alocasia is prone to rot and an oversized pot makes that far more likely. Snug is better.

This is the natural moment to separate offset corms, which is easiest when the root ball is out and washed. Set the main tuber at the same depth, water lightly, and keep humidity high for a few weeks. Wait six weeks before feeding. Expect a pause before new growth appears.
varieties: Alocasia × amazonica 'Polly' is a compact hybrid with arrow-shaped dark leaves and bold white veining and scalloped margins. Despite the name it is not from the Amazon — it is a nursery hybrid.

Alocasia 'Amazonica' is the larger form of the same cross. A. zebrina has plain leaves on striking striped stems, A. frydek is velvety dark green with white veins, and A. macrorrhiza is the giant elephant ear. All Alocasia are toxic to cats and dogs, and notably so: the calcium oxalate content is high, causing intense mouth burning, swelling and drooling. This is one of the more seriously toxic common houseplants and is worth keeping well out of reach.

light: Calathea orbifolia wants medium to bright indirect light with no direct sun at all. The large round leaves scorch readily, and the silver banding bleaches out in strong light.

A north-facing window is often ideal, or a position well back from an east window. In light that is too low the leaves lose contrast, the plant stops producing new growth, and the stems stretch. Orbifolia is somewhat more forgiving about light than other calatheas — it is water and humidity that cause most of the trouble with this species.
water: Keep the mix evenly moist — never soggy, never dry. Water when the top half-inch feels dry, which in spring and summer usually means every five to seven days. Reduce to every ten days or so in winter but never let the root ball dry out completely.

Water quality is the decisive factor with orbifolia, more so than with almost any other houseplant. It is extremely sensitive to fluoride, chlorine and dissolved salts, and hard tap water produces the brown crispy edges this plant is notorious for. Use filtered, distilled or rainwater from the start; switching after damage appears only prevents further browning rather than fixing existing leaves.

Humidity of 60% or higher is genuinely required. The large thin leaves lose moisture fast, and this is not a plant that will do well in a dry room whatever else you get right. A humidifier is the realistic answer.
soil: Use a moisture-retentive but airy mix — two parts coir or peat-based compost to one part perlite, with a little fine bark. It should stay damp without compacting into a wet block.

Plastic or glazed ceramic pots hold moisture better than terracotta, which dries the root ball too fast. Drainage holes are still essential. Feed at quarter to half strength monthly through spring and summer only, and flush the pot with clean water every couple of months — orbifolia is as sensitive to fertiliser salts as it is to tap water.

propagation: Calathea orbifolia is propagated by division only. Stem and leaf cuttings will not root, because the plant grows from a clumping rhizome rather than from nodes — a cut leaf simply rots.

Divide in spring, ideally while repotting, and only once the plant has formed a substantial clump. Slide it out of the pot and gently wash or tease away the mix so you can see where rhizome sections separate naturally. Work them apart by hand where possible, using a clean knife only where necessary.

Each division needs its own roots and at least two or three leaves — smaller pieces rarely survive, and orbifolia is less forgiving of division than most calatheas. Pot each into fresh moisture-retentive mix, water with filtered water, and keep warm, shaded and very humid for the first month, ideally under a clear cover. Expect the divisions to sulk, droop and possibly drop a leaf before new growth begins. If your orbifolia is thriving, think carefully before dividing it — this species resents disturbance.

problems.symptom: Brown crispy leaf edges
problems.cause: The defining orbifolia complaint. Minerals in tap water, low humidity, or fertiliser salt buildup — usually all three.
problems.fix: Switch to filtered, distilled or rainwater, raise humidity to 60% or more with a humidifier, and flush the pot with clean water every couple of months. Trim damaged edges following the leaf's curve.

problems.symptom: Leaves curling inward along the midrib
problems.cause: Underwatering, low humidity, or too much light. Note that some folding at night is normal — calatheas raise their leaves in darkness.
problems.fix: Check the soil first. If dry, water. If moist and the curl persists in daylight, raise humidity and move out of direct light.

problems.symptom: Yellowing leaves with constantly wet soil
problems.cause: Overwatering and root rot.
problems.fix: Confirm the pot drains and is not standing in water. Let the top half-inch dry before each watering. Trim soft roots and repot if rot is present.

problems.symptom: Faded, washed-out silver banding
problems.cause: Too much light. Direct sun bleaches the pattern.
problems.fix: Move to a shadier position. Existing faded leaves stay as they are; new growth comes in properly marked.

problems.symptom: New leaves emerging smaller than older ones
problems.cause: Insufficient light, nutrients or humidity, or a pot-bound root system.
problems.fix: Improve humidity first, then check light and feeding. Repot in spring if roots have filled the container.

problems.symptom: Fine webbing under the leaves
problems.cause: Spider mites, which thrive in exactly the dry air that also causes brown edges.
problems.fix: Rinse thoroughly, paying attention to the undersides, then treat with insecticidal soap every five days for three cycles. Fixing humidity is what stops them returning.

problems.symptom: Whole plant drooping
problems.cause: Either thirst or root rot — the two look identical in calatheas, which catches people out.
problems.fix: Feel the soil before acting. Dry means water; wet means stop and check the roots immediately.

repotting: Calathea orbifolia dislikes root disturbance and should be repotted only every two years, or when roots have completely filled the pot and it dries out much faster than before.

Repot in spring into a plastic or glazed pot one size larger. Disturb the root ball as little as possible — loosen the outer roots and leave the core intact rather than washing the soil away, unless you are deliberately dividing.

Water with filtered water, keep humidity high, and expect a period of sulking. Do not feed for six to eight weeks. If the plant is otherwise healthy, leaving it alone is usually the better choice; orbifolia responds badly to routine disturbance.
varieties: Calathea orbifolia, now formally Goeppertia orbifolia, has the largest and roundest leaves in the commonly sold group, with broad alternating silver and green bands. There are no cultivars — the species is grown as it is.

Within the genus, Calathea lancifolia (rattlesnake plant) is the most forgiving, C. makoyana (peacock plant) has fine translucent patterning, and C. 'White Fusion' is the most demanding of all with its unstable white variegation. All calatheas are non-toxic to cats and dogs, which is why they remain popular despite the care requirements — there are very few pet-safe plants with this kind of foliage.

light: Watermelon peperomia wants bright indirect light to keep the silver striping crisp and the leaves compact. This is one of the more light-responsive peperomias.

An east window is ideal, or near a south or west window behind a sheer curtain. Direct sun scorches the leaves and fades the pattern to a washed-out grey. In low light the red petioles stretch dramatically, the leaves space out, and the plant loses its dense rosette form — the most common complaint with this species.
water: The thick leaves store water, so treat this as a semi-succulent. Let the top inch or two of mix dry before watering, then water thoroughly and drain fully. In spring and summer that usually means every ten to fourteen days.
Reduce to every three weeks or so in winter. Overwatering is by far the main cause of failure, and peperomias fail suddenly rather than gradually — stems collapse at the base with little warning.

Water at soil level rather than over the leaves, since water sitting in the crown where the petioles meet causes rot. Bottom-watering suits this plant well. Average household humidity is fine; it does not need the levels a calathea demands, though above 50% produces slightly better growth.
soil: Use a light, airy, fast-draining mix — two parts standard compost to one part perlite, with a little orchid bark. Peperomia roots are fine and sparse and rot quickly in dense wet soil.

Keep the pot small. This is the single most important practical point with peperomias: the root system is modest and an oversized pot holds a reservoir of wet mix the plant cannot use. Terracotta helps. Feed monthly at half strength through spring and summer only; over-feeding causes leaf drop.

propagation: Watermelon peperomia propagates from leaf cuttings, and the technique is slightly unusual — it is one of the few houseplants where cutting the leaf in half actually improves results.

Take a healthy leaf with an inch of petiole attached. You can either insert the petiole into damp mix at an angle so the leaf blade sits just above the surface, or cut the leaf blade in half across the middle and stand the cut edge in damp mix. The cut-half method produces plantlets along the whole cut edge rather than just at the petiole base, so one leaf yields several plants.

Cover with a clear bag or propagator to maintain humidity, and keep warm in bright indirect light. Tiny plantlets emerge at the base after four to eight weeks — slower than stem cuttings on other plants, so patience is needed. Note that because this species grows as a rosette rather than a vine, there are no long stems to take conventional cuttings from; leaf propagation and division of a mature clump are the options.

problems.symptom: Stems suddenly collapsing at the base
problems.cause: Stem and root rot from overwatering. Peperomias fail abruptly, which is why this catches people out.
problems.fix: Take healthy leaves immediately for propagation as insurance. Unpot, cut away all soft tissue, and repot any healthy material into fresh airy mix in a smaller pot. Water far less often.

problems.symptom: Long leggy petioles and a sparse, open rosette
problems.cause: Insufficient light. The leaf stalks stretch toward the source.
problems.fix: Move to a brighter position with indirect light. Stretched petioles stay as they are, but new growth comes in compact. Removing the longest stalks tidies the plant.

problems.symptom: Silver striping fading to plain green or grey
problems.cause: Too little light fades the pattern; too much direct sun bleaches it.
problems.fix: Check the position. A plant in medium light should be moved brighter; one in direct sun should be filtered.

problems.symptom: Leaves wrinkled and soft
problems.cause: Underwatering — the plant is drawing on the water stored in its leaves.
problems.fix: Water thoroughly until it drains. Leaves firm up within a few days.

problems.symptom: Leaves dropping at a touch
problems.cause: Overwatering most commonly, sometimes a sudden cold draught.
problems.fix: Check the soil. Wet means stop watering and inspect the roots. Move away from draughty windows.

problems.symptom: Corky brown bumps on leaf undersides
problems.cause: Oedema — cells rupturing after the plant took up water faster than it could transpire, typically from heavy watering in low light.
problems.fix: Water less and increase light. The marks are permanent but harmless, and new leaves come in clean.

problems.symptom: Small flies around the pot
problems.cause: Fungus gnats in soil kept too damp, which for this plant is a clear signal the watering routine is wrong.
problems.fix: Let the mix dry out properly between waterings, use sticky traps, and repot into a grittier mix and a smaller pot if the problem persists.

repotting: Peperomias have small root systems and like being snug, so repot only every two to three years, or when roots have genuinely filled the pot.
Move up one small size and no more. Overpotting is the commonest mistake with this genus and leads directly to rot. A small terracotta pot is ideal.

Repot in spring into fresh airy mix, handling the brittle petioles carefully. Water lightly afterwards and wait six weeks before feeding. This is the natural moment to divide a mature clump into two plants if it has become crowded.
varieties: Peperomia argyreia is the watermelon peperomia, with rounded leaves striped silver and dark green on bright red petioles. There are no widely sold cultivars — the species is distinctive enough on its own.

The genus is large and varied: P. obtusifolia is the baby rubber plant with thick glossy oval leaves, P. caperata 'Rosso' has deeply corrugated dark leaves with red undersides, P. polybotrya is the raindrop peperomia with teardrop-shaped leaves, and P. prostrata is the string of turtles. Care is broadly similar across the genus — bright indirect light, dry out between waterings, small pot. All peperomias are non-toxic to cats and dogs, making this one of the safest and most varied groups for a pet household.

light: Purple shamrock wants bright indirect light with a few hours of gentle direct sun. Light is what keeps the deep purple colour saturated and the plant compact.

An east or south window works well, filtered in the hottest part of summer. In insufficient light the stems stretch into long thin stalks that flop over, and the purple pales. One of this plant's charms is its nyctinasty — the triangular leaflets fold down like closed umbrellas at night and open again in the morning, a daily rhythm driven by light that is quite visible and happens reliably in a well-lit plant.
water: Water when the top inch of mix has dried, then water thoroughly and drain. In spring and summer that is usually every five to seven days. Oxalis grows from small bulb-like rhizomes and rots if kept saturated.

The important seasonal point is dormancy. Oxalis triangularis naturally goes dormant once or twice a year, usually after a period of heavy growth or in response to heat. The foliage dies back completely and the plant looks dead. This is normal and expected — do not discard it.

When dormancy begins, stop watering, cut the dead foliage back to soil level, and put the pot somewhere cool and dark for four to six weeks. Then bring it back into the light and resume watering, and fresh growth appears within a couple of weeks. Humidity is not important; average household air suits it.
soil: Use a standard well-draining potting mix with added perlite. The rhizomes want a medium that drains freely rather than staying wet.

Drainage holes are essential. Feed monthly at half strength through the active growing period and stop entirely during dormancy. Oxalis is not a heavy feeder. A pot that is wide rather than deep suits the shallow spreading rhizomes, and a crowded pot actually looks better since the foliage forms a dense mound.

propagation: Oxalis triangularis is propagated by dividing the rhizomes, which is easy and very reliable — the plant multiplies readily on its own.

The best time is at the end of a dormant period, just before you bring the pot back into growth. Tip the pot out and sift through the mix: you will find small pale rhizomes that look like tiny pine cones or scaly bulbs, usually far more of them than you expected.

Separate them and pot them in groups of five or six, about an inch deep, in fresh well-draining mix. Water lightly and place in bright light. Shoots appear within one to three weeks. Because each rhizome produces a cluster of leaves, planting several together gives a full pot immediately rather than a sparse one. Handle them gently — they snap easily, though broken pieces often grow anyway. Individual rhizomes can also be shared or stored dry for a few weeks between plantings.

problems.symptom: All foliage dies back and the plant looks dead
problems.cause: Dormancy, which is a normal part of this plant's cycle and happens once or twice a year, often triggered by heat.
problems.fix: Stop watering, cut the dead growth back to soil level, and rest the pot somewhere cool and dark for four to six weeks. Then resume light and water. Do not throw the plant away — the rhizomes are alive.

problems.symptom: Long floppy stems that cannot hold the leaves up
problems.cause: Insufficient light. The stalks stretch and weaken.
problems.fix: Move to a brighter position with some gentle direct sun. Cut the floppy growth back to soil level and the plant regrows compact from the rhizomes.

problems.symptom: Purple colour fading toward green or bronze
problems.cause: Too little light. The purple pigment is a light response.
problems.fix: Increase light gradually. New growth comes in properly coloured.

problems.symptom: Leaves not opening during the day
problems.cause: Too little light, or the plant entering dormancy.
problems.fix: Move somewhere brighter. If the leaves also begin yellowing and dying back, it is dormancy rather than a light problem, and should be allowed to run its course.

problems.symptom: Mushy stems and rhizomes
problems.cause: Overwatering, particularly if it continued into dormancy when the plant needs none.
problems.fix: Stop watering, let the mix dry out, and sift out any firm healthy rhizomes to replant in fresh mix. Discard soft ones.

problems.symptom: Brown crispy leaf edges
problems.cause: Underwatering, or scorch from harsh direct sun.
problems.fix: Water more consistently and filter the strongest midday light. Damaged leaves can be trimmed at the base; the plant replaces foliage rapidly.

problems.symptom: Powdery white coating on the leaves
problems.cause: Powdery mildew, encouraged by crowded growth and poor air circulation.
problems.fix: Remove affected leaves, thin the clump, and improve airflow. Avoid wetting the foliage when watering.

repotting: Repot every one to two years, ideally at the end of a dormant period when the rhizomes can be handled without disturbing active growth.

Choose a wide, shallow pot rather than a deep one, since the rhizomes spread sideways near the surface. Move up one size, or simply refresh the mix in the same pot and replant a selection of the best rhizomes.

Plant the rhizomes about an inch deep and several to a pot for a full look. Water lightly until growth appears, then resume normal care. This is also the easiest moment to divide and share the surplus, of which there is usually plenty.
varieties: Oxalis triangularis is the purple shamrock, with deep burgundy triangular leaflets and small pale pink or white flowers. 'Atropurpurea' is the darkest form. A green-leaved form, Oxalis regnellii, has the same habit with plain green foliage and white flowers.

Oxalis tetraphylla, the iron cross plant, has green leaves with a dark purple marking at the centre of each leaflet. The plant is sometimes sold as false shamrock or love plant. Important safety note: Oxalis contains oxalic acid and is toxic to cats and dogs in quantity, causing drooling, vomiting and in serious cases kidney effects — despite its delicate appearance and common gift-plant status it is worth keeping out of reach.

light: Staghorn fern wants bright indirect light. It grows epiphytically on tree trunks and branches in tropical forests, receiving filtered light through the canopy rather than direct sun or deep shade.

An east window is close to ideal, or bright light from a north window. Direct sun scorches the fronds, particularly the flat shield fronds at the base. In too little light the plant produces few new fronds and the growth is pale and weak. If mounted on a wall, remember that light falls off sharply with distance from the window — a staghorn on a shaded wall is often in much lower light than it appears.
water: Staghorn fern has two distinct kinds of frond and understanding them is the key to watering it. The flat, round shield fronds at the base press against the mounting surface, collect debris, and turn brown and papery as they mature — this is completely normal and they should never be removed. The antler-shaped fronds are the growing, photosynthesising ones.

For a mounted plant, the usual method is soaking: submerge the mount or root ball in water for ten to twenty minutes, then let it drain thoroughly. Do this when the mount feels light and dry, typically every one to two weeks in summer and every two to three weeks in winter. A potted plant is watered conventionally when the top inch of medium is dry.
Humidity above 50% suits it well, and misting the antler fronds is genuinely useful for this epiphyte, unlike most houseplants. Avoid letting water sit in the centre of the crown.
soil: Staghorn fern is not grown in soil in the conventional sense. Mounted plants sit on a board with sphagnum moss packed behind the shield fronds, which is the traditional and best-looking method. Potted plants need a very loose epiphytic mix — mostly orchid bark and sphagnum moss with some perlite.

Ordinary potting compost will kill this plant by suffocating the roots. Feed monthly at half strength through spring and summer, applying diluted liquid feed during a soak, or push a banana peel or slow-release pellets behind the shield fronds, which is a traditional approach that works well. Stop feeding in winter.

propagation: Staghorn fern is propagated from pups — offsets that appear around the base of a mature plant — and this is the only practical home method. Spore propagation is possible but extremely slow.

Wait until a pup has developed its own shield frond and at least one antler frond, which usually means it is several inches across. Using a clean sharp knife, cut the pup away from the parent, taking a portion of the root mass and shield frond material with it. Cutting too close to the parent or taking a pup without roots usually fails.

Mount the pup by packing damp sphagnum moss around its roots against a board, and securing it with fishing line or soft wire wrapped over the moss — not over the shield frond, which needs to press flat against the mount. Keep it humid and shaded for the first month while it attaches itself. Over time the shield fronds grow over the fixings and anchor the plant naturally. A pup can also be potted in a loose bark mix while it establishes.

problems.symptom: Shield fronds turning brown and papery
problems.cause: Completely normal. The flat basal fronds are designed to brown, harden and form a protective layer over the roots.
problems.fix: Leave them alone. Removing them exposes the roots and damages the plant. This is the single most common mistake made with staghorn ferns.

problems.symptom: Antler fronds turning brown at the tips
problems.cause: Underwatering, low humidity, or salts in the water.
problems.fix: Soak more regularly, raise humidity, and use filtered or rainwater. Trim brown tips if you wish, following the frond shape.

problems.symptom: Black spots at the base of the antler fronds
problems.cause: Rot from overwatering, or water sitting in the crown where the fronds emerge.
problems.fix: Reduce watering frequency, let the mount dry properly between soaks, and improve air circulation. Remove badly affected fronds.

problems.symptom: Fronds wilting and limp
problems.cause: Underwatering, which is common with mounted plants because it is hard to judge moisture.
problems.fix: Soak the mount thoroughly for twenty minutes. Learn the weight of the mount when freshly watered versus dry — lifting it is a more reliable gauge than looking at it.

problems.symptom: Grey fuzzy coating on the fronds
problems.cause: Normal. Staghorn fronds are covered in fine hairs that reduce water loss and reflect light.
problems.fix: Do not wipe them off — this damages the plant's natural protection. Resist the urge to polish the leaves as you might with a rubber plant.

problems.symptom: Brown circular patches with distinct edges
problems.cause: Rhizoctonia fungal infection, which spreads fast in wet, still conditions.
problems.fix: Remove affected fronds immediately, dry the plant out, and increase air circulation substantially. This can kill a staghorn quickly if left.

problems.symptom: Small brown bumps on frond undersides
problems.cause: Either spores, which form in patches near the frond tips and are normal on mature plants, or scale insects, which are scattered irregularly.
problems.fix: Spores need no action. For scale, wipe off with a cotton bud and diluted rubbing alcohol — be cautious with chemical treatments, since ferns are sensitive to neem and soaps.

repotting: Mounted staghorn ferns need remounting every three to five years, when the plant has outgrown its board or the sphagnum behind the shield fronds has broken down entirely.

Remount onto a larger board in spring. Do not attempt to remove the old shield fronds or clean the root mass — simply pack fresh damp sphagnum around and behind the existing root ball and secure the whole thing to the new board.

Potted plants should be moved up one size every two to three years into fresh loose bark mix. In both cases keep humidity high for a few weeks afterwards and hold off feeding for six weeks while the plant reattaches.
varieties: Platycerium bifurcatum is the common staghorn fern, the hardiest and most forgiving, with drooping grey-green antler fronds. P. superbum is the giant staghorn, forming huge crown-shaped shield fronds, and P. veitchii has upright silvery fronds and tolerates more light and drier air.

P. grande and P. ridleyi are collector species needing higher humidity. Staghorn ferns are non-toxic to cats and dogs, and because they are usually mounted on a wall they are physically out of reach anyway — a practical advantage in a pet household. The mounting also makes them one of the few houseplants that genuinely work as wall decor.

light: Kentia palm is the most shade-tolerant of the large indoor palms and handles medium light comfortably, which is why Victorian drawing rooms were full of them long before electric lighting. Bright indirect light produces faster growth, but it does not decline in a moderately lit room the way areca or majesty palm does.

Keep it out of direct sun, which yellows and scorches the fronds. A position a few feet back from an east or north window suits it well. Rotate the pot every few weeks so the crown develops evenly rather than leaning toward the light.
water: Water when the top two inches of mix are dry, then water thoroughly until it runs from the drainage holes. In spring and summer that is usually every ten to fourteen days; in winter, every three weeks or so.

Kentia is noticeably more drought-tolerant than areca or majesty palm and considerably more sensitive to overwatering. The thick fleshy roots rot in saturated soil, and yellowing lower fronds with damp mix is the classic warning. When in doubt, wait a few more days.

It also tolerates dry indoor air better than most palms, which is a large part of why it succeeds where others fail. Humidity above 40% is preferred but not critical. Like most palms it is sensitive to fluoride and salts, so filtered water and an occasional flush help prevent brown frond tips.
soil: Use a well-draining potting mix with added perlite and a little coarse sand. Kentia wants a medium with structure that drains freely rather than one that stays damp.

Choose a heavy, stable pot — a mature kentia is tall and top-heavy. Feed only every six to eight weeks at half strength through spring and summer, and not at all in winter. Kentia is a slow grower and a light feeder; over-fertilising causes tip burn and accumulated salts. Flush the pot with clean water a couple of times a year.

propagation: Kentia palm cannot be propagated by cuttings or by division of a single stem. Each stem grows from one terminal point, so cutting it kills that stem, and a severed frond will not root.

Propagation is from seed, which is genuinely difficult at home: kentia seed is slow and erratic, often taking two to twelve months to germinate and requiring consistent bottom heat around 27°C. Seedlings then take several years to reach any size, which is why kentia palms are relatively expensive.

What you can do is separate a multi-stemmed pot. Kentias are almost always sold with three to five seedlings planted together for a fuller look. In spring you can divide the root mass into smaller clumps, keeping at least two or three stems per division. Kentia roots are thick and brittle and resent disturbance, so expect a setback of several months and some frond browning. Most people are better off leaving the clump intact — it looks better and the plant is happier.

problems.symptom: Yellowing lower fronds
problems.cause: Overwatering if widespread with damp soil; normal ageing if it is the oldest frond alone as new ones emerge.
problems.fix: Let the top two inches dry before watering and confirm the pot drains freely. Cut spent fronds at the base — they will not green up again.

problems.symptom: Brown frond tips
problems.cause: Fluoride and salts in tap water, dry air, or over-fertilising.
problems.fix: Switch to filtered or rainwater, reduce feeding, and flush the pot with clean water a couple of times a year. Trim the brown tip following the natural taper, leaving a sliver of dead tissue.

problems.symptom: Fronds pale and washed out
problems.cause: Too much light, or a nutrient shortage in a plant that has been in the same mix for years.
problems.fix: Move out of direct sun. If light is already moderate, feed lightly through the growing season and repot into fresh mix.

problems.symptom: Fine webbing and stippled fronds
problems.cause: Spider mites, though kentia is less prone than areca or majesty palm thanks to its tolerance of drier air.
problems.fix: Rinse the plant thoroughly including frond undersides, then treat with insecticidal soap every five days for three cycles.

problems.symptom: No new fronds for a long period
problems.cause: Usually just the plant's pace — kentia is genuinely slow, producing only two or three new fronds a year even in good conditions.
problems.fix: Be patient. Ensure adequate light and light feeding in the growing season, but do not respond by watering more, which is the damaging mistake.

problems.symptom: Stems soft and brown at soil level
problems.cause: Root rot from waterlogged mix or a pot standing in water.
problems.fix: Confirm drainage, empty the saucer, trim soft roots, and repot into fresh free-draining mix. Affected stems will not recover and should be cut at the base.

problems.symptom: Small brown bumps along the fronds and stems
problems.cause: Scale insects, which are the most common kentia pest.
problems.fix: Scrape them off with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol and follow with neem oil weekly for a month.

repotting: Kentia palms are slow and strongly dislike root disturbance, so repot only every three to four years, or when roots are clearly emerging from the drainage holes and water runs straight through.

Repot in spring into a pot one size larger and heavy enough to keep a tall plant stable. Handle the thick brittle roots gently and avoid teasing the root ball apart — kentia sulks badly after disturbance.

Keep the clump of stems together rather than separating them. Water thoroughly afterwards, keep out of direct sun for a few weeks, and do not feed for two months. For a very large specimen, top-dressing with fresh compost each spring is far kinder than repotting.
varieties: Howea forsteriana is the kentia palm, native only to Lord Howe Island off Australia, with gracefully arching dark green fronds. Howea belmoreana, the curly palm or sentry palm, is a related species from the same island with more upright, arching fronds and a slightly more compact habit.

There are no cultivars — what varies commercially is age and the number of stems per pot. Kentia is non-toxic to cats and dogs, and between that, its shade tolerance, its tolerance of dry air and its resistance to neglect, it is arguably the best large palm for an ordinary home. The only real drawbacks are its price and how slowly it grows.

light: Guzmania wants bright indirect light. It grows as an epiphyte on tree branches in Central and South American forests, receiving filtered light rather than direct sun.

An east window is ideal, or a position near a south or west window behind a sheer curtain. Direct sun scorches the strappy leaves and bleaches the colourful bract. In light that is too low the plant survives but the bract colour fades faster and pups are produced more slowly. Good light also helps the plant dry properly between waterings, which matters for rot prevention.
water: Bromeliads are watered differently from every other houseplant, and getting this right is most of the battle. Guzmania takes up water through the central cup formed by its overlapping leaves, not primarily through its roots — the roots exist mainly to anchor it to a tree.

Keep the central cup filled with about an inch of water at all times, and flush it out completely every one to two weeks by tipping the plant to empty it before refilling. Stagnant water in the cup causes rot and smells. Keep the potting medium only lightly damp, watering it sparingly every week or two.

Water quality matters: use filtered, distilled or rainwater, since bromeliads are sensitive to salts and minerals which accumulate in the cup. Humidity above 50% is appreciated and misting the foliage is genuinely beneficial for an epiphyte.
soil: Use a very free-draining epiphytic mix — orchid bark with some perlite and a little peat or coir. Ordinary potting compost holds far too much water around the small root system and causes rot.

The pot should be small; bromeliad roots are minimal and an oversized pot of wet medium is the main hazard. Feed very sparingly — a quarter-strength liquid feed poured into the cup or over the medium every couple of months during growth is ample. Over-feeding causes the leaves to lose colour and grow loose and floppy.

propagation: This is the essential thing to understand about bromeliads: the plant you buy will flower once and then die. That is its natural life cycle, not a failure of care. The colourful central structure is a bract, not a flower, and it lasts for several months before slowly fading.

As the parent declines, it produces pups — offsets around its base. This is how the plant continues, and it is the only method of propagation available at home. Wait until a pup is at least one third to one half the size of the parent and has begun forming its own small roots; taking them too early is the commonest reason they fail.

Cut the pup away from the parent with a clean sharp knife, cutting as close to the parent as possible to include a little of its base. Pot into free-draining bark mix, using a small pot, and support the pup with stakes if it is unsteady — its roots will not anchor it for some weeks. Keep the cup filled and the medium barely damp. Pups typically take one to three years to reach flowering size.

problems.symptom: The colourful bract fades and the plant slowly dies
problems.cause: Normal life cycle. Guzmania is monocarpic — it flowers once, then dies over the following months.
problems.fix: Nothing to fix. Let the parent decline naturally while it feeds its pups, and separate the pups once they are a third to half the parent's size. Do not discard the pot when the bract fades.

problems.symptom: Base of the plant rotting, leaves pulling away easily
problems.cause: Overwatering the potting medium, or a pot that holds too much water around the roots.
problems.fix: Keep the medium only lightly damp and water primarily into the cup. Repot into a smaller pot of pure bark mix if the medium stays wet.

problems.symptom: Brown crispy leaf tips
problems.cause: Dry air, or minerals and salts in tap water accumulating in the cup.
problems.fix: Use filtered, distilled or rainwater, flush the cup every one to two weeks, and raise humidity. Trim tips following the leaf shape.

problems.symptom: Water in the cup smelling stagnant
problems.cause: The cup has not been flushed and bacteria have built up.
problems.fix: Tip the plant to empty the cup completely, rinse it out, and refill with fresh water. Do this every one to two weeks as routine.

problems.symptom: Leaves pale, loose and floppy
problems.cause: Over-feeding, or too little light.
problems.fix: Stop fertilising and move to brighter indirect light. Bromeliads need very little feed and respond badly to standard houseplant doses.

problems.symptom: Bleached or scorched patches on leaves
problems.cause: Direct sun through glass.
problems.fix: Move back from the window or filter the light. Damaged tissue does not recover.

problems.symptom: Pup wilting after separation
problems.cause: Taken too early, before it had roots of its own, or its cup is not being kept filled.
problems.fix: Keep the pup's cup topped up, maintain humidity, and support it upright. Take future pups only once they are at least a third the parent's size.

repotting: Bromeliads rarely need repotting, because each plant lives only a few years and has a tiny root system. Repot only if the pot is unstable or the medium has broken down.
When you do, use a small pot with fresh free-draining bark mix. Set the plant at the same depth, and stake it if it will not stand on its own — the shallow roots take time to anchor.

The more relevant operation is potting up separated pups, which effectively replaces repotting in this plant's life cycle. Do that in spring or summer, keep the cup filled and the medium barely damp, and expect the pup to take a year or more to establish and eventually bloom.
varieties: Guzmania lingulata is the most commonly sold, with a long-lasting bract in red, orange, yellow, pink or purple above a rosette of glossy green strappy leaves. Named cultivars are usually distinguished only by bract colour.

Related bromeliads include Vriesea, the flaming sword, with a flattened bright bract; Neoregelia, grown for coloured leaf centres rather than a bract; Aechmea fasciata, the urn plant, with silver-banded leaves and a pink bract; and Tillandsia, the air plants, which need no pot at all. All are monocarpic and pup in the same way. Guzmania and most bromeliads are non-toxic to cats and dogs, making them one of the few genuinely pet-safe sources of long-lasting indoor colour.

light: Ficus Audrey wants bright indirect light and tolerates a little gentle direct sun, particularly morning light. It is noticeably more forgiving than the fiddle leaf fig, which is a large part of its appeal as an alternative.

Place it in front of an east window, or a few feet from a south or west window. In medium light it survives but grows slowly and may drop lower leaves. Rotate the pot a quarter turn every couple of weeks, since it leans toward light and develops a one-sided crown otherwise. It handles a change of position better than a fiddle leaf fig, but still prefers to be left where it is.
water: Water when the top two inches of mix are dry, then water thoroughly until it drains. In spring and summer that is usually every seven to ten days; in winter, every two to three weeks.

Audrey is more drought-tolerant than the fiddle leaf fig and considerably less prone to dramatic leaf drop, but it still dislikes both extremes. The velvety leaves show underwatering as drooping and edge browning, and overwatering as yellowing lower leaves with damp soil.

Humidity above 40% is preferred and the plant appreciates a little extra in winter. Wipe the leaves with a damp cloth every few weeks — the soft matte surface collects dust readily, and a clean leaf photosynthesises noticeably better. Keep it away from cold draughts and heating vents.
soil: Use a well-draining potting mix with plenty of structure — roughly two parts quality compost to one part perlite and one part bark. Ficus roots need air, and a dense peat-heavy mix that stays soggy leads to root rot.

The pot must drain freely. Feed every four weeks through spring and summer with a balanced fertiliser at half strength, and stop from autumn through winter. Audrey is a moderately vigorous grower in good light and responds well to feeding during the growing season.

propagation: Ficus Audrey propagates from stem cuttings, with the same latex caveat as other figs — the cut bleeds a milky sap that irritates skin and stains, so wear gloves and rinse the cut end before potting.

Take a cutting six to eight inches long with two or three leaves, cutting just below a node in spring or early summer. Remove the lowest leaves and let the cut end stop bleeding. Dip in rooting hormone and pot into damp free-draining mix, or stand in water.

Cover a soil-potted cutting with a clear bag to maintain humidity and keep it warm in bright indirect light. Roots take four to eight weeks — slower than a pothos, so resist tugging at it. Air layering is the better technique for a tall plant that has gone bare at the base: wound the stem, pack damp sphagnum moss around it inside a plastic sleeve, and cut below the roots once they fill the moss. This gives you a substantial plant immediately and encourages the parent to branch below the cut.

problems.symptom: Lower leaves yellowing and dropping
problems.cause: Overwatering most commonly, particularly in winter. Losing an occasional oldest leaf is normal.
problems.fix: Let the top two inches dry properly before watering and confirm the pot drains. Reduce watering substantially from autumn.

problems.symptom: Brown crispy leaf edges
problems.cause: Dry air, underwatering, or salt buildup from fertiliser and hard water.
problems.fix: Water more consistently, raise humidity slightly, and flush the pot with plain water every few months.

problems.symptom: Leaf drop after being moved
problems.cause: Shock from a change in light or temperature. Less severe than with fiddle leaf fig, but Audrey still dislikes relocation.
problems.fix: Settle it in one position away from draughts and keep watering consistent. It usually stabilises within a few weeks.

problems.symptom: Tall bare stem with leaves only at the top
problems.cause: Natural growth habit combined with low light and no pruning. Ficus grows as a single leader unless encouraged to branch.
problems.fix: Cut the main stem back by a third in spring. It branches from below the cut, and the removed section can be rooted or air-layered.

problems.symptom: Dull, dusty-looking leaves
problems.cause: Dust on the soft matte leaf surface, which this species collects more readily than glossy-leaved figs.
problems.fix: Wipe both sides with a damp cloth every few weeks. This is genuine maintenance for Audrey rather than cosmetic.

problems.symptom: Leaves drooping with damp soil
problems.cause: Root rot from prolonged overwatering.
problems.fix: Unpot, trim soft brown roots, and repot into fresh free-draining mix. Water sparingly until new growth appears.

problems.symptom: Fine webbing or small brown bumps on leaf undersides
problems.cause: Spider mites or scale, both of which colonise the undersides unnoticed.
problems.fix: Wipe every leaf on both sides, then treat with insecticidal soap or neem weekly for three to four weeks.

repotting: Repot every one to two years while young, then every two to three years once mature. Signs are roots through the drainage holes, water running straight through, and stalled growth in the growing season.

Repot in spring into a pot one size larger. Audrey becomes top-heavy as it grows, so choose a substantial pot that will not tip. Handle the root ball gently — ficus dislikes root disturbance and may drop a few leaves afterwards.

Water thoroughly, keep out of direct sun for a fortnight, and hold off fertiliser for six weeks. For a large specimen that cannot practically be repotted, top-dress by replacing the top two inches of mix each spring.
varieties: Ficus benghalensis is the Indian banyan, sold as Ficus Audrey, with soft matte green leaves, pale veining and a light grey trunk. It is the national tree of India and grows to enormous size outdoors, though indoors it stays manageable.

There are few cultivars; 'Audrey' is the commonly sold selection. Within the genus, Ficus lyrata is the fiddle leaf fig, F. elastica the rubber plant, and F. benjamina the weeping fig — Audrey is generally regarded as the most forgiving of the large-leaved ones. All Ficus are toxic to cats and dogs, and the milky sap irritates skin on contact, so gloves are sensible when pruning.

light: Angel wing begonia wants bright indirect light. Good light is what produces the silver spotting on the leaves, the red undersides and, importantly, the clusters of flowers that this group is grown for.

An east window is ideal, or near a south or west window behind a sheer curtain. Direct midday sun scorches the leaves and fades the spotting. In low light the canes stretch, the leaves space out, the spotting dulls and flowering stops entirely. This is a plant where more light, short of direct sun, almost always improves things.
water: Water when the top inch of mix has dried, then water thoroughly and drain fully. In spring and summer that is usually every five to seven days; in winter, every ten to fourteen days.

Begonias are prone to both root rot and crown rot, so the balance matters. Water at soil level rather than over the foliage — water sitting on begonia leaves encourages powdery mildew and bacterial leaf spot, which are the most common diseases in this genus.

Humidity above 50% suits them, but do not achieve it by misting, for the reason just given. A pebble tray or humidifier is the right approach. Good air circulation is as important as humidity for begonias, because still damp air is what mildew needs.
soil: Use a light, well-draining mix — two parts standard compost to one part perlite, with a little bark. Begonias have relatively fine roots and want a medium that drains freely.

Keep the pot snug; begonias flower better slightly pot-bound and rot in an oversized pot of wet mix. Drainage holes are essential. Feed every two to four weeks at half strength through spring and summer with a balanced fertiliser, switching to something higher in potassium if you want to push flowering. Stop in winter.

propagation: Angel wing begonias are cane begonias, which makes them among the easiest in the genus to propagate — unlike rex begonias, which are propagated from leaves, these root readily from stem cuttings.

Take a cutting four to six inches long from a healthy cane, cutting just below a node, with two or three leaves. Remove the lowest leaf and any flower buds, which divert energy from rooting. Large leaves can be cut in half across to reduce water loss.

Root in water, changing it weekly, where roots appear in two to three weeks, or push directly into damp mix under a clear bag. Both work reliably. Pot several rooted cuttings together for a full plant. Because angel wings become tall and bare at the base over time, taking cuttings from the tips and replanting them is the standard way to keep a good-looking plant — treat it as routine renewal every couple of years rather than an occasional project.

problems.symptom: White powdery coating on leaves
problems.cause: Powdery mildew, the signature begonia disease, caused by damp still air and crowded growth.
problems.fix: Improve air circulation immediately, remove affected leaves, space plants apart, and stop misting. Water at soil level only. A fungicide helps but airflow is the real fix.

problems.symptom: Tall bare canes with leaves only at the top
problems.cause: Natural habit accelerated by low light and a lack of pruning.
problems.fix: Cut the canes back by a third to a half in spring — begonias branch readily from below a cut. Root the removed sections and replant them into the same pot to thicken it. Pinching tips regularly prevents the problem.

problems.symptom: No flowers
problems.cause: Insufficient light most commonly, then too large a pot or too much nitrogen fertiliser.
problems.fix: Move to a brighter position, keep the plant slightly pot-bound, and switch to a higher-potassium feed during the growing season.

problems.symptom: Brown crispy leaf edges
problems.cause: Low humidity or inconsistent watering.
problems.fix: Raise humidity with a pebble tray or humidifier rather than misting, and water on a more regular schedule.

problems.symptom: Stems collapsing and rotting at soil level
problems.cause: Overwatering, or water sitting against the stem bases.
problems.fix: Take tip cuttings immediately as insurance. Let the mix dry out more between waterings and repot into fresher, more open mix if needed.

problems.symptom: Brown or black spots with yellow halos on leaves
problems.cause: Bacterial leaf spot, spread by water splashing on the foliage.
problems.fix: Remove affected leaves with sterile scissors, water at soil level only, and improve airflow. Isolate the plant if it spreads quickly.

problems.symptom: Silver spotting fading and leaves turning plain green
problems.cause: Too little light. The spotting and red undersides are both light responses.
problems.fix: Move to a brighter position. New growth comes in properly marked.

repotting: Repot every one to two years in spring. Angel wings grow reasonably fast in good conditions, and the signs are roots through the drainage holes and rapid drying between waterings.
Move up one pot size only — begonias flower better slightly snug and rot in oversized pots. Choose a stable container, since tall canes make the plant top-heavy.

This is a good moment to prune the canes back and replant rooted cuttings around the parent, which is how you keep an angel wing looking full rather than bare-legged. Water thoroughly and wait a month before feeding.
varieties: Angel wing begonias are cane begonias, typically Begonia coccinea hybrids, with asymmetrical wing-shaped leaves, silver spotting and red undersides, and drooping clusters of pink, red or white flowers. 'Lucerna' is a classic large-leaved form.

Other cane begonias include the dragon wing types, which are more compact and flower prolifically. Different groups within the genus need quite different care: rex begonias are grown for foliage and propagated from leaves, rhizomatous begonias spread from surface rhizomes, and tuberous begonias go dormant annually. All begonias are toxic to cats and dogs — the tubers and rhizomes most of all — causing mouth irritation and vomiting if chewed.

light: String of bananas wants bright light with several hours of direct sun. It is noticeably tougher and more sun-tolerant than its relative string of pearls, which is why it is usually the better choice for a beginner.

A south or east-facing window suits it well. In insufficient light the strands stretch, the banana-shaped leaves space out along bare stems, and growth becomes thin and sparse. Good light produces dense strands packed with plump crescents. It handles more direct sun than string of pearls but can still scorch in intense unfiltered afternoon light in summer.
water: Treat it as the succulent it is. Water thoroughly, then let the mix dry out almost completely before watering again — typically every two to three weeks in spring and summer, and once a month or less in winter.

The leaves are the gauge: plump and firm means well watered, slightly flattened and soft means it is time. Mushy translucent leaves mean serious overwatering, by which point root rot is usually underway.

Water at the soil surface rather than over the strands, and drain completely. The root system is shallow, so a deep soak followed by a long dry period suits it far better than frequent light watering. String of bananas is genuinely more forgiving of both drought and occasional overwatering than string of pearls. Humidity is irrelevant.
soil: Use a gritty cactus or succulent mix, or two parts succulent compost to one part perlite or coarse sand. Fast drainage is essential.

A wide shallow pot suits the shallow spreading roots far better than a deep one, which holds a wet reservoir underneath them. Terracotta helps. Feed sparingly — a half-strength succulent feed twice during the growing season is ample, and none in winter. Hanging pots work well; check they actually drain rather than holding water in a sealed base.

propagation: String of bananas is very easy to propagate and does so more readily than string of pearls, which is another reason it makes a better starting point.

Take a strand four to six inches long and strip the leaves from the last inch or two to expose bare stem. You can then either lay the strand flat on the surface of damp cactus mix and press the bare section into contact — roots form at each node where stem touches soil — or insert the bare end an inch into the mix.

The laying method is more productive, because a single strand roots at multiple points and produces a much fuller plant. Let cut ends callus for a day first. Keep the mix barely moist rather than wet, in bright indirect light; roots take two to three weeks. Planting several rooted strands around the edge of the parent pot is the standard way to thicken a plant that has gone sparse at the crown. Avoid water propagation, which tends to rot the strands.

problems.symptom: Leaves shrivelling and going flat
problems.cause: Underwatering, or root rot preventing uptake despite damp soil.
problems.fix: Check the soil. Dry means water thoroughly and the leaves plump up within days. Wet and still shrivelled means the roots have failed — take healthy strand cuttings and restart.

problems.symptom: Leaves mushy and translucent
problems.cause: Overwatering. The leaves take up more water than they can hold.
problems.fix: Stop watering and let the mix dry out completely. Check the crown for rot and take cuttings from healthy strands as insurance.

problems.symptom: Bare stems with leaves widely spaced
problems.cause: Insufficient light — the strands stretch toward the source.
problems.fix: Move to a much brighter position with some direct sun. Stretched sections will not fill in; trim them and lay the cuttings back onto the soil surface to root.

problems.symptom: Plant thinning and dying back at the crown
problems.cause: Natural ageing of the centre, worsened by water collecting among the strands there.
problems.fix: Normal for mature plants. Lay cuttings from the healthy outer strands onto the surface to fill in, or start a fresh pot. Water at the pot edge rather than over the centre.

problems.symptom: Reddish or purple tinge to the leaves
problems.cause: Sun stress, which is generally harmless and often considered attractive, though it can also indicate underwatering.
problems.fix: Check the soil. If watering is adequate, no action is needed — move slightly out of the strongest sun if you prefer green.

problems.symptom: White cottony clusters among the strands
problems.cause: Mealybugs, which hide well in the dense tangle.
problems.fix: Dab each cluster with rubbing alcohol on a cotton bud and inspect weekly for a month.

problems.symptom: Strands browning and drying from the base
problems.cause: Stem rot at soil level from overwatering or water sitting against the stems.
problems.fix: Cut affected strands away entirely, let the soil dry, and salvage healthy strands as cuttings. Improve drainage.

repotting: String of bananas has a shallow root system and is happy pot-bound, so repot only every two to three years, or when the mix has broken down and stopped draining.
Choose a wide, shallow pot rather than a deep one, in terracotta or another breathable material. Spring is the right time.

Handle the strands carefully — they detach easily and every broken strand is a free cutting. Use dry mix, wait a week before the first watering, and skip fertiliser for a couple of months. Repotting is a good opportunity to lay cuttings onto the fresh surface to fill in bare areas.
varieties: Curio radicans, formerly Senecio radicans, is the string of bananas, with crescent-shaped leaves along trailing stems. It grows faster and more robustly than string of pearls and tolerates a wider range of conditions.

Close relatives with near-identical care include string of pearls with spherical beads, string of dolphins with curved leaves resembling leaping dolphins, string of tears with teardrop beads, and string of fishhooks, a larger-leaved form. All these Curio species are toxic to cats and dogs, and because the trailing strands are so attractive to a playful cat, a high hanging position genuinely matters in a pet household.

light: Rex begonia wants bright indirect light with no direct sun. It is grown entirely for its foliage — the metallic silvers, purples, pinks and reds — and light level controls how vivid those colours are.

An east or north window is ideal. Direct sun scorches the thin textured leaves within hours and bleaches the metallic sheen. In light that is too low the colours dull toward green and the plant becomes leggy. Rex begonias also grow well under artificial light, which makes them a good option for a room with poor natural light.
water: Water when the top inch of mix has dried, then water thoroughly and drain fully. In spring and summer that is usually every five to seven days; in winter, every ten to fourteen days.

Water at soil level and keep water off the leaves entirely. Rex begonias are more prone to powdery mildew and bacterial leaf spot than almost any other houseplant, and wet foliage in still air is exactly what those need. Bottom-watering suits them well.

They want humidity above 50%, but — crucially — not achieved by misting. Use a pebble tray or humidifier. Good air circulation is as important as the humidity itself: still, damp air is the combination that causes mildew, while moving humid air is what rex begonias actually want.
soil: Use a light, airy, free-draining mix — two parts peat or coir-based compost to one part perlite, with a little bark. Rex begonias grow from a shallow surface rhizome with fine roots and rot easily in dense wet soil.

A shallow, wide pot suits the rhizome far better than a deep one. Keep the pot snug. Feed every three to four weeks at quarter to half strength through spring and summer only — rex begonias are light feeders and over-fertilising causes leaf edge burn. Stop entirely in winter when many go semi-dormant.

propagation: Rex begonias are propagated from leaf cuttings, not stem cuttings, and this is one of the most satisfying propagations in houseplant growing — a single leaf can produce a dozen plants.

The classic method is leaf wedges. Take a healthy mature leaf and cut it into triangular wedges, each containing a section of a main vein running to the point of the wedge. Insert the pointed end into damp propagation mix so the vein is in contact with the surface. Plantlets emerge from the vein.

The alternative is vein cutting: lay a whole leaf face up on damp mix, slice across the main veins with a sharp blade in several places, and pin the leaf flat so the cuts touch the medium. A plantlet forms at each cut. Either way, cover with a clear lid or bag and keep warm in bright indirect light. Plantlets appear after four to eight weeks. Mature plants can also be divided by separating sections of the surface rhizome, each with roots and a leaf or two.

problems.symptom: White powdery coating on leaves
