problems.cause: Powdery mildew, which rex begonias are exceptionally prone to. Caused by damp, still air and crowding.
problems.fix: Improve air circulation immediately — a small fan on low nearby makes a real difference. Remove affected leaves, space plants apart, stop misting entirely, and water at soil level only.

problems.symptom: Brown crispy leaf edges
problems.cause: Low humidity, over-fertilising, or salts in tap water.
problems.fix: Raise humidity with a pebble tray or humidifier rather than misting, reduce feeding to quarter strength, and flush the pot occasionally with clean water.

problems.symptom: Leaves losing their metallic colour and turning plain green
problems.cause: Insufficient light.
problems.fix: Move to a brighter position with indirect light, or add a grow light. New growth comes in properly coloured.

problems.symptom: Plant dying back in autumn, losing most leaves
problems.cause: Semi-dormancy, which many rex begonias undergo in winter. Normal rather than terminal.
problems.fix: Reduce watering substantially and stop feeding. Keep the rhizome just barely damp and somewhere warm. Growth resumes in spring. Do not discard the pot.

problems.symptom: Stems and rhizome going soft and mushy
problems.cause: Overwatering and rhizome rot, made worse by a deep pot or dense mix.
problems.fix: Take leaf cuttings immediately as insurance. Unpot, cut away soft rhizome, and repot healthy sections into fresh airy mix in a shallow pot.

problems.symptom: Brown or black spots with yellow halos
problems.cause: Bacterial leaf spot, spread by water splashing onto leaves.
problems.fix: Remove affected leaves with sterile scissors, water at soil level only, and improve airflow. Isolate the plant if it spreads.

problems.symptom: Leggy growth with long bare stretches of rhizome
problems.cause: Too little light.
problems.fix: Increase light. Cut the rhizome into sections and replant them to make a denser pot, which is standard renewal for this plant.

repotting: Repot every one to two years in spring, into a shallow, wide pot one size larger. Rex begonias grow from a surface rhizome that spreads sideways rather than rooting deeply, so pot shape matters more than depth.
Set the rhizome at or just below the surface — burying it causes rot. Use fresh airy mix and handle the brittle leaves and rhizome gently.

Water at soil level afterwards, keep humidity up but airflow good, and wait six weeks before feeding. This is the natural moment to divide a congested rhizome into several plants, and to take leaf cuttings from any leaves that come off in the process.
varieties: Begonia rex-cultorum covers hundreds of named cultivars, bred entirely for leaf colour and texture. 'Escargot' has leaves that spiral into a snail shell shape, 'Fireworks' is silver with purple veining, and 'Red Kiss' is deep burgundy with a black centre.

Spiral, ruffled and pointed leaf forms are all available. Rex begonias do exceptionally well in terrariums, which solves the humidity problem — though airflow must still be adequate or mildew follows. Other begonia groups need quite different care: cane begonias root from stem cuttings, and tuberous ones go fully dormant. All begonias are toxic to cats and dogs, with the rhizome the most concentrated part.

light: Ti plant needs bright indirect light with some gentle direct sun to develop and hold its pink, red and burgundy colouring. Light is the primary factor in whether the foliage stays vivid or fades.

An east window is ideal, or near a south or west window behind a sheer curtain. In insufficient light new leaves emerge green and the plant loses the colour it was bought for. Harsh unfiltered afternoon sun scorches the leaves, so the aim is bright but filtered. Rotate the pot regularly, since the canes lean toward light.
water: Keep the mix evenly moist through spring and summer, watering when the top inch is dry — usually every five to seven days. Ti plant comes from tropical Pacific islands and does not tolerate drying out well.
Reduce to every ten to fourteen days in winter but do not let the root ball go dry. Drooping leaves and crisping edges follow quickly from drought.

The critical point for this species is water quality. Cordyline is among the most fluoride-sensitive houseplants there is, and fluoridated tap water produces the brown, burnt leaf tips that almost every specimen eventually develops. Use filtered, distilled or rainwater from the start. Humidity above 50% is also genuinely needed, and dry air compounds the tip-burn problem.
soil: Use a well-draining potting mix with added perlite. Avoid mixes containing superphosphate or perlite-heavy blends that have been treated with fluoridated water, since both contribute to tip burn.

Drainage holes are essential. Feed monthly at half strength through spring and summer, and stop in winter. Ti plant is a moderate feeder, but salt accumulation worsens the tip-burn issue, so flush the pot thoroughly with clean water every couple of months.

propagation: Ti plant propagates readily from cane cuttings, and this doubles as the remedy for a plant that has grown tall and bare — a very common outcome.

In spring, cut the cane wherever you want the plant to branch. The stump usually sprouts two or three new shoots from just below the cut, making the parent bushier. The removed section can be cut into pieces three to five inches long, each with at least one node, keeping track of orientation — a piece planted upside down will not root.

The leafy top roots directly in water or damp mix. Bare cane sections, traditionally called ti logs, can be laid horizontally half-buried in damp mix with the nodes facing up, or stood upright the right way round. Keep warm and humid in bright indirect light; shoots and roots appear in three to six weeks. Cordyline roots noticeably faster than most dracaenas, and a single tall cane can yield four or five new plants.

problems.symptom: Brown, burnt leaf tips
problems.cause: Fluoride in tap water, which this genus is more sensitive to than almost any other houseplant. Dry air and salt buildup compound it.
problems.fix: Switch to filtered, distilled or rainwater immediately, raise humidity above 50%, and flush the pot with clean water every couple of months. Trim tips at an angle. New growth will be clean.

problems.symptom: New leaves emerging plain green
problems.cause: Insufficient light. The pink and red pigments are a light response.
problems.fix: Move to a brighter position with filtered light. Existing green leaves stay as they are; new growth colours up.

problems.symptom: Leaves dropping from the lower cane
problems.cause: Natural ageing as the cane lengthens, or a response to drought, cold or a sudden move.
problems.fix: Some bare lower cane is the normal habit. If shedding is rapid, check watering consistency and move away from draughts. Cut the cane back in spring to force branching.

problems.symptom: Leaves drooping and crisping
problems.cause: Underwatering or low humidity.
problems.fix: Water more consistently and raise humidity. Ti plant is less drought-tolerant than the dracaenas it resembles.

problems.symptom: Fine webbing and stippled leaves
problems.cause: Spider mites, drawn by dry air — the most common Cordyline pest.
problems.fix: Rinse the plant thoroughly including leaf undersides, treat with insecticidal soap every five days for three cycles, and raise humidity to prevent recurrence.

problems.symptom: Soft, mushy cane at soil level
problems.cause: Stem rot from waterlogged soil.
problems.fix: Cut the cane above the rot into firm tissue and root the healthy top as a cutting. Repot into fresher, faster-draining mix.

problems.symptom: Pale or bleached patches on leaves
problems.cause: Scorch from harsh direct sun.
problems.fix: Filter the strongest light while keeping overall brightness high. Damaged tissue does not recover.

repotting: Repot every two years in spring. Ti plant grows moderately fast in good conditions, and the signs are roots through the drainage holes and water running straight through.
Move up one pot size into a stable container — tall canes make the plant top-heavy. Loosen circling roots and trim any that are soft.

Use this as the moment to cut a leggy plant back and propagate the removed cane, since the parent will branch from the cut as it recovers. Water with filtered water, keep humidity up, and wait six weeks before feeding.
varieties: Cordyline fruticosa comes in many cultivars distinguished by leaf colour. 'Red Sister' has vivid pink-red new growth, 'Kiwi' is green striped with cream and edged in pink, and 'Black Magic' is a deep purple-bronze.

'Chocolate Queen' and 'Florica' offer further colour variations. The plant is sometimes sold as Hawaiian ti or good luck plant. Cordyline is frequently confused with Dracaena, and they are related, but Cordyline has more fluoride sensitivity and needs more humidity. Important: Cordyline fruticosa is toxic to cats and dogs, with saponins causing vomiting, drooling and, in cats especially, dilated pupils.

light: Coffee plant wants bright indirect light. In its native Ethiopian highlands it grows as an understorey shrub beneath taller trees, so it is adapted to filtered light rather than full exposure.

An east window is ideal, or a few feet back from a south or west window. Direct sun scorches the glossy leaves, producing brown patches and yellowing — this is the most common mistake, since people assume a tropical crop plant wants full sun. In low light it survives but grows slowly and will not flower. Rotate the pot regularly for even growth.
water: Keep the mix consistently moist but never soggy, watering when the top inch is dry — usually every five to seven days in spring and summer. Coffee dislikes drying out and responds by dropping leaves.
Reduce to every ten to fourteen days in winter, but never let the root ball dry through. The balance is evenly damp; both drought and waterlogging cause leaf loss.

Humidity above 50% is important. Coffee comes from a misty highland climate and dry indoor air produces browning leaf edges and invites spider mites. A humidifier helps considerably. Use filtered or rainwater if your tap water is hard, since coffee prefers slightly acidic conditions and is sensitive to accumulated salts.
soil: Use a slightly acidic, well-draining potting mix — a peat or coir-based compost with added perlite works well, and an ericaceous compost blended with perlite is even better. Coffee prefers a pH around 6 to 6.5.

Drainage holes are essential. Feed every two to four weeks through spring and summer with a balanced fertiliser at half strength, ideally one formulated for acid-loving plants. Coffee is a moderately hungry grower. Stop feeding in winter. Flush the pot with clean water every couple of months to prevent salt buildup.

propagation: Coffee propagates from seed and from stem cuttings, with an important caveat about seed that catches people out.

Seed must be genuinely fresh — green, unroasted coffee beans still in their parchment. Roasted supermarket beans will never germinate, and even green beans lose viability within a few months. Fresh seed sown in damp mix at 25°C germinates in two to four months, which requires patience.

Stem cuttings are more practical. In spring or early summer, take a cutting six to eight inches long from a healthy upright stem — and specifically from a vertical shoot rather than a side branch, because cuttings from lateral branches grow permanently sideways and never form an upright plant. Remove the lower leaves, dip in rooting hormone, and pot into damp free-draining mix under a clear bag. Keep warm and humid in bright indirect light. Roots take two to three months, which is slower than most houseplants.

problems.symptom: Brown patches and yellowing on leaves
problems.cause: Direct sun. Coffee is an understorey plant and scorches readily, contrary to what most people assume.
problems.fix: Move out of direct light into bright filtered conditions. Damaged leaves do not recover.

problems.symptom: Leaves dropping suddenly
problems.cause: The soil dried out, a cold draught, or a sharp temperature change. Coffee is sensitive to temperatures below about 15°C.
problems.fix: Keep the mix evenly moist, move away from draughty windows and doors, and maintain a warm stable position.

problems.symptom: Brown crispy leaf edges
problems.cause: Low humidity or salt buildup from fertiliser and hard water.
problems.fix: Raise humidity above 50%, flush the pot with clean water every couple of months, and use filtered water.

problems.symptom: Yellowing leaves with green veins
problems.cause: Iron deficiency, common in coffee when the soil pH has drifted too alkaline — often from hard tap water.
problems.fix: Repot into an acidic mix, use filtered or rainwater, and feed with a fertiliser for acid-loving plants containing chelated iron.

problems.symptom: No flowers or berries
problems.cause: The plant is too young — coffee needs three to five years before flowering — or light and humidity are insufficient.
problems.fix: Be patient, maintain bright indirect light and good humidity, and feed through the growing season. Indoor plants do flower and fruit, but it takes years.

problems.symptom: Fine webbing and stippled leaves
problems.cause: Spider mites, encouraged by dry indoor air.
problems.fix: Rinse the plant thoroughly, treat with insecticidal soap every five days for three cycles, and raise humidity.

problems.symptom: Leggy stem with leaves only at the top
problems.cause: Insufficient light and no pruning.
problems.fix: Increase light and prune the top back in spring to encourage branching. Prune vertical shoots rather than side branches if you plan to root the cuttings.

repotting: Repot every one to two years in spring while the plant is growing, then less often. Signs are roots through the drainage holes and rapid drying between waterings.
Move up one pot size into fresh slightly acidic, free-draining mix. Coffee has a deep taproot when young, so a pot with reasonable depth suits it better than a shallow one.

Handle the roots gently and water thoroughly afterwards. Keep humidity up and out of direct sun for a couple of weeks while it settles. Do not feed for six weeks. Prune to shape at the same time if the plant has grown leggy.
varieties: Coffea arabica is the species grown as a houseplant, with glossy dark green leaves and, on mature plants, fragrant white flowers followed by red berries. 'Nana' is a dwarf cultivar better suited to indoor growing, staying around three feet.

Coffea canephora, robusta coffee, is occasionally sold but is larger and less ornamental. Two practical notes: harvesting usable coffee from a houseplant is possible but a mature indoor plant produces only a handful of beans a year, so grow it for the foliage rather than the crop. And all parts of the coffee plant except the ripe berry flesh are toxic to cats and dogs due to caffeine content, causing vomiting, rapid heartbeat and restlessness.

light: Norfolk Island pine needs bright light, including several hours of direct sun, and this is where most of them fail. It is commonly sold as a Christmas decoration and placed in a dim corner, where it slowly thins and drops branches.

A south or west window is the right position, or directly in front of an east window. In insufficient light the branches space out widely, lower branches yellow and drop, and the plant becomes sparse and lopsided. Rotate the pot a quarter turn every week — this plant leans toward light noticeably, and an uneven specimen cannot be corrected because lost branches never regrow.
water: Keep the mix evenly moist, watering when the top inch is dry — usually every five to seven days in spring and summer. Norfolk Island pine does not tolerate drying out, and branches that brown from drought are lost permanently.
Reduce to every ten to fourteen days in winter but never let the root ball dry through. Equally, do not let it stand in water; the roots rot in saturated soil.

Humidity above 50% is genuinely important. This is a subtropical island species used to moist ocean air, and dry winter heating is what causes the browning, dropping branches that so many indoor specimens suffer. A humidifier makes a real difference, and grouping it with other plants helps.
soil: Use a well-draining, slightly acidic potting mix with added perlite and a little sand. Norfolk Island pine wants a medium that holds moisture while draining freely.

Choose a stable pot — the plant grows tall and its shallow root system makes it prone to tipping. Feed every four to six weeks at half strength through spring and summer, and stop in winter. It is a light feeder. Flush the pot occasionally with clean water, since salt buildup contributes to needle browning.

propagation: Norfolk Island pine is very difficult to propagate at home, and it is worth knowing why before attempting it.

Cuttings taken from side branches will root, but they grow permanently sideways — producing a flat, sprawling plant that never develops the upright symmetrical form. This is called plagiotropic growth and it is a genuine, irreversible characteristic of the species. Only a cutting from the vertical leading shoot produces an upright plant, and taking that cutting destroys the parent's growing point, after which the parent cannot recover its shape.

Seed is the practical method, though seed is rarely available and germination is slow and erratic, needing warmth and fresh seed. Realistically, this is a plant to buy rather than propagate. If you do want to try, sow fresh seed in damp free-draining mix at around 20°C, keep humid, and expect germination over one to three months and years of growth to reach any size.

problems.symptom: Lower branches yellowing and dropping
problems.cause: Low humidity, insufficient light, or the soil drying out. Some loss of the lowest branches with age is natural, but rapid shedding is not.
problems.fix: Raise humidity above 50%, move to a much brighter position, and keep the soil evenly moist. Critically, lost branches never regrow — the bare section is permanent, so prevention is the only remedy.

problems.symptom: Brown, crispy needle tips throughout
problems.cause: Dry air, most commonly from central heating in winter.
problems.fix: Run a humidifier nearby, move away from radiators and vents, and group with other plants. This is the single most common Norfolk Island pine complaint.

problems.symptom: Branches spaced widely with a sparse, stretched look
problems.cause: Insufficient light.
problems.fix: Move to the brightest position available. The stretched growth stays as it is, but new growth comes in more compact.

problems.symptom: Plant leaning permanently to one side
problems.cause: Growing toward a single light source without rotation.
problems.fix: Rotate a quarter turn every week from the start. An established lean cannot be corrected, since the plant grows from a single leader and the shape is fixed.

problems.symptom: Whole plant browning from the bottom upward
problems.cause: Root rot from waterlogged soil, or severe drought at some point.
problems.fix: Check drainage and the roots. Trim soft roots and repot into fresh mix. If the root ball has shrunk from the pot sides, submerge the pot to rehydrate it.

problems.symptom: Fine webbing between branches
problems.cause: Spider mites, which thrive in the dry air that also causes needle browning.
problems.fix: Rinse the plant thoroughly in the shower, treat with insecticidal soap every five days for three cycles, and fix the humidity.

problems.symptom: No growth at the top, or a damaged leader
problems.cause: The vertical growing tip has been damaged or cut.
problems.fix: Unfortunately there is no fix. Norfolk Island pine grows from a single leader and cannot replace it, so the plant stops gaining height. Never prune the top.

repotting: Repot every two to three years in spring. Norfolk Island pine grows slowly indoors and has a shallow root system, so it does not need frequent moves.
Choose a pot one size larger that is heavy and wide rather than deep — the shallow roots and tall form make it prone to tipping. Handle the root ball gently.

Water thoroughly afterwards, keep humidity high, and wait six weeks before feeding. Never prune the growing tip at any point; unlike most houseplants, this one cannot branch from a cut and pruning the leader permanently stops upward growth.
varieties: Araucaria heterophylla is the Norfolk Island pine, from a single small island in the Pacific, with soft needle-like foliage in symmetrical tiers. There are no meaningful cultivars — what varies is size and age.

Related species include Araucaria araucana, the monkey puzzle tree, which is a hardy outdoor conifer, and Araucaria bidwillii, the bunya pine. Note that despite the name and appearance, this is not a true pine and is not frost-hardy — it must stay indoors above about 10°C. Norfolk Island pine is non-toxic to cats and dogs, which makes it a genuinely safe alternative to a real Christmas tree in a pet household.

light: Stromanthe Triostar wants bright indirect light — more than most of its prayer plant relatives, because the cream and pink variegation contains little chlorophyll and the plant needs the extra light to compensate.

An east window is ideal, or near a south or west window behind a sheer curtain. Direct sun scorches the thin leaves and bleaches the pink, which burns before the green does. In light that is too low, new leaves emerge with less variegation and the pink undersides dull. Like other Marantaceae, the leaves fold upward at night and open again by morning.
water: Keep the mix evenly moist — never soggy, never dry. Water when the top half-inch feels dry, usually every four to six days in spring and summer, and every seven to ten days in winter.

Water quality is critical. Stromanthe is as sensitive to fluoride, chlorine and dissolved salts as any calathea, and hard tap water produces the brown crispy edges this family is known for — damage that shows first and worst on the pale variegated sections. Use filtered, distilled or rainwater from the start.

Humidity of 60% or more is genuinely required rather than preferred. The thin variegated leaves lose moisture fast, and this plant will not look good in a dry room whatever else you get right. A humidifier is the realistic solution; misting is not.
soil: Use a moisture-retentive but airy mix — two parts coir or peat-based compost to one part perlite, with a little fine bark. It should stay damp without compacting.

Plastic or glazed ceramic pots hold moisture better than terracotta, which dries too fast. Drainage holes are still essential. Feed at quarter to half strength monthly through spring and summer only, and flush the pot with clean water every couple of months — Stromanthe is as sensitive to fertiliser salts as it is to tap water.

propagation: Stromanthe Triostar is propagated by division only. Stem and leaf cuttings will not root, because the plant grows from a clumping rhizome rather than from nodes along a stem — a cut leaf simply rots.

Divide in spring, ideally while repotting, and only once the plant has formed a decent clump. Slide it from the pot and gently tease or wash the mix away so you can see where rhizome sections separate. Pull them apart by hand where possible, using a clean knife only where necessary.

Each division needs its own roots and at least three or four leaves — small pieces struggle. Choose divisions with balanced variegation; a section that is almost entirely cream lacks the chlorophyll to establish. Pot into fresh moisture-retentive mix, water with filtered water, and keep warm, shaded and very humid for the first month, ideally under a clear cover. Expect the divisions to sulk and possibly drop a leaf before new growth begins.

problems.symptom: Brown crispy leaf edges
problems.cause: Minerals in tap water, low humidity, or fertiliser salt buildup — usually all three, and most visible on the pale variegated areas.
problems.fix: Switch to filtered, distilled or rainwater, raise humidity above 60%, and flush the pot with clean water every couple of months. Trim damaged edges following the leaf shape.

problems.symptom: Leaves curling inward and not opening flat in the day
problems.cause: Underwatering, low humidity, or too much light. Note that folding upward at night is normal and not a problem.
problems.fix: Check the soil first, then humidity, then position. Leaves usually resume their daily rhythm within a week of conditions improving.

problems.symptom: New leaves emerging plain green
problems.cause: Insufficient light. The plant favours chlorophyll-rich tissue when short of energy.
problems.fix: Move to brighter indirect light. Prune out fully green shoots to redirect energy into variegated growth.

problems.symptom: Pink and cream sections browning before the green does
problems.cause: Sunburn or low humidity. The unpigmented tissue is thinner and more vulnerable.
problems.fix: Move out of direct sun and raise humidity. This pattern of damage is characteristic of variegated Marantaceae.

problems.symptom: Yellowing leaves with wet soil
problems.cause: Overwatering and root rot.
problems.fix: Confirm the pot drains and is not standing in water. Let the top half-inch dry before each watering. Trim soft roots and repot if needed.

problems.symptom: Whole plant drooping
problems.cause: Either thirst or root rot — they look identical in this family.
problems.fix: Feel the soil before acting. Dry means water; wet means stop and check the roots.

problems.symptom: Fine webbing under the leaves
problems.cause: Spider mites, which thrive in exactly the dry air that also causes brown edges.
problems.fix: Rinse thoroughly, treat with insecticidal soap every five days for three cycles, and fix the humidity to prevent recurrence.

repotting: Stromanthe dislikes root disturbance and should be repotted only every two years, or when roots have filled the pot and it dries out much faster than before.
Repot in spring into a plastic or glazed pot one size larger. Disturb the root ball as little as possible — loosen the outer edge and leave the core intact unless you are deliberately dividing.

Water with filtered water, keep humidity high, and expect a period of sulking with some leaf loss. Do not feed for six to eight weeks. If the plant is thriving, leaving it alone is usually better than repotting on schedule.
varieties: Stromanthe sanguinea 'Triostar', also sold as 'Tricolor', has long lance-shaped leaves splashed cream and green on top with deep magenta-pink undersides — the pink underside is the most striking feature and shows when the leaves fold up at night.

Within the wider prayer plant family, Calathea offers patterned foliage with similar demands, Maranta trails and roots from nodes making it much easier to propagate, and Ctenanthe has a more upright branching habit. All Marantaceae, including Stromanthe, are non-toxic to cats and dogs — which is the main reason this demanding group remains so popular in pet households.
